In the first three chapters we collected three kinds of equations. Strains follow from displacements (chapter 1), stresses must balance the load (chapter 2), and Hooke's law connects stresses with strains (chapter 3). Chapter 4 derived the energy principles from them and showed that a load has at most one solution. Chapter 5 solved beams with them, but with an assumption about the form of the field: how a cross-section moves was assumed in advance.

How do we find the field of a real body, for example the steel tube of a hydraulic cylinder, a plate with a hole or a curved hook, without assuming in advance how it deforms? This is the question of this chapter.

The route is the following. First we collect all the equations and all the conditions on the surface into one problem and show that it has only one solution. Without this, every solution we found would be only one of several possible ones. Then we reduce the problem in two ways to fewer unknowns, to displacements or to stresses, and on the hanging bar we show how a solution is really found: we guess the field and check whether it satisfies all the equations. Round bodies, such as the tube and the sphere, call for coordinates that fit them. With them we solve the thick tube and the thick sphere. Plane problems we reduce to a single function, the Airy stress function (Airyjeva napetostna funkcija), which chapter 4 already named. With it we solve the beams of chapter 5 once more, this time as solutions of the equations of elasticity. Here the question of why we may replace real supports and loads by their resultants arises by itself, and the answer will be Saint-Venant's principle, which we will test on numbers. With all this we solve the plate with a hole and the curved beam, and at the end the body on several separate supports, which chapter 4 promised.

What is new in this chapter is thus five things: the complete set of equations as one problem, two ways to reduce it, coordinates that fit round bodies, plane problems with one function and the principle that justifies replacing the real load by its resultant.

11.1 The boundary value problem of elasticity

Take a steel tube with an inner radius of 40 mm and an outer radius of 60 mm, filled with oil at a pressure of 30 MPa (figure 11.1). The radii are the same as for the ring of section 1.18.5 and for the thick spherical shell of section 4.3.7. The tube is made of steel with \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\). Which equations and which conditions on the surface determine the field of displacements, strains and stresses in its wall? And do they determine it uniquely, or could the same data give two different fields?

First let us count the unknowns and the equations. The unknowns are the three components of displacement \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\), the six components of the tensor of small strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and the six components of stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), fifteen functions of the point of the body in all. There are just as many equations (SADD §5.1, PDF p. 103-104). Six connect the strains with the displacements (definition 1.115),

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) ,\]

where the indices \(i\), \(j\) are each equal to \(x\), \(y\) or \(z\) and \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\), \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\). Six connect the stresses with the strains, this is Hooke's law for an isotropic material (theorem 3.11),

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \lambda\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}})\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} ,\]

where \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is one for \(i = j\) and zero otherwise. Three are the equilibrium equations (theorem 2.28),

\[\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + b_{\mathrm{i}} = 0 , \qquad i = x, y, z ,\]

where \(\vek b\) is the body force. Six plus six plus three is fifteen, so there are as many equations as unknowns. The compatibility equations (theorem 1.127) are not among them. Strains computed from displacements satisfy them automatically, and we need them only when the strains or the stresses are the unknowns and we look for the displacements afterwards (SADD §5.1, PDF p. 104). The constants \(E\) and \(\nu\) and the body force are given in advance.

The equations alone do not determine the problem, however. Every tube, every beam and every body has the same equations, but a different field of displacements, because it is held and loaded differently. The data on holding and loading are conditions on the surface, as in section 4.5.1. On a part of the surface \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) a displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) is prescribed, and on the remaining part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) a force per unit area \(\bar{\vek t}\) is prescribed. Chapter 4 always took the prescribed displacement on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) to be zero. Here we may prescribe any displacement, for example a support that settles by a known distance. According to what is prescribed where, we distinguish three kinds of problems (figure 11.2, SADD §5.2, PDF p. 108-109). In a traction problem (problem sil) the force is prescribed on the whole surface and \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is empty. In a displacement problem (problem pomikov) the displacement is prescribed on the whole surface and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) is empty. In a mixed problem (mešani problem) both are nonempty. The tube of figure 11.1 is a traction problem. There is one more kind of condition, which we only name: at the same point a component of displacement in one direction and a component of force in another are prescribed, for example for a body sliding along a smooth rigid wall, or on a plane of symmetry (SADD §5.2, PDF p. 104). We will not use it.

Now we can write everything said so far as one problem. The data about the body are the same as in section 4.5.1, so here we only list them.

Definition 11.1 Boundary value problem of elasticity (robni problem elastičnosti)

Let the body \(V\) be as in section 4.5.1: a body made of boxes (definition 4.11) or a body cut into pieces between two graphs and curved boxes, its interior points form a connected open set (definition 1.130), every point of the body is the limit of a sequence of interior points, and the surface \(S\) is the union of two parts \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) that do not overlap and are made of whole outer pieces of the surface. Let the material be linearly elastic, with stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}}\) (definition 3.16, for an isotropic material theorem 3.11). The data are the body force \(\vek b\), continuous on \(V\), the prescribed force per unit area \(\bar{\vek t}\), continuous on each outer face of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), and the prescribed displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\), a field continuously differentiable (definition 1.90) on an open set that contains \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). A displacement field \(\vek u\) is a solution of the boundary value problem of elasticity (rešitev robnega problema elastičnosti) for the data \((\vek b, \bar{\vek t}, \bar{\vek u})\) if:

  1. \(\vek u\) is continuously differentiable on an open set that contains the body together with its surface, and at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) it equals \(\bar{\vek u}\),
  2. the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), computed from the components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) of the tensor of small strains of the field \(\vek u\), are continuously differentiable on an open set that contains the body together with its surface, and at every interior point of the body they satisfy the equilibrium equations (2.31),
  3. at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) Cauchy's formula \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\) holds, where \(\vek n\) is the outer unit normal of the surface.

If \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is empty this is a traction problem, if \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) is empty a displacement problem, if both are nonempty a mixed problem.

Source: SADD §5.2, (5.2.1) and (5.2.2) (PDF p. 108-109). The requirements of continuous differentiability are ours, so that the proved principles of chapter 4 apply.

For \(\bar{\vek u} = \vek 0\) we already had this definition (definition 4.132). Only the value of \(\bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is new.

May we prescribe any load we like? If we push the tube of figure 11.1 at one end with a force of 100 kN and do not hold it at the other, it starts to move, and the equilibrium equations have no solution. The condition that excludes this is in fact a consequence of the equations.

Lemma 11.2 Equilibrium of the whole body (ravnovesje celega telesa)

Let \(\vek u\) be a solution of the boundary value problem of elasticity (definition 11.1) and \(\vek t = \ten\sigma\,\vek n\) the stress vector on the surface \(S\) (on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) this is \(\bar{\vek t}\)). Let \(\vek r\) be the position vector of a point from a chosen fixed point \(O\). Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek t\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\,\mathrm{d}V = \vek 0 , \qquad \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek r\times\vek t\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek r\times\vek b\,\mathrm{d}V = \vek 0 . \tag{11.1}\]
Proof

We must show six equalities, three for the force and three for the moment. We obtain each by multiplying an equilibrium equation by a suitable function, integrating over the body and using the divergence theorem.

  1. The stresses of the solution are symmetric, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}\) (lemma 3.17, point 2, as in the text after definition 4.132). At every interior point \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + b_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) holds (requirement 2). Both sides are continuous on \(V\) and every point of the body is a limit of interior points, so this equation holds at every point of the body.
  2. The field \(\vek v = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}})\) is continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(V\), and by step 1 its divergence equals \(-b_{\mathrm{x}}\). By the divergence theorem 4.14 for bodies made of boxes, or by corollary 4.68 for other bodies, it follows that \(-\int_{\mathrm{V}} b_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\).
  3. By symmetry \(\vek v\cdot\vek n = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}n_{\mathrm{z}} = t_{\mathrm{x}}\), because \(\vek t = \ten\sigma\,\vek n\) (Cauchy's formula, theorem 2.24), hence \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} t_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{V}} b_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\). For the components \(y\) and \(z\) we repeat steps 2 and 3 with the fields \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}})\) and \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}})\). This is the first equality.
  4. The component \(x\) of the moment is \((\vek r\times\vek t)_{\mathrm{x}} = y\,t_{\mathrm{z}} - z\,t_{\mathrm{y}}\) (equation (2.32)). Take the field \(\vek v\) with components \(v_{\mathrm{j}} = y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{jz}} - z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{jy}}\) for \(j = x, y, z\). It is continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(V\), and by symmetry \(\vek v\cdot\vek n = y\,t_{\mathrm{z}} - z\,t_{\mathrm{y}}\).
  5. By the product rule its divergence is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \partial v_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = y\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{jz}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} - z\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{jy}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\), because \(\partial y/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) equals one for \(j = y\) and zero otherwise, and likewise for \(z\). By step 1 the two sums are \(-b_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(-b_{\mathrm{y}}\), and by symmetry \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\) cancel. What remains is \(-(y\,b_{\mathrm{z}} - z\,b_{\mathrm{y}})\).
  6. The divergence theorem as in step 2 gives \(-\int_{\mathrm{V}} (y\,b_{\mathrm{z}} - z\,b_{\mathrm{y}})\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} (y\,t_{\mathrm{z}} - z\,t_{\mathrm{y}})\,\mathrm{d}A\), which is the component \(x\) of the second equality. The components \(y\) and \(z\) follow by exchanging the letters in the cycle \(x \to y \to z \to x\), as for the vector product.

Source: SADD §3.7, (3.7.1)-(3.7.3) (PDF p. 77-78), where the argument is reversed: from the equilibrium of every part the equilibrium equations follow. The condition on the data of the traction problem is not stated in SADD §5.2. The proof with the divergence theorem is not from the source. The force for a body made of boxes was already proved by corollary 4.41.

The lemma says that the data of a traction problem may not be chosen arbitrarily. When \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is empty, \(S = S_{\mathrm{t}}\) and the data \((\vek b, \bar{\vek t})\) must satisfy both equalities by themselves. In a mixed problem they satisfy them only together with the forces of the supports on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), which we do not know in advance. Let us check this on three bodies.

The tube of figure 11.1 is a traction problem. There is no body force. The pressure in the bore acts on the wall equally from all sides, so the forces on opposite sides of the bore cancel and the resultant of the pressure is zero, and so is its moment about a point on the axis. If the ends of the tube are free there is no other load and both equalities hold. If a plug closes each end of the tube, the plug receives from the oil in the bore of radius \(a = 40\) mm the force \(p\pi a^2 = 150{,}8\) kN and passes it on to the tube. Let this force be distributed uniformly over the annulus of the end face with area \(\pi(b^2 - a^2)\), where \(b = 60\) mm is the outer radius. The force per unit area is then \(p a^2/(b^2 - a^2) = 24\) MPa. The lower annulus pulls the tube downwards, the upper one upwards, each with the force \(24\ \text{MPa} \cdot 6{,}283 \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2 = 150{,}8\) kN, and the sum of the forces is zero. The moment about the axis is zero because the force on an annulus is distributed uniformly along its circumference, and about a point on the axis it is zero because both forces lie on the axis and have equal magnitude and opposite direction. The plug is an idealization here: we do not compute its field, we only prescribe the force it passes on. How a real plug would change the field near the ends we will say later in this chapter.

The hanging bar of chapter 1, 10 m long with a diameter of 10 mm, is also a traction problem. The body force is the weight \(\vek b = \rho g\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), where the axis \(x\) points downwards, and its resultant is \(\rho g A L = 7800 \cdot 9{,}81 \cdot 7{,}854 \cdot 10^{-5} \cdot 10 = 60{,}10\) N. The top face is pulled upwards uniformly by the force per unit area \(\rho g L = 0{,}7652\) MPa, which on the area \(A = 78{,}54\) mm\(^2\) gives exactly 60,10 N. The lateral surface and the bottom face are free. The weight and the force on the top face cancel. The moment about the centre of the top face is zero, because the weight and the force on the top face are distributed symmetrically about the axis.

The cantilever of chapter 5 is a mixed problem. The face of the clamp is \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and the displacement there is zero, the remaining faces are \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), and at the end a force of 500 N acts downwards. The data on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) do not balance by themselves: a force of 500 N and its moment of 500 N m about the clamp remain, because the arm is 1 m. The lemma says that the clamp must supply a force of 500 N upwards and a moment of 500 N m that cancel them. We did not prescribe these forces, the solution must supply them itself.

Now the question we posed at the tube: is the field only one? Let us see what would happen if there were two. Their difference would be a displacement field without load and without prescribed displacement, and chapter 4 showed that such a field has no strain. For this we first need that solutions may be subtracted.

Corollary 11.3 Superposition for boundary value problems (seštevanje rešitev robnih problemov)

Let \(\vek u^{(1)}\) be a solution of the boundary value problem of elasticity for the data \((\vek b^{(1)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(1)}, \bar{\vek u}^{(1)})\) and \(\vek u^{(2)}\) a solution for the data \((\vek b^{(2)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(2)}, \bar{\vek u}^{(2)})\) of the same body with the same parts \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), and let \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) be numbers. Then \(\alpha\,\vek u^{(1)} + \beta\,\vek u^{(2)}\) is a solution for the data \((\alpha\,\vek b^{(1)} + \beta\,\vek b^{(2)},\ \alpha\,\bar{\vek t}^{(1)} + \beta\,\bar{\vek t}^{(2)},\ \alpha\,\bar{\vek u}^{(1)} + \beta\,\bar{\vek u}^{(2)})\), and its strains and stresses are the same linear combinations.

Proof

We must show the three requirements of definition 11.1. The only difference from lemma 4.134 is the value of the field on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\).

  1. By lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation, the field \(\alpha\,\vek u^{(1)} + \beta\,\vek u^{(2)}\) is continuously differentiable on the intersection of the two open sets that contain the body together with its surface, and this intersection is an open set with the same property. On \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) the field equals \(\alpha\,\bar{\vek u}^{(1)} + \beta\,\bar{\vek u}^{(2)}\). This is requirement 1.
  2. Steps 2, 3 and 4 of the proof of lemma 4.134 on the principle of superposition show that the strains and stresses of the field \(\alpha\,\vek u^{(1)} + \beta\,\vek u^{(2)}\) are the same linear combinations, that the stresses are continuously differentiable and that they satisfy the equilibrium equations with the body force \(\alpha\,\vek b^{(1)} + \beta\,\vek b^{(2)}\). These steps use only the rules for derivatives and the linearity of the elastic constants, not the value of the field on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). This is requirement 2.
  3. Step 5 of the same lemma gives on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the equality \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \alpha\,\bar{\vek t}^{(1)} + \beta\,\bar{\vek t}^{(2)}\) and does not use the field on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) either. This is requirement 3.

Source: EP §4.6.1, (4.6.1)-(4.6.4) (p. 218), where prescribed displacements are also part of the data. The proof is an adaptation of lemma 4.134, not from the source.

Theorem 11.4 Uniqueness of the boundary value problem (enoličnost robnega problema)

Let the body be as in definition 11.1 and the material ideally elastic (definition 3.43) with a strain energy density that is positive for every small strain that is not zero (for an isotropic material theorem 3.48 on the bounds on the elastic constants guarantees this). Let \(\vek u\) and \(\tilde{\vek u}\) be solutions of the boundary value problem for the same data \((\vek b, \bar{\vek t}, \bar{\vek u})\). Then:

  1. the strains and stresses of the two solutions are equal at every point of the body,
  2. the difference \(\tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\) is a small rigid displacement (definition 1.11) that is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), and for every such displacement \(\vek w\) the field \(\vek u + \vek w\) is also a solution,
  3. if the only small rigid displacement that is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is the field \(\vek 0\), then \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u\).
Proof

We must show that the difference of the two solutions solves the problem with zero data, and apply the lemma of chapter 4 about such a problem.

  1. By corollary 11.3 with \(\alpha = 1\) and \(\beta = -1\) the field \(\vek w = \tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\) is a solution for the data \((\vek 0, \vek 0, \bar{\vek u} - \bar{\vek u}) = (\vek 0, \vek 0, \vek 0)\). Its strains and stresses are the differences of the strains and stresses of the fields \(\tilde{\vek u}\) and \(\vek u\).
  2. The field \(\vek 0\) is also a solution for the data \((\vek 0, \vek 0, \vek 0)\): its strains and stresses are zero, the equilibrium equations are \(0 + 0 = 0\), and on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) we have \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\).
  3. By lemma 4.133 (valid for bodies made of curved boxes by the remark at the end of section 4.5.4), applied to the solutions \(\vek w\) and \(\vek 0\) for the same load \((\vek 0, \vek 0)\), the strains and stresses of the field \(\vek w\) equal those of the field \(\vek 0\), so they are zero, and \(\vek w\) is a small rigid displacement that is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\).
  4. The strains of the field \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u + \vek w\) are the sum of the strains of the fields \(\vek u\) and \(\vek w\), so they equal the strains of the field \(\vek u\), and the stresses are equal by Hooke's law. This is point 1. The first part of point 2 is step 3.
  5. Let \(\vek w\) be a small rigid displacement that is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). The field \(\vek w = \vek a + \mat W\,\overrightarrow{OP}\) is a polynomial in the coordinates, hence continuously differentiable, and its tensor of small strains is \(\tfrac12(\mat W + \mat W^\T) = \mat 0\), because \(\mat W\) is antisymmetric. The stresses are zero by Hooke's law, the equilibrium equations are \(0 + 0 = 0\) and the condition on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) is \(\vek 0 = \vek 0\), so \(\vek w\) is a solution for zero data. By corollary 11.3, \(\vek u + \vek w\) is therefore a solution for the data \((\vek b, \bar{\vek t}, \bar{\vek u} + \vek 0)\). This is the second part of point 2.
  6. If the only small rigid displacement that is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is the field \(\vek 0\), then by step 3 \(\vek w = \vek 0\), so \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u\). This is point 3.

Source: SADD §6.2, (6.2.1)-(6.2.5) (PDF p. 133), CM §7.3.6, (7.3.38)-(7.3.45) (PDF p. 313-314), BARBER §33.8 (PDF p. 515-516), where the difference of the solutions is inserted into the strain energy. The reduction to lemma 4.133 is ours.

The proof showed that no new energy estimate is needed: the difference of two solutions solves the problem with zero data, and that has no strain, which we proved in chapter 4. Let us see what the theorem says about the bodies.

For the cantilever, \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is the face of the clamp, on which the displacement is zero. A small rigid displacement \(\vek a + \mat W\,\overrightarrow{OP}\) is zero at three points \(P_1\), \(P_2\), \(P_3\) of the face that do not lie on one line only if \(\vek a = \vek 0\) and \(\mat W = \mat 0\). We show this as follows. From \(\vek a + \mat W\,\overrightarrow{OP_{\mathrm{i}}} = \vek 0\) for \(i = 1, 2, 3\) it follows by subtraction that \(\mat W\,\vek d_2 = \vek 0\) and \(\mat W\,\vek d_3 = \vek 0\), where \(\vek d_2 = \overrightarrow{P_1P_2}\) and \(\vek d_3 = \overrightarrow{P_1P_3}\) are independent vectors. Let \(\vek d_1\) be a vector that is not in their plane. Since \(\mat W\) is antisymmetric, \(\vek d_{\mathrm{j}}\cdot\mat W\,\vek d_1 = -(\mat W\,\vek d_{\mathrm{j}})\cdot\vek d_1 = 0\) for \(j = 2, 3\) and \(\vek d_1\cdot\mat W\,\vek d_1 = 0\) (corollary 1.104, point 1). The vector \(\mat W\,\vek d_1\) is therefore perpendicular to the three independent vectors \(\vek d_1\), \(\vek d_2\), \(\vek d_3\), which span space, so it is perpendicular to every vector, itself included, and it is \(\vek 0\). The matrix \(\mat W\) maps three independent vectors to zero, so it is the zero matrix, and \(\vek a = \vek 0\). The cantilever therefore satisfies point 3 and the field of displacements is unique. The same holds for a beam on three supports, which is also a mixed problem: each support is a piece of a flat surface with an area, which contains three points not on one line. The equilibrium equations of the whole beam do not determine the three support forces, because there are more unknowns than equations, but the elastic field is nevertheless unique, and with it the support forces.

For the tube, for the hanging bar and for every traction problem \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is empty. All small rigid displacements are then allowed, point 3 does not apply, point 2 does: the stresses and strains are unique, but the displacements only up to a small rigid displacement (figure 11.3). The tube can move and turn as a whole, and every such displacement adds a new solution to a solution. The hanging bar is fixed only at the centre \(O\) of the top face. The condition \(\vek u(O) = \vek 0\) removes the translation but not the rotation about \(O\), so \(\mat W = \mat 0\) must also be required (CM, PDF p. 306).

And existence? The theorem says that there cannot be two solutions, not that there is at least one. A proof of existence in general is beyond this book, because it requires Sobolev spaces and the Lebesgue integral, which we only named in section 6.2.3, and theorems of functional analysis. The sources say the following. BOWER §5.1.4 (PDF p. 279) states that the boundary value problem with displacements prescribed on the whole surface always has a solution and that it is unique, that with mixed conditions a static solution exists and is unique if the prescribed displacements prevent rigid motion, and that with tractions only a solution exists only if the tractions are in equilibrium, which is just our lemma 11.2. BARBER §33.8 (PDF p. 516), after the proof of uniqueness, says that the question of existence is much more challenging and that he will not pursue it, and cites Sokolnikoff, according to whom existence has been satisfactorily resolved for domains of great generality. BATHE §4.3.4 (PDF p. 253-255) shows what stands behind this: the bilinear form of the problem (definition 6.4) has two properties on the space of functions that are zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and have integrable squares of themselves and of their first derivatives. Continuity says that the value of the form for two fields is bounded above by the product of their sizes, ellipticity says that the value of the form for one field in both arguments is at least a constant multiple of the square of its size. Ellipticity holds because the structure is properly supported, and for the proof BATHE refers to Ciarlet. That existence follows from these properties is a theorem of functional analysis, which BATHE does not summarize on these pages, so we do not prove existence here and do not claim it for every body. In this chapter every solution is constructed: we find a field that satisfies all three requirements of definition 11.1, and by theorem 11.4 it is the solution. Where we would really need general existence, we will say so as a conjecture.

From history

The proof that the equations for the equilibrium of an elastic body have no more than one solution was first published by Kirchhoff in a memoir of 1858 (TP2B, PDF p. 18). Neumann repeated it in the tenth section of his Vorlesungen, which is entitled Kirchhoffs allgemeine Lehrsätze (Kirchhoff's general theorems). Paragraph 60 reproduces Kirchhoff's proof for equilibrium, and the section stems from lectures of 1859 and 1860 and is therefore older than Clebsch's textbook (TP2B, PDF p. 18). In §61 Neumann extended the proof to the vibration of a body. TP2B thinks that neither Kirchhoff nor Clebsch had done this before him (TP2B, PDF p. 18). Neumann assumes an isotropic material, takes two solutions and finds that the difference of their displacements \(U\), \(V\), \(W\) satisfies the equations without body force and surface force. He considers the quadruple integral (over the body and over time) of a sum of three terms: the equation of motion of the difference in the direction of each axis, multiplied by the time derivative of the displacement in that direction. The integral is zero because of the equations in the interior of the body. He integrates the stress terms by parts, the surface integrals vanish because of the conditions on the surface, and after inserting the relation between stresses and strains the whole is a complete differential with respect to time. After integrating over time he obtains the equality that the sum of two integrals of squared terms (squares of the time derivatives of the displacements and squared terms of the strain energy) equals zero. Hence every squared term must be zero at every point of the body, the displacements do not depend on time and can express only a translation and a rotation of the body as a whole (TP2B, PDF p. 18-19).

We were looking at whether the equations and the conditions on the surface determine the field uniquely. The conclusion that two solutions can differ only by a translation and a rotation of the body as a whole is, at rest, exactly point 2 of our theorem: the stresses and strains are unique, and the displacements up to a small rigid displacement, which the supports remove if they prevent it.

For the tube of figure 11.1 this means the following. The tube with open ends and the tube with ends closed by a plug are two different traction problems, because the data at the ends differ, and each has a single field of stresses and strains. How to find this field we will see later in this chapter. For now we know that it is enough to find one field that satisfies all three requirements of the definition, because that field is the one. We use exactly this in every solution of the chapter.

11.2 The Navier-Lamé equations (Navier-Laméjeve enačbe)

In the previous section we wrote down the boundary value problem of elasticity (definition 11.1). Its unknowns are the three components of the displacement, the six components of the strain and the six components of the stress, fifteen functions in all. For them we have fifteen equations: six relations between strains and displacements (chapter 1), six equations of Hooke's law (chapter 3) and three equilibrium equations (chapter 2). Can the fifteen equations be replaced by three, for the three unknown components of the displacement?

The idea is simple. The strains are already written with displacements, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}})\) (definition 1.115). Hooke's law (equation (3.13)) gives the stresses from the strains, so the stresses are written with displacements as well. The three equilibrium equations are equations for the stresses, so they become three equations for the displacements, and the six strains and six stresses drop out of the calculation. The resulting system has the advantage that we mentioned with the compatibility equations (section 1.18.3): the strains are computed from the displacements, so they fit together by themselves and we need no compatibility equations.

The equilibrium equations will contain the second derivatives of a displacement component with respect to all three coordinates, in the sum \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x^2 + \partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial y^2 + \partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial z^2\). This sum appears so often in mechanics and physics that it gets a name.

Definition 11.5 Laplace operator (Laplaceov operator)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points of space and \(f\) a function of three variables that has continuous second partial derivatives at every point of \(D\). The Laplace operator (Laplaceov operator) assigns to \(f\) the function whose value at every point of \(D\) is the sum of the three second partial derivatives at that point,

\[\nabla^2 f = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2} . \tag{11.2}\]

For a vector field \(\vek u = (u_{\mathrm{x}}, u_{\mathrm{y}}, u_{\mathrm{z}})\) whose components have continuous second partial derivatives, \(\nabla^2\vek u\) is the vector field with components \(\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{z}}\). So the operator is applied to each component separately. If \(f\) also has continuous fourth partial derivatives, \(\nabla^4 f = \nabla^2(\nabla^2 f)\).

Source: CM (2.4.36) (PDF p. 76), where \(\nabla^2 = \nabla\cdot\nabla\) is called the Laplace operator, SADD (5.4.5) (PDF p. 111), KREYSZIG §9.7 (PDF p. 427).

The operator has two views. The gradient \(\nabla f\) is the column of partial derivatives (chapter 8), and its divergence (definition 4.13) is exactly \(\partial^2 f/\partial x^2 + \partial^2 f/\partial y^2 + \partial^2 f/\partial z^2\), so \(\nabla^2 f = \operatorname{div}(\nabla f)\). The symbol \(\Delta\), which KREYSZIG gives as another name for the same operator (§9.7, PDF p. 427), is not used in this book, because \(\Delta\) means a difference (\(\Delta L\), \(\Delta T\)). We write \(\nabla^2\). As an example take \(f = x^2 + 3yz\). Its second derivatives are \(\partial^2 f/\partial x^2 = 2\), \(\partial^2 f/\partial y^2 = 0\) and \(\partial^2 f/\partial z^2 = 0\), so \(\nabla^2 f = 2\), the same at every point.

Now we can write the equations. Let the material be the same everywhere, so homogeneous (definition 3.5), and let it behave the same in all directions at every point, so isotropic (definition 3.4). The constants \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) of definition 3.10 are then the same numbers everywhere, so we may leave them in front of the derivative when we differentiate the stresses. Because \(\nu \neq -1\) and \(\nu \neq \tfrac12\), Hooke's law holds in the form (3.13). The definition of the boundary value problem asks only for continuously differentiable displacements and stresses, while the theorem asks for continuous second derivatives of the displacements, because the stresses will be differentiated once more. Whether the second follows from the first we do not prove. The solutions that we build in this chapter have continuous second derivatives, because they are written with smooth functions, such as polynomials and powers of the distance from the axis, which we check for every solution.

Theorem 11.6 Navier-Lamé equations (Navier-Laméjeve enačbe)

Let the material be homogeneous, isotropic and linearly elastic, with Lamé constants \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) (theorem 3.11, \(\nu \neq -1\) and \(\nu \neq \tfrac12\)). Let \(D\) be an open set of points of the body and \(\vek u = (u_{\mathrm{x}}, u_{\mathrm{y}}, u_{\mathrm{z}})\) a displacement field with continuous second partial derivatives on \(D\). Let \(\ten\sigma\) be the stresses that we obtain from the displacements \(\vek u\) by definition 1.115 and Hooke's law (3.13), and \(\vek b\) a vector at a point \(P\) of \(D\). Then the stresses \(\ten\sigma\) at \(P\) satisfy the equilibrium equations (2.31) with body force \(\vek b\) exactly when at \(P\)

\[\mu\,\nabla^2\vek u + (\lambda + \mu)\,\nabla(\operatorname{div}\vek u) + \vek b = \vek 0 , \tag{11.3}\]

in components, for \(\ix{i} = x, y, z\),

\[\mu\,\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{i}} + (\lambda + \mu)\,\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z}\Big) + b_{\mathrm{i}} = 0 .\]
Proof

We must show that the left side of the \(\ix{i}\)-th equilibrium equation, when we insert the stresses of the field \(\vek u\), equals the left side of the \(\ix{i}\)-th equation of the theorem. We write \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\), \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\) (definition 1.109).

  1. By definition 1.115, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}})\), and the trace is \(\tr\ten\varepsilon = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \partial u_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}} = \operatorname{div}\vek u\) (definition 4.13). The identity matrix \(\mat I\) has the element \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), which is \(1\) for \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\) and \(0\) otherwise. So Hooke's law (3.13), \(\ten\sigma = \lambda\,(\tr\ten\varepsilon)\,\mat I + 2\mu\,\ten\varepsilon\), reads in components
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \lambda\,(\operatorname{div}\vek u)\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} + \mu\left(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\right) . \tag{11.4}\]
    Since \(\vek u\) has continuous second derivatives on the open set \(D\), the stresses have continuous first derivatives at every point of \(D\).
  2. The left side of the \(\ix{i}\)-th equilibrium equation (2.31) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + b_{\mathrm{i}}\). For \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}\) we insert (11.4) with the indices swapped, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ji}} = \lambda\,(\operatorname{div}\vek u)\,\delta_{\mathrm{ji}} + \mu\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}})\), differentiate with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) and sum over \(\ix{j}\). The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives and the constants \(\lambda\), \(\mu\) stay in front of the derivative, so the three terms of the sum are those of steps 3 to 5.
  3. First term: \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \partial\big(\lambda\,(\operatorname{div}\vek u)\,\delta_{\mathrm{ji}}\big)/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = \lambda\,\partial(\operatorname{div}\vek u)/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\), because \(\delta_{\mathrm{ji}}\) differs from zero only for \(\ix{j} = \ix{i}\).
  4. Second term: \(\mu\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \partial^2 u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\). For \(\ix{j} = \ix{i}\) the mixed derivative is just a second derivative with respect to one variable. For \(\ix{j} \neq \ix{i}\) the two mixed second derivatives of the component \(u_{\mathrm{j}}\) are continuous, so by theorem 1.125 on the symmetry of mixed derivatives we may swap them, \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}} = \partial^2 u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\). In both cases the sum over \(\ix{j}\) equals \(\mu\,\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} = \mu\,\dfrac{\partial(\operatorname{div}\vek u)}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\).
  5. Third term: \(\mu\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}^2 = \mu\,\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}\) by definition 11.5.
  6. We add steps 3 to 5:
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} = \mu\,\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{i}} + (\lambda + \mu)\,\frac{\partial(\operatorname{div}\vek u)}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} .\]
  7. The equilibrium equations (2.31) at the point \(P\) are \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + b_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) for \(\ix{i} = x, y, z\). By step 6 the left side equals the left side of the equation of the theorem. All steps are equalities, so one equation holds exactly when the other does. The three equations together are the vector equation (11.3), because \(\nabla(\operatorname{div}\vek u)\) is a vector with components \(\partial(\operatorname{div}\vek u)/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\).

Source: SADD (5.4.2)-(5.4.5) (PDF p. 111), CM (7.2.16)-(7.2.17) (PDF p. 299), where CM keeps the acceleration term, zero in equilibrium. SADD writes the body force \(F\) and CM writes \(\rho_0 f_{\mathrm{i}}\), which is our \(b_{\mathrm{i}}\). SADD summarizes the derivation in one sentence, we wrote out the steps.

The proof showed that the equilibrium equations for the stresses of a displacement field are three second-order equations for the displacement itself: we removed the stresses with Hooke's law and the strains with their definition by displacements.

From history

For a long time it did not seem that anyone had tried to obtain general equations of equilibrium and motion of elastic bodies (LOVE, PDF p. 23). At the end of 1820, according to Love, all the effort spent on elastic problems could be summed up as an inadequate theory of flexure, an erroneous theory of torsion, an unproved theory of the vibrations of bars and plates and the definition of Young's modulus, and Love at once adds that such an estimate would give a wrong impression of the value of the older researches (LOVE, PDF p. 23). Navier was the first to investigate the general equations of equilibrium and vibration of elastic bodies. His memoir was read in May 1821 and published in 1827 (LOVE, PDF p. 23). He set out from Newton's conception of bodies: he regarded the molecules as material points and assumed that the force between two molecules whose distance is slightly increased is proportional to the product of the increase of the distance and some function of the initial distance. The elastic reactions arose, in his view, from variations of the forces between molecules when the arrangement of the molecules changes (LOVE, PDF pp. 23-24). He expressed all the forces on a displaced molecule and from them obtained the equations of motion of the molecule, and with them the equations for the displacements of the molecule. He assumed the material to be isotropic, and the equations of equilibrium and vibration contained a single constant of the same kind as Young's modulus (LOVE, PDF p. 24).

Navier's memoir was not generally accepted. The objections were aimed at his expression for the force between two molecules and at his replacing triple sums over molecules by integrals, since the validity of this replacement is disputed (LOVE, PDF p. 24). By the autumn of 1822 Cauchy had discovered most of the elements of the pure theory of elasticity: stress at a point, strain at a point, the equilibrium equations and, from the relation between stresses and strains, the equations for the displacements (LOVE, PDF p. 25). In a later published version he obtained the relation for an isotropic material from two assumptions, that it is linear and that the principal planes of stress are normal to the principal axes of strain. He used no hypothesis of material points and central forces. His equations contain two constants, Navier's only one (LOVE, PDF pp. 25-26). Later Cauchy also used the molecular picture with central forces. In the first memoir the equations for an isotropic body contained two constants. In the second memoir he expressed the stresses across any plane, and for an isotropic body without initial stress the stress was expressed through the strain with a single constant, so one of the constants of the first memoir had to vanish. The equations then agreed with Navier's (LOVE, PDF p. 26). Cauchy's derivation from linearity and isotropy thus gave two constants, and the molecular picture with central forces gave one (LOVE, PDF pp. 25-26).

Lamé and Clapeyron wrote a memoir on the internal equilibrium of homogeneous solid bodies in St. Petersburg. Poinsot and Navier reviewed it in 1828 and it was published in 1833 (TIMO, PDF p. 123). The memoir is important because it contains not only a derivation of the equilibrium equations, which Navier and Cauchy already knew, but also their application to practical problems (TIMO, PDF p. 123). In the first part they derived the equations with Navier's molecular forces and showed that Cauchy's stresses give the same ones. A single elastic constant appeared in their equations (TIMO, PDF pp. 123-124). In 1852 Lamé's book on the theory of elasticity appeared, the first book on this subject. The results of the memoir are in it, but the form of the equations is somewhat changed, because Lamé had concluded that two elastic constants determine the properties of an isotropic material. Cauchy had reached this conclusion earlier (TIMO, PDF pp. 124-125).

Let us return to the three equations for the displacements in the form of theorem 11.6, with the two Lamé constants (definition 3.10). What do the terms \(\mu\,\nabla^2\vek u\) and \((\lambda + \mu)\,\nabla(\operatorname{div}\vek u)\) mean? Together they are the force per unit volume that the stresses give to a piece of the body because they vary from place to place. The term \(\mu\,\nabla^2\vek u\) is nonzero when the sum of the second derivatives of a displacement component is nonzero, and the term \((\lambda + \mu)\,\nabla(\operatorname{div}\vek u)\) when the volumetric strain \(\operatorname{div}\vek u\) varies from place to place. Let us look at two simple displacements of a small cube with edge \(h\) and centre at height \(z > 0\) (figure 11.4).

In the first, \(\vek u = (c\,z^2, 0, 0)\) with a constant \(c\). The displacement \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) depends only on \(z\), so \(\operatorname{div}\vek u = 0\) and the cube only deforms in shear. The strains are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12\,\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z = c\,z\) and zero elsewhere, so by Hooke's law the only nonzero stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2\mu c\,z\). On the top face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) a force per unit area \(2\mu c\,(z + h/2)\) acts in the direction of the \(x\) axis, on the bottom face with normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) the force is \(-2\mu c\,(z - h/2)\). The total force divided by the volume \(h^3\) is

\[\frac{h^2\,\big[\,2\mu c\,(z + h/2) - 2\mu c\,(z - h/2)\,\big]}{h^3} = 2\mu c = \mu\,\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} ,\]

because \(\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} = \partial^2(c\,z^2)/\partial z^2 = 2c\). The term with the divergence is zero, because \(\nabla(\operatorname{div}\vek u) = \vek 0\). On the faces perpendicular to \(x\) and \(y\) there is no force in the direction of the \(x\) axis, because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\). The force comes from the shear stresses, which are larger at the top than at the bottom.

In the second, \(\vek u = (c\,x^2, 0, 0)\). The cube stretches more along the \(x\) axis on the right than on the left, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 2c\,x\) and \(\operatorname{div}\vek u = 2c\,x\). By Hooke's law \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \lambda\cdot 2c\,x + 2\mu\cdot 2c\,x = (\lambda + 2\mu)\,2c\,x\). The stress on the right face is larger than on the left, so the force per unit volume is \((\lambda + 2\mu)\,2c\). The theorem splits it into two parts, \(\mu\,\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\mu c\) and \((\lambda + \mu)\,\partial(\operatorname{div}\vek u)/\partial x = (\lambda + \mu)\,2c\), which together give the same, \(2c\,(\lambda + 2\mu)\). Here both terms are nonzero at once. There are no shear stresses in this case, yet the term \(\mu\,\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{x}}\) is nonzero. The split of the force into the two terms of the theorem is therefore not a split into a shear and a volumetric contribution, but a consequence of writing the equations with displacements.

The theorem holds in the interior of the body. On the surface either a displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) is prescribed on a part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), which is already a condition on the displacement, or a traction vector \(\bar{\vek t}\) on a part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) (definition 11.1). The second condition is written with stresses. We can write it with displacements too, from the same step 1 as the equations.

Corollary 11.7 Traction condition in terms of displacements (robni pogoj z napetostnim vektorjem v pomikih)

Let the material be as in theorem 11.6. Let \(P\) be a point of the part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) of the surface of the body with unit outward normal \(\vek n\) and \(\bar{\vek t}\) the prescribed traction vector at \(P\). Let the displacement field \(\vek u\) be continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(P\), with displacement gradient \(\mat H\) (definition 1.109). Then the condition \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\) at the point \(P\) holds exactly when

\[\lambda\,(\operatorname{div}\vek u)\,\vek n + \mu\,(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t} , \tag{11.5}\]

in components \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \big[\lambda\,(\operatorname{div}\vek u)\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} + \mu\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}})\big]\,n_{\mathrm{j}} = \bar t_{\mathrm{i}}\).

Proof

We must show that \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) equals the left side of (11.5).

  1. By definition 1.115, \(\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\) and \(\tr\ten\varepsilon = \operatorname{div}\vek u\). Hooke's law (3.13) gives \(\ten\sigma = \lambda\,(\operatorname{div}\vek u)\,\mat I + \mu\,(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\), which is (11.4) written with matrices. We multiply the matrix by the vector \(\vek n\) and use \(\mat I\vek n = \vek n\).

Source: CM (7.2.18) (PDF p. 299), SADD (5.2.1), (5.2.2) (PDF pp. 108-109) for the boundary conditions. The matrix form is ours.

Let us test the theorem and the corollary on three fields. The first is the field of the hanging bar. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m and diameter 10 mm, with the \(x\) axis pointing down from the centre \(O\) of the top face, is held in the idealized way of section 1.7.1: only the point \(O\) is fixed and a uniform force acts upward on the top face. The body force is the weight, \(\vek b = (\rho g, 0, 0)\) with \(\rho g = 7800 \cdot 9{,}81 = 76\,518\ \text{N/m}^3\). The field (1.18) of chapter 1 has \(a = \rho g/(2E) = 1{,}95199 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\) (chapter 1 rounded it to \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\)) and \(\nu = 0{,}3\). Let us examine the terms of equation (11.3) for the component \(x\).

  1. The second derivatives of \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\) with respect to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) are \(-2a\), \(-0{,}6\,a\) and \(-0{,}6\,a\), so \(\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} = -3{,}2\,a\). The components \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) are linear in each coordinate, so \(\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} = \nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\).
  2. The divergence is \(\operatorname{div}\vek u = 2a\,(L - x) - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) = 0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\). It depends only on \(x\), so \(\nabla(\operatorname{div}\vek u) = (-0{,}8\,a, 0, 0)\).
  3. With \(\mu = 75{,}385\) GPa and \(\lambda + \mu = 188{,}46\) GPa (section 3.2.6) we have \(\mu\,\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} = -3{,}2 \cdot 1{,}95199 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot 75{,}385 \cdot 10^9 = -47\,088\ \text{N/m}^3\) and \((\lambda + \mu)\,\partial(\operatorname{div}\vek u)/\partial x = -0{,}8 \cdot 1{,}95199 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot 188{,}46 \cdot 10^9 = -29\,430\ \text{N/m}^3\).
  4. The sum is \(-47\,088 - 29\,430 + 76\,518 = 0\). The components \(y\) and \(z\) are \(0 + 0 + 0 = 0\), because \(\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\), \(\partial(\operatorname{div}\vek u)/\partial y = 0\) and \(b_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\). The Navier-Lamé equations hold (checked with SymPy, the residual is zero).

Why exactly \(0{,}3\) in the field? If the number \(k\) stood in the field instead of \(0{,}3\), that is \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -2k\,a\,(L - x)\,y\) and \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = a\,(2Lx - x^2) - k\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\), the residual of the component \(x\) by the theorem would be \(2\nu\rho g\,(k - \nu)/\big((1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)\big)\), which is zero only for \(k = \nu\) (SymPy). For \(k = 0\), that is for a bar that does not get thinner, the residual would be \(-26\,487\ \text{N/m}^3\), which is 35 % of the weight. Equilibrium itself requires the thinning by the Poisson's ratio of the material.

Let us also examine the boundary condition. For the field \(\mat H + \mat H^\T = \operatorname{diag}(4s, -1{,}2\,s, -1{,}2\,s)\) with \(s = a\,(L - x)\), because \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x = -0{,}6\,a\,y + 0{,}6\,a\,y = 0\) and the same for \(z\), and \(\operatorname{div}\vek u = 0{,}8\,s\). On the mantle \(\vek n = (0, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\) and by (11.5)

\[\lambda \cdot 0{,}8\,s\,\vek n + \mu\,(-1{,}2\,s)\,\vek n = s\,(0{,}8 \cdot 113{,}08 - 1{,}2 \cdot 75{,}385)\ \text{GPa}\;\vek n = s\,(90{,}46 - 90{,}46)\ \text{GPa}\;\vek n = \vek 0 .\]

So the mantle is free, as it must be. On the bottom face \(s = 0\) and the traction vector is zero. On the top face \(\vek n = (-1, 0, 0)\) and \(s = aL\), so the traction vector is \(-aL\,(0{,}8\lambda + 4\mu)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). Here \(0{,}8\lambda + 4\mu = 392\) GPa \(= 2E\), so the vector equals

\[-1{,}95199 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} \cdot 10\ \text{m} \cdot 392\ \text{GPa}\;\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = (-0{,}7652\ \text{MPa},\,0,\,0) = -\rho g L\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} .\]

Since the \(x\) axis points down, this means a force upward, uniform over the top face, as we described it in chapter 1 (figure 11.5). The area of the top face is \(\pi\,(5\ \text{mm})^2 = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\), so the force is \(0{,}7652\ \text{MPa} \cdot 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2 = 60{,}1\) N, which is the weight of the bar, \(\rho g\,L\,A\) with \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\). The field is therefore a solution of the problem with the force prescribed on the whole surface (the traction vector is prescribed everywhere on the surface). Here we only checked the field. We will derive it in section 11.4, where it is also shown that, up to a rigid displacement, it is the only solution of this problem.

The second field is the ball in oil of section 4.3.7 in chapter 4, checked there with the divergence and here with the equations of this chapter. A steel ball of radius \(R = 10\) mm lies in oil at pressure \(p = 100\) MPa. In a fluid at rest the stress is \(-p\,\mat I\) (section 3.2.4), so the traction vector of the fluid on the surface of the ball is \(\bar{\vek t} = -p\,\vek n\). The weight of the ball is not important at this pressure, \(\rho g R = 0{,}77\) kPa, which is \(8 \cdot 10^{-6}\) of the pressure, so we take \(\vek b = \vek 0\). For the cube in water Hooke's law gave \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -(1 - 2\nu)\,p/E\) (section 3.2.4). Let us try the same for the ball, that is the displacement \(\vek u = \varepsilon_0\,(x, y, z)\) with the origin at the centre and \(\varepsilon_0 = -(1 - 2\nu)\,p/E = -0{,}4 \cdot 100/196\,000 = -2{,}0408 \cdot 10^{-4}\).

All components are linear, so \(\nabla^2\vek u = \vek 0\), \(\operatorname{div}\vek u = 3\varepsilon_0\) is constant and \(\nabla(\operatorname{div}\vek u) = \vek 0\). The Navier-Lamé equations hold with \(\vek b = \vek 0\). The boundary condition: \(\mat H = \varepsilon_0\,\mat I\), so the left side of (11.5) equals \((3\lambda + 2\mu)\,\varepsilon_0\,\vek n = 490\ \text{GPa} \cdot (-2{,}0408 \cdot 10^{-4})\,\vek n = -100\ \text{MPa}\,\vek n = -p\,\vek n\). The field is a solution, the ball shrinks, and its edge moves by \(\varepsilon_0 R = -2{,}041\ \mu\text{m}\) towards the centre. The solution is unique up to a rigid displacement (theorem 11.4), since this is a traction problem.

The third field is uniform. The shifted cube of section 1.6.2 has \(\vek u = (0{,}001\,z, 0, 0)\). The components are linear, so \(\nabla^2\vek u = \vek 0\), \(\operatorname{div}\vek u = 0\) and \(\nabla(\operatorname{div}\vek u) = \vek 0\), and the equations hold with \(\vek b = \vek 0\). The stress is the same everywhere, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \mu \cdot 0{,}001 = 75{,}38\) MPa, as we computed in chapter 3. The same holds for every field \(\vek u = \vek c + \mat A\,\vek x\) with a constant vector \(\vek c\) and a constant matrix \(\mat A\): the second derivatives are zero and the divergence is constant, so such a field is in equilibrium without body force.

Let us collect what we have. The unknowns are only the three components of the displacement. The three equations (11.3) are coupled, because the term \(\nabla(\operatorname{div}\vek u)\) contains all three components in every equation. Together with the boundary conditions, the displacement on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and (11.5) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), they form the displacement form of the boundary value problem. Let the field \(\vek u\) have continuous second derivatives on an open set that contains the body, let it satisfy (11.3) at every interior point, let \(\vek u = \bar{\vek u}\) hold on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and the condition (11.5) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). By theorem 11.6 and corollary 11.7 the stresses of the field are in equilibrium and satisfy the condition on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), so \(\vek u\) is a solution of the boundary value problem by definition 11.1. By theorem 11.4 (for steel the condition of the theorem on positive energy holds, theorem 3.48) it is the only solution if \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) prevents every small rigid displacement, and otherwise unique up to a rigid displacement. Since the strains are computed from the displacements, we need no compatibility equations, so the displacement form is the natural one when displacements are prescribed (SADD, PDF p. 110). Solving three coupled second-order equations is difficult, though. According to SADD, direct integration of the field equations meets great mathematical difficulties, so it is useful only for simple shapes of the body (SADD, PDF p. 115). Later in this chapter we therefore mostly find solutions by partly assuming the form of the field and computing the rest from the equations, and then checking all equations and conditions, as we did above for the hanging bar.

11.3 Beltrami-Michell equations (Beltrami-Michellove enačbe)

In section 11.2 we collected the equations of the boundary value problem (definition 11.1) into three equations for the displacement. The displacement is the only unknown there, and the strains and stresses are computed from it. Can it also be done the other way, with the stresses as the only unknown? This route is natural when forces are prescribed on the surface, because the stress gives them directly (Cauchy's formula, theorem 2.24). A question appears at once that did not arise with displacements: which equations must a stress field satisfy for it to be possible at all?

Let us look at an example. Take a bar of rectangular cross section lying along the \(x\) axis, with depth \(2c = 40\) mm, the \(y\) axis pointing up along the depth and the \(z\) axis perpendicular to the plane of the drawing. The material is the steel of the book, \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\). Let the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\) be the only nonzero component, with the constant \(k = 2{,}5 \cdot 10^{10}\ \text{N/m}^4\), so that at the top and bottom edges \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(\pm c) = k\,c^2 = 10\) MPa. The equilibrium equations (theorem 2.28) hold without body force, because the field does not depend on \(x\), so \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial x = 0\), and the other components are zero. For comparison take the field \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y\), which equals the pure bending of chapter 5. This field is in equilibrium too. We believe pure bending, because a bar really does bend. Do we believe the parabola as well?

We look for the answer through the strains. By Hooke's law (theorem 3.11) \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E\), so the fibre at height \(y\) stretches or shortens in proportion to \(k\,y\) in the first field and in proportion to \(k\,y^2\) in the second. We imagine the bar as a bundle of fibres along the \(x\) axis and let each fibre lengthen by its own amount (figure 11.6). In the first field the elongations are linear in \(y\). The upper fibres are longer, the lower ones shorter, and a surface that was flat stays flat and only turns. The fibres fit against each other if we bend them about a common centre, which is bending. In the second field the upper and the lower fibre are both longer than the middle one. The two outer fibres would both have to lie outside the curved middle fibre, which is impossible for any bending with one centre. The gap between fibres would be too narrow everywhere or too wide everywhere after loading. It seems that no displacement field gives such strains. We know the exact condition for this from chapter 1: strains that come from a displacement field satisfy the compatibility equations (1.68) (theorem 1.127), and in a simply connected body these equations are also sufficient (theorem 4.119). In a simply connected body, stresses are therefore possible exactly when the strains we get from them by Hooke's law are possible. The compatibility equations for these strains are the condition we are looking for on the stresses.

This section answers the question what compatibility demands of the stresses. First we transform the compatibility equations into a form that fits the equilibrium equations, then we insert Hooke's law and equilibrium.

11.3.1 Contracted compatibility equations (Skrčene enačbe kompatibilnosti)

The compatibility equations (1.68) contain the second derivative of the shear strain, for example \(\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial x\,\partial y\). If we insert Hooke's law in it, we get the second derivative of the shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), which the equilibrium equations do not know: they contain only first derivatives, in the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ik}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\). Such sums arise in expressions where one index is summed. Lemma 4.105 showed that the compatibility equations are the same as the vanishing of all numbers \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\). Take the numbers \(Z_{\mathrm{ikjk}}\), where the second and fourth index are equal, and for fixed \(i\), \(j\) sum them over \(k\). We get nine numbers, of which by symmetry only six are different. Did we lose information by summing? The lemma says we did not.

Lemma 11.8 Contracted compatibility equations (skrčene enačbe kompatibilnosti)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points and let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}}\), where the indices run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), be functions whose partial derivatives of the first and second order exist and are continuous at every point of \(D\). For the indices \(i\), \(j\) let

\[\begin{aligned} &R_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} Z_{\mathrm{ikjk}} \\ &\quad = \nabla^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} \\ &\quad + \frac{\partial^2(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}})}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} \\ &\quad - \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} \\ &\quad - \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} , \end{aligned} \tag{11.6}\]

where \(Z_{\mathrm{ikjk}}\) is the expression (4.71) with the indices \(i\), \(k\), \(j\), \(k\) and \(\nabla^2\) is the operator of definition 11.5. At a point \(P\) of \(D\) the compatibility equations (1.68) hold exactly when the number \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is zero at \(P\) for all nine choices of the indices \(i\), \(j\).

Proof

We must show that compatibility implies \(R_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) and that \(R_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) implies compatibility. We express the six expressions whose zeros are the compatibility equations by the \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and the other way round.

  1. The expression (4.71), in which \(i\), \(k\), \(j\), \(k\) stand in place of \(i\), \(j\), \(k\), \(l\), is
    \[Z_{\mathrm{ikjk}} = \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}^2} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kj}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} .\]
    The sum over \(k\) of the first term is \(\nabla^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\), of the second \(\partial^2(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}})/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\). In the third and fourth term we exchange the order of differentiation (theorem 1.125) and use \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kj}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}\). This is (11.6).
  2. Let \(S_1, \dots, S_6\) be the difference of the left and right side of the equations (1.68) in order. By steps 7 and 8 of the proof of lemma 4.105, \(S_1 = Z_{\mathrm{xyxy}}\), \(S_2 = Z_{\mathrm{yzyz}}\), \(S_3 = Z_{\mathrm{zxzx}}\), \(S_4 = Z_{\mathrm{xyxz}}\), \(S_5 = Z_{\mathrm{yzyx}}\), \(S_6 = Z_{\mathrm{zxzy}}\).
  3. In the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} Z_{\mathrm{ikjk}}\) the term with \(k = i\) is zero, because the first two indices are equal, and the term with \(k = j\) is zero, because the last two indices are equal (step 4 of the proof of lemma 4.105). The terms with \(k\) different from \(i\) and \(j\) remain. For \(R_{\mathrm{xx}}\) these are \(k = y\) and \(k = z\):
    \[R_{\mathrm{xx}} = Z_{\mathrm{xyxy}} + Z_{\mathrm{xzxz}} = S_1 + S_3 .\]
    Here \(Z_{\mathrm{xzxz}} = \partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial z^2 + \partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}/\partial x^2 - 2\,\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}/\partial x\,\partial z\) is the difference of the left and right side of the third equation (1.68), so \(S_3\), and \(Z_{\mathrm{xyxy}} = S_1\) by step 2.
  4. In the same way, with the exchange of pairs, \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = Z_{\mathrm{klij}}\), and of both orders, \(Z_{\mathrm{jikl}} = -Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) and \(Z_{\mathrm{ijlk}} = -Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) (steps 1 to 3 of the proof of lemma 4.105), we get
    \[R_{\mathrm{yy}} = Z_{\mathrm{yxyx}} + Z_{\mathrm{yzyz}} = S_1 + S_2 , \qquad R_{\mathrm{zz}} = Z_{\mathrm{zxzx}} + Z_{\mathrm{zyzy}} = S_3 + S_2 ,\]
    \[R_{\mathrm{yz}} = Z_{\mathrm{yxzx}} = -Z_{\mathrm{xyzx}} = Z_{\mathrm{xyxz}} = S_4 ,\]
    \[R_{\mathrm{xz}} = Z_{\mathrm{xyzy}} = Z_{\mathrm{zyxy}} = -Z_{\mathrm{yzxy}} = Z_{\mathrm{yzyx}} = S_5 ,\]
    \[R_{\mathrm{xy}} = Z_{\mathrm{xzyz}} = Z_{\mathrm{yzxz}} = -Z_{\mathrm{zyxz}} = Z_{\mathrm{zyzx}} = Z_{\mathrm{zxzy}} = S_6 .\]
    By the same steps \(R_{\mathrm{ji}} = R_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so the nine numbers \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are only six different ones.
  5. If the compatibility equations hold, then \(S_1 = \dots = S_6 = 0\) and by step 4 \(R_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) for all \(i\), \(j\).
  6. Conversely, if \(R_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) for all \(i\), \(j\), then by step 4 \(S_4 = S_5 = S_6 = 0\), and
    \[\begin{aligned} S_1 &= \tfrac12\,(R_{\mathrm{xx}} + R_{\mathrm{yy}} - R_{\mathrm{zz}}) , \\ S_2 &= \tfrac12\,(R_{\mathrm{yy}} + R_{\mathrm{zz}} - R_{\mathrm{xx}}) , \\ S_3 &= \tfrac12\,(R_{\mathrm{xx}} + R_{\mathrm{zz}} - R_{\mathrm{yy}}) , \end{aligned}\]
    which on insertion from step 4 indeed gives \(S_1\), \(S_2\), \(S_3\) (for example \(R_{\mathrm{xx}} + R_{\mathrm{yy}} - R_{\mathrm{zz}} = 2S_1 + S_2 + S_3 - S_2 - S_3 = 2S_1\)). So \(S_1\), \(S_2\), \(S_3\) are zero as well and all compatibility equations hold.

Source: SADD §5.3 (PDF p. 109): the six meaningful equations are obtained with \(k = l\) in the general form (5.1.2), so by contraction over one index. The converse direction, the solution in step 6, is ours. The proof by inversion is not from the sources. SymPy checked all six relations of step 4 for general functions.

The lemma showed that the nine contracted numbers carry the same content as the six compatibility equations, only in a form where the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\) appears. Let us test it on the bar of the introduction. The strains of the field \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\) are by Hooke's law \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2/E\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nu\,k\,y^2/E\), the other components are zero. The derivatives are \(\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial y^2 = 2k/E\), \(\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}/\partial y^2 = -2\nu k/E\), all other second derivatives are zero. The first compatibility equation gives \(S_1 = \partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial y^2 + \partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}/\partial x^2 - 2\,\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial x\,\partial y = 2k/E = 0{,}2551\ \text{m}^{-2}\), the second \(S_2 = \partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}/\partial z^2 + \partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}/\partial y^2 - 2\,\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}/\partial y\,\partial z = -2\nu k/E = -0{,}0765\ \text{m}^{-2}\), the third \(S_3 = 0\), the fourth to sixth are zero. By the lemma the contracted values are \(R_{\mathrm{xx}} = S_1 + S_3 = 0{,}2551\ \text{m}^{-2}\), \(R_{\mathrm{yy}} = S_1 + S_2 = 0{,}1786\ \text{m}^{-2}\) and \(R_{\mathrm{zz}} = S_2 + S_3 = -0{,}0765\ \text{m}^{-2}\). They are not zero, so the parabola is not a possible stress field. For the field \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y\) every second derivative of the strains is zero and compatibility holds, as figure 11.6 shows. SymPy checked the computation.

11.3.2 Stress formulation (Napetostna formulacija)

Now we insert Hooke's law and equilibrium into \(R_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\), so that only the stresses remain as unknowns. The sum \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), that is the trace (sled) of the stress tensor, we will write \(\Theta\). The equations also contain first derivatives of the body force, which the equilibrium equations connect with the stresses.

Theorem 11.9 Beltrami-Michell equations (Beltrami-Michellove enačbe)

Let the material be isotropic and homogeneous (definitions 3.4 and 3.5) with modulus of elasticity \(E\) and Poisson's ratio \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\) (theorem 3.48), with Hooke's law (3.12). Let \(D\) be an open set of points, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}\) functions with continuous partial derivatives up to the second order on \(D\) and \(\Theta = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\). Let the equilibrium equations (2.31) \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + b_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) hold at every point of \(D\) with a body force \(\vek b = (b_{\mathrm{x}}, b_{\mathrm{y}}, b_{\mathrm{z}})\) whose components have continuous first partial derivatives. Let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) be the strains that the stresses determine by Hooke's law. Then at a point \(P\) of \(D\) the compatibility equations (1.68) hold exactly when at \(P\) for all nine choices of the indices \(i\), \(j\)

\[\nabla^2\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} + \frac{1}{1 + \nu}\,\frac{\partial^2\Theta}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} = -\frac{\nu}{1 - \nu}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{div}\,\vek b - \Big(\frac{\partial b_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial b_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) . \tag{11.7}\]

Here \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) equals \(1\) for \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\) and \(0\) otherwise. From these equations follows, by summing over \(i = j\) (step 6 of the proof),

\[\nabla^2\Theta = -\frac{1 + \nu}{1 - \nu}\,\mathrm{div}\,\vek b . \tag{11.8}\]
Proof

We must show that \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\) for stresses that satisfy equilibrium equals, up to a constant factor, the difference of the left and right side of (11.7), if (11.8) holds. First we express \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\) by the stresses, then we show that (11.8) follows from each of the two sides of the claim.

  1. Hooke's law (3.12) can be written for all six components as \(E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = (1 + \nu)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} - \nu\,\Theta\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\). For \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) this is \(\big((1 + \nu)\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \nu(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}})\big)/E = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \nu(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}))/E\), for the shear components \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) and we get \((1 + \nu)\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}/E\). The sum of the diagonal components is \(E\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}) = (1 + \nu)\,\Theta - 3\nu\,\Theta = (1 - 2\nu)\,\Theta\).
  2. Because \(E\) and \(\nu\) are the same at every point (homogeneity), the derivatives of the strains are the derivatives of the stresses divided by \(E\). The first term of \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\) from (11.6) is by step 1
    \[E\,\nabla^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = (1 + \nu)\,\nabla^2\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} - \nu\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\nabla^2\Theta ,\]
    the second is \(E\,\partial^2(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}})/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = (1 - 2\nu)\,\partial^2\Theta/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  3. The third term contains the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ik}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\). By the equilibrium equations \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ik}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}} = -b_{\mathrm{i}}\) (the stress is symmetric, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ik}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ki}}\), so the order of the indices in the equation does not matter). We exchange the derivatives, because the second derivatives of the stresses are continuous (theorem 1.125), and get
    \[\begin{aligned} E\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} &= (1 + \nu)\,\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} - \nu\,\frac{\partial^2\Theta}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} \\ &= -(1 + \nu)\,\frac{\partial b_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \nu\,\frac{\partial^2\Theta}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} . \end{aligned}\]
    The fourth term is the same with \(i\) and \(j\) exchanged.
  4. We assemble \(E\,R_{\mathrm{ij}}\) from the terms of steps 2 and 3, the third and fourth term with the sign reversed:
    \[\begin{aligned} &E\,R_{\mathrm{ij}} = (1 + \nu)\,\nabla^2\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} \\ &\quad + \frac{\partial^2\Theta}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \nu\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\nabla^2\Theta \\ &\quad + (1 + \nu)\Big(\frac{\partial b_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} \\ &\quad + \frac{\partial b_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) . \end{aligned} \tag{11.9}\]
    For the second term we have \((1 - 2\nu) + \nu + \nu = 1\): the first term gives \(1 - 2\nu\), and the third and fourth have a minus in front and contain \(-\nu\,\Theta\), so each contributes \(+\nu\).
  5. We sum (11.9) over \(i = j\). The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \nabla^2\sigma_{\mathrm{ii}}\) is \(\nabla^2\Theta\), the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \partial^2\Theta/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}^2\) is \(\nabla^2\Theta\), \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \delta_{\mathrm{ii}} = 3\), the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} 2\,\partial b_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\) is \(2\,\mathrm{div}\,\vek b\). Therefore
    \[E\sum_{\mathrm{i}} R_{\mathrm{ii}} = 2\,(1 - \nu)\,\nabla^2\Theta + 2\,(1 + \nu)\,\mathrm{div}\,\vek b ,\]
    because \((1 + \nu) + 1 - 3\nu = 2\,(1 - \nu)\). If all \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are zero, the sum is zero, and since \(1 - \nu > 0\), (11.8) follows.
  6. If the equations (11.7) hold for all \(i\), \(j\), then (11.8) follows from them as well: their sum over \(i = j\) is \(\nabla^2\Theta + \nabla^2\Theta/(1 + \nu) = -3\nu\,\mathrm{div}\,\vek b/(1 - \nu) - 2\,\mathrm{div}\,\vek b\). The left side is \(\frac{2 + \nu}{1 + \nu}\,\nabla^2\Theta\), the right side \(-\frac{2 + \nu}{1 - \nu}\,\mathrm{div}\,\vek b\), and since \(2 + \nu > 0\), this gives (11.8).
  7. So let (11.8) hold, either from step 5 or from step 6. The term \(-\nu\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\nabla^2\Theta\) in (11.9) is then \(+\nu\,(1 + \nu)\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{div}\,\vek b/(1 - \nu)\) and
    \[E\,R_{\mathrm{ij}} = (1 + \nu)\Big[\nabla^2\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} + \frac{1}{1 + \nu}\,\frac{\partial^2\Theta}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\nu}{1 - \nu}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{div}\,\vek b + \frac{\partial b_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial b_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big] ,\]
    which is \((1 + \nu)\) times the left side of (11.7) from which we subtracted the right side. Therefore \(R_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) exactly when (11.7) holds.
  8. Let the compatibility equations hold. By lemma 11.8 \(R_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\), by step 5 (11.8) holds, and by step 7 (11.7). Conversely, let the equations (11.7) hold. By step 6 (11.8) holds, by step 7 \(R_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) for all \(i\), \(j\), and by lemma 11.8 the compatibility equations hold.

Source: SADD (5.3.3), (5.3.4) (PDF pp. 109 to 110), CM (7.2.26) (in vector form, with \(\rho_0\,\mathbf f = \vek b\)) and (7.2.27) (constant body force) (PDF p. 300). The sources write the equations with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij},\mathrm{kk}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{kk},\mathrm{ij}}/(1 + \nu)\) on the left, as (11.7). The converse direction and step 6 are ours, not from the sources.

The proof showed that for stresses in equilibrium the compatibility equations are the same as the six equations (11.7). Equilibrium is not just an assumption, the computation needs it: it removed the derivatives of the stresses that cannot be expressed in any other way, and the body force remained only in first derivatives.

Let us test the theorem on examples. For \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y\) we have \(\nabla^2\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\), \(\Theta = k\,y\) and its second derivatives are zero, \(\vek b = \vek 0\). All six equations are satisfied, as we saw with the strains. For \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\) we have \(\Theta = k\,y^2\) and \(\vek b = \vek 0\), and

\[\text{equation } xx:\ \nabla^2\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \frac{1}{1 + \nu}\,\frac{\partial^2\Theta}{\partial x^2} = 2k = 5{,}0 \cdot 10^{10}\ \text{N/m}^4 \ne 0 , \qquad \text{equation } yy:\ 0 + \frac{1}{1 + \nu}\,\frac{\partial^2\Theta}{\partial y^2} = \frac{2k}{1 + \nu} = 3{,}85 \cdot 10^{10}\ \text{N/m}^4 \ne 0 .\]

The equations \(zz\), \(xy\), \(xz\) and \(yz\) are satisfied. Two equations fail, so the parabola is not a possible stress field, and the trace of the stress is not harmonic, \(\nabla^2\Theta = 2k \ne 0\), which contradicts (11.8) at \(\vek b = \vek 0\). The answer is the same as from the strains, as it must be. A body force would not give a solution: from the equilibrium equation for \(x\), \(b_{\mathrm{x}} = -\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial x = 0\), and the other two components are also zero by equilibrium.

For the hanging bar of chapter 1 \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\), the other components are zero, and the body force \(\vek b = \rho g\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) is constant, so all its derivatives and \(\mathrm{div}\,\vek b\) are zero. The stress is linear in \(x\), so all second derivatives are zero and both sides of (11.7) are zero for all nine index pairs. The strains are compatible, which chapter 1 already checked, and here we obtained this without strains. For a bar of length \(L = 10\) m the stress at the top is \(\rho g L = 0{,}7652\) MPa.

Chapter 5, in the elastic solution of a simply supported beam, required \(\nabla^2(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}) = 0\) and called it the compatibility condition of the plane problem. Now we see where it comes from: for a field that does not depend on \(z\) and has \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) we have \(\Theta = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\partial^2\Theta/\partial x^2 + \partial^2\Theta/\partial y^2 = \nabla^2\Theta\). The sum of the equations \(xx\) and \(yy\) from (11.7) is therefore \(\frac{2 + \nu}{1 + \nu}\,\nabla^2\Theta = 0\) at \(\vek b = \vek 0\), and since \(2 + \nu > 0\), this gives the condition of chapter 5. The condition is thus only one consequence, the sum of two of the six equations. That it does not suffice by itself is shown by the cantilever of chapter 5 with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = F\,(L - x)\,y/I\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -F\,(c^2 - y^2)/(2I)\) and the other components zero. For it \(\Theta = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is a linear function, so \(\nabla^2\Theta = 0\) and the condition of chapter 5 holds. The equation \(xy\) from (11.7), however, is \(\nabla^2\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} + \frac{1}{1 + \nu}\,\partial^2\Theta/\partial x\,\partial y = F/I - F/\big((1 + \nu)I\big) = \nu F/\big((1 + \nu)I\big)\) and is not zero. For \(F = 500\) N and \(I = 1{,}0667 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^4\) (cross section \(20 \times 40\) mm) this is \(1{,}082 \cdot 10^9\ \text{N/m}^4\). By step 7 of the proof \(R_{\mathrm{xy}} = \nu F/(EI) = 7{,}175 \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{-2}\), which is exactly \(\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}/\partial x\,\partial y\) for \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nu\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E\).
