TIMO writes that Maxwell had already shown how stresses are measured photoelastically, but that the engineers of his time did not appreciate his work, and that the next attempt to measure stresses by photoelasticity was made after an interval of forty years by Carus Wilson (TIMO, PDF pp. 290-291). He investigated a rectangular beam loaded at the middle and found a considerable discrepancy between the measured stresses and the predictions of the usual beam formula (TIMO, PDF p. 291, the paper in Phil. Mag. in 1891 according to the note on the same page). The explanation was given by Stokes, who advocated adding the stresses from two fields. The first is the simple radial stress field in a semi-infinite plate (TIMO, figure 210a), the second the field in a freely supported beam loaded by radial tensile stresses equal and opposite to the compressive stresses in the semi-infinite plate. The resultant of these tensile stresses on each half of the beam is balanced by the reaction \(P/2\) at the support and by a horizontal force at the point \(m\), so at the cross section \(mn\) there is a bending moment and an axial force (TIMO, PDF p. 291). With this sum Wilson obtained the results of his experiments with sufficient accuracy (TIMO, PDF p. 291).

We looked at how far from the place of loading two statically equivalent distributions still differ. Lemma 11.45 gave decaying solutions for the strip, and if completeness holds, the difference decays like \(\mathrm{e}^{-(\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda)x}\) with \(\lambda b = 2{,}106 + 1{,}125\,\mathrm{i}\) or \(3{,}749 + 1{,}384\,\mathrm{i}\), which after the distance of one height of the strip is \(1{,}5\,\%\) or \(0{,}055\,\%\). The rule of one length of the loaded part suffices for the cantilever and both bars, and later in this chapter we shall meet it again at the hole in a plate.

Two warnings for what follows. First: the principle requires a self-equilibrated difference. If the resultants of the loads do not agree, part of the force must go by longer paths to distant parts of the boundary and the stresses in the intermediate regions do not fall (BARBER, PDF p. 56). Second: a computation that takes the weak condition for a part of the boundary is good only outside the neighbourhood of that part. Where we use it, we shall write which condition is replaced and at what distance the solution holds.

11.12 The Airy function in polar coordinates

In section 11.10 we wrote the three stresses of the plane problem, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), with one function \(\varphi(x, y)\) that satisfies \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\). For beams this form is suitable, because the edges are the lines \(x = \text{constant}\) and \(y = \text{constant}\). The tube of section 11.7, the ring of chapter 4 and a plate with a hole have a circle for an edge. The condition of a free edge on a circle is complicated in Cartesian coordinates, because the normal changes from point to point. In the coordinates \(r\), \(\theta\) it is simple: on the circle \(r = a\) we have \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\) at every \(\theta\). So there are three questions. How are the stresses and the equation \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\) written with \(r\) and \(\theta\)? Which functions solve the equation? And which of them may we use in a ring, that is, in a body that surrounds a hole?

Throughout this section the plane problem without body force holds, as in theorem 11.36: the stresses are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial x^2\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial y\).

11.12.1 Stresses and the equation in polar coordinates

Polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\) are cylindrical coordinates without the coordinate \(z\) (lemma 11.15). The stresses in the local axes (krajevne osi) \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(\vek e_\theta\) are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\) (definition 11.19), the first index gives the normal of the face, as in chapter 2. The component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) is the normal stress on the face \(r = \text{constant}\), that is, on the circle. The component \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) is the normal stress on the face \(\theta = \text{constant}\), that is, on the radius. The component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\) is the shear stress between them (figure 11.34, left).

How do the stresses from the same function \(\varphi\) read in these axes? In Cartesian axes \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2\) is the curvature of the surface \(z = \varphi(x, y)\) in the direction \(y\), that is, perpendicular to the normal of the face on which the stress acts. The same holds for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\). The shear stress is \(-\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial y\). In polar axes we expect the same: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) is the curvature along the circle and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) the curvature along the radius. The following lemma says this exactly, and its proof also shows why the rule holds in every rotated system.

Lemma 11.46 Airy stresses in polar coordinates (Airyjeve napetosti v polarnih koordinatah)

Let \(\varphi\) be a four times continuously differentiable function in a region of plane polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\) (lemma 11.15), written as a function of the point (lemma 11.16, item 3), and let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial x^2\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial y\) be the stresses of a plane problem without body force. Then the local components of the stress are

\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} &= \frac1r\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial r} \\ &\quad + \frac{1}{r^2}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial\theta^2} , \\ \sigma_{\theta\theta} &= \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial r^2} , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} &= -\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\Big(\frac1r\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\theta}\Big) , \end{aligned} \tag{11.59}\]

and the equation \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\) reads

\[\Big(\frac{\partial^2}{\partial r^2} + \frac1r\,\frac{\partial}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r^2}\,\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\Big)\Big(\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial r^2} + \frac1r\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r^2}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial\theta^2}\Big) = 0 . \tag{11.60}\]
Proof

We must show that the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) can be written with \(\varphi\) independently of the axes, and that their local components are computed from the derivatives of \(\varphi\) with respect to \(r\) and \(\theta\).

  1. Let \(\mat H\) be the matrix of second derivatives of \(\varphi\) (the Hessian matrix, Hessova matrika), \(H_{\mathrm{kl}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\) with \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\). It is symmetric, because the second derivatives are continuous (theorem 1.125). The stress matrix is
    \[\ten\sigma = \begin{bmatrix}\varphi_{\mathrm{yy}} & -\varphi_{\mathrm{xy}} \\ -\varphi_{\mathrm{xy}} & \varphi_{\mathrm{xx}}\end{bmatrix} = (\varphi_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varphi_{\mathrm{yy}})\,\mat I - \mat H = (\nabla^2\varphi)\,\mat I - \mat H ,\]
    which we check element by element: the element \(xx\) of the right-hand side is \(\varphi_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varphi_{\mathrm{yy}} - \varphi_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{yy}}\), the element \(yy\) is \(\varphi_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and the element \(xy\) is \(-\varphi_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The form contains no axes, so it holds in every orthonormal system.
  2. By definition 11.19 \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\ten\sigma\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\), and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\mat I\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}} = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), because the local basis is orthonormal. From step 1 it follows that
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \nabla^2\varphi - H_{\mathrm{rr}} , \qquad \sigma_{\theta\theta} = \nabla^2\varphi - H_{\theta\theta} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -H_{\mathrm{r}\theta} ,\]
    where \(H_{\mathrm{ij}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\mat H\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  3. The matrix \(\mat H\) is the matrix of derivatives of the field \(\vek v = \nabla\varphi\), \(H_{\mathrm{kl}} = \partial v_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\), and the field \(\vek v\) is continuously differentiable. Its local components are, by lemma 11.16, item 1, \(v_{\mathrm{r}} = \partial\varphi/\partial r\) and \(v_\theta = (1/r)\,\partial\varphi/\partial\theta\). Because \(\mat H\) is symmetric, \(\mat H = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\), and this is the strain matrix of the field \(\vek v\) if we take \(\vek v\) as a displacement field (definition 1.115). Corollary 11.21 (without derivatives with respect to \(z\)) therefore gives
    \[H_{\mathrm{rr}} = \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{r}}}{\partial r} = \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial r^2} , \qquad H_{\theta\theta} = \frac1r\Big(v_{\mathrm{r}} + \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial\theta}\Big) = \frac1r\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r^2}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial\theta^2} ,\]
    \[H_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = \tfrac12\Big(\frac1r\,\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{r}}}{\partial\theta} + \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial r} - \frac{v_\theta}{r}\Big) = \tfrac12\Big(\frac{2}{r}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial r\,\partial\theta} - \frac{2}{r^2}\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\theta}\Big) = \frac{\partial}{\partial r}\Big(\frac1r\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\theta}\Big) ,\]
    in the last one by the rule for the derivative of a quotient \(\partial_{\mathrm{r}}(\varphi_\theta/r) = \varphi_{\mathrm{r}\theta}/r - \varphi_\theta/r^2\), and the second derivatives are interchanged by theorem 1.125.
  4. By corollary 11.18 (without derivatives with respect to \(z\)) \(\nabla^2\varphi = \varphi_{\mathrm{rr}} + \varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/r + \varphi_{\theta\theta}/r^2\). Inserting into step 2: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/r + \varphi_{\theta\theta}/r^2\) (the term \(\varphi_{\mathrm{rr}}\) cancels), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \varphi_{\mathrm{rr}}\) (\(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/r + \varphi_{\theta\theta}/r^2\) cancels) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -\partial_{\mathrm{r}}(\varphi_\theta/r)\). This is (11.59).
  5. The function \(\psi = \nabla^2\varphi\) is twice continuously differentiable, because \(\varphi\) is four times, and it is a function of the point. Corollary 11.18 applied to \(\psi\) gives \(\nabla^4\varphi = \nabla^2\psi = \psi_{\mathrm{rr}} + \psi_{\mathrm{r}}/r + \psi_{\theta\theta}/r^2\), which is (11.60).

Source: SADD (7.6.7) and (7.6.8) (PDF p. 161-162, crop (7.6.7) read). SADD writes the components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(\sigma_\theta\), \(\tau_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\), while here each has two indices, the first is the normal of the face. The derivation through \(\ten\sigma = (\nabla^2\varphi)\mat I - \mat H\) is ours, SADD refers to Exercise 3.3 and the chain rule.

Let us test the lemma on a field we already know. Uniform tension \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_0\), everything else zero, has \(\varphi = \sigma_0 y^2/2\), since \(\varphi_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_0\) and the other second derivatives are zero. With \(y = r\sin\theta\) and \(\sin^2\theta = (1 - \cos 2\theta)/2\) (corollary 8.15) we get \(\varphi = (\sigma_0/4)\,r^2\,(1 - \cos 2\theta)\). The lemma gives

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}\,(1 - \cos 2\theta) + \sigma_0\cos 2\theta = \sigma_0\cos^2\theta , \qquad \sigma_{\theta\theta} = \tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}\,(1 - \cos 2\theta) = \sigma_0\sin^2\theta , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -\tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}\sin 2\theta .\]

So we obtained \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) from \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/r = (\sigma_0/2)(1 - \cos 2\theta)\) and \(\varphi_{\theta\theta}/r^2 = \sigma_0\cos 2\theta\), and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\) from \(\varphi_\theta/r = (\sigma_0/2)\,r\sin 2\theta\). Directly from definition 11.19, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\cdot\ten\sigma\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} = \sigma_0\cos^2\theta\), because \(\ten\sigma = \sigma_0\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}^\T\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \cos\theta\). Similarly \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = \sigma_0\cos\theta\,(-\sin\theta)\). At \(\sigma_0 = 50\) MPa and \(\theta = 30^\circ\) we get \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = 37{,}5\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = 12{,}5\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -21{,}65\) MPa, and the sum of the normal stresses is \(50\) MPa, as it must be (\(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} + \sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), the trace of a matrix does not change under a rotation of the axes). We will use the same field at a circular hole as the stress far from it. With a computer we also checked the lemma on three other functions (\(r^3\cos\theta\), \(r^4\cos 2\theta + r^2\sin 3\theta\) and \(r^2\ln r\cos\theta + r^{-1}\sin 2\theta\)): at the point with \(x = 0{,}7\) and \(y = -1{,}3\) the stresses from the rotation of the Cartesian stresses and from (11.59) agree to \(10^{-14}\).

The lemma says that in polar axes it is the same as in Cartesian ones: a normal stress is the curvature of the surface \(\varphi\) in the perpendicular direction, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = H_{\theta\theta}\) (curvature along the circle) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = H_{\mathrm{rr}}\) (curvature along the radius), and the shear stress is \(-H_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\). For the tube of section 11.7, \(\varphi\) is a function of \(r\) only and figure 11.34 (right) shows it: the slope of the curve divided by \(r\) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\), and its curvature is \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\).

11.12.2 Biharmonic functions in polar coordinates

A function is biharmonic (biharmonična) if \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\). Which functions of \(r\) and \(\theta\) are such? One way is to try functions in which \(r\) and \(\theta\) are separated. The second derivative of \(\cos n\theta\) with respect to \(\theta\) is \(-n^2\cos n\theta\), and the Laplace operator lowers the power \(r^k\) by \(2\). So we expect that the functions \(r^k\cos n\theta\) and \(r^k\sin n\theta\) have a simple Laplace operator and that the condition on \(k\) will be a polynomial. We take integer \(n\) so that the stresses are equal again after going around the angle \(2\pi\), since they are at the same point.

Lemma 11.47 Biharmonic functions in polar coordinates (biharmonične funkcije v polarnih koordinatah)

For \(r > 0\) the following functions are biharmonic.

  1. \(1\), \(\ln r\), \(r^2\) and \(r^2\ln r\) (\(n = 0\)). Every four times continuously differentiable biharmonic function that depends only on \(r\) is, on the interval \(r > 0\), a linear combination of them.
  2. \(r^3\), \(r^{-1}\), \(r\) and \(r\ln r\), each multiplied by \(\cos\theta\) or \(\sin\theta\) (\(n = 1\)).
  3. \(r^n\), \(r^{n+2}\), \(r^{-n}\) and \(r^{2-n}\), each multiplied by \(\cos n\theta\) or \(\sin n\theta\), for every integer \(n \ge 2\). For \(n = 2\) these are \(r^2\), \(r^4\), \(r^{-2}\) and \(1\), multiplied by \(\cos 2\theta\) or \(\sin 2\theta\).
Proof

We must show that \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\) holds for the listed functions, and that there are no others among the functions of \(r\) alone. For the Laplace operator we use corollary 11.18 without derivatives with respect to \(z\).

  1. Let \(\varphi = r^k\cos n\theta\) with real \(k\) and integer \(n \ge 0\). By corollary 11.18 \(\nabla^2\varphi = \big(k(k-1) + k - n^2\big)\,r^{k-2}\cos n\theta = (k^2 - n^2)\,r^{k-2}\cos n\theta\), since the second derivative of \(\cos n\theta\) with respect to \(\theta\) is \(-n^2\cos n\theta\). The same computation with \(\sin n\theta\) gives the same product. Applying it again to the function \(r^{k-2}\cos n\theta\) gives
    \[\begin{gathered} \nabla^4\varphi = (k^2 - n^2)\,\big((k-2)^2 - n^2\big)\,r^{k-4}\cos n\theta \\ = (k - n)(k + n)(k - 2 - n)(k - 2 + n)\,r^{k-4}\cos n\theta . \end{gathered}\]
    This expression is zero for \(r > 0\) exactly when \(k \in \{n,\ -n,\ n + 2,\ 2 - n\}\). For \(n \ge 2\) these are four different values, which is item 3. For \(n = 1\) the values are \(1, -1, 3, 1\), so we get \(r\), \(r^{-1}\) and \(r^3\), and the value \(1\) is double. For \(n = 0\) the values are \(0, 0, 2, 2\), so we get \(1\) and \(r^2\), each twice.
  2. The double values give one function more each, which we check directly. For \(n = 0\): \(\nabla^2\ln r = \frac1r\,(r\cdot\frac1r)' = 0\), so \(\nabla^4\ln r = 0\). Next \(\nabla^2(r^2\ln r) = \frac1r\,\big(r\,(2r\ln r + r)\big)' = \frac1r\,(2r^2\ln r + r^2)' = 4\ln r + 4\), which is the sum of a harmonic function and a constant, so \(\nabla^4(r^2\ln r) = 0\). For \(n = 1\) and \(f(r)\cos\theta\), corollary 11.18 gives \(\nabla^2\big(f\cos\theta\big) = (f'' + f'/r - f/r^2)\cos\theta\). For \(f = r\ln r\) we have \(f' = \ln r + 1\), \(f'' = 1/r\) and the expression is \(\frac1r + \frac{\ln r + 1}{r} - \frac{\ln r}{r} = \frac2r\). Next \(\nabla^2(r\ln r\cos\theta) = \frac2r\cos\theta\), and for \(f = 2/r\) we have \(f' = -2/r^2\), \(f'' = 4/r^3\) and the expression \(\frac{4}{r^3} - \frac{2}{r^3} - \frac{2}{r^3} = 0\). So \(\nabla^4(r\ln r\cos\theta) = 0\), and the same with \(\sin\theta\). Thus the functions \(\ln r\), \(r^2\ln r\) and \(r\ln r\cos\theta\), \(r\ln r\sin\theta\) are added to those from step 1, which gives items 1 and 2. All twenty functions of items 1 to 3 at \(n \le 2\) were also checked with SymPy.
  3. Let \(\varphi\) be a function of \(r\) only with four continuous derivatives on an interval and \(\psi = \nabla^2\varphi\). By corollary 11.18 \(\psi = \varphi'' + \varphi'/r = \frac1r\,(r\varphi')'\), and \(\nabla^4\varphi = \frac1r\,(r\psi')'\). From \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\) we get \((r\psi')' = 0\), so by corollary 1.85 \(r\psi' = c_1\) and \(\psi' = c_1/r\). Because \((\ln r)' = 1/r\) (definition 9.10), the difference \(\psi - c_1\ln r\) is constant, \(\psi = c_1\ln r + c_2\). Then \((r\varphi')' = r\psi = c_1\,r\ln r + c_2\,r\). Because \(\big(\tfrac{r^2}{2}\ln r - \tfrac{r^2}{4}\big)' = r\ln r\), by the same corollary \(r\varphi' = c_1\big(\tfrac{r^2}{2}\ln r - \tfrac{r^2}{4}\big) + \tfrac{c_2}{2}\,r^2 + c_3\), so \(\varphi' = c_1\big(\tfrac r2\ln r - \tfrac r4\big) + \tfrac{c_2}{2}\,r + \tfrac{c_3}{r}\). Because \(\big(\tfrac{r^2}{4}\ln r - \tfrac{r^2}{4}\big)' = \tfrac r2\ln r - \tfrac r4\), applying the corollary again gives
    \[\varphi = \frac{c_1}{4}\,r^2\ln r + \frac{c_2 - c_1}{4}\,r^2 + c_3\ln r + c_4 ,\]
    which is a linear combination of the four functions of item 1.

Source: SADD (8.3.1)-(8.3.7) (PDF p. 186-187, crop (8.3.6) read). The listed functions are terms of the general solution (8.3.6), which SADD credits to Michell. SADD adds terms with \(\theta\) as a factor (\(\theta\), \(\theta\ln r\), \(r\theta\cos\theta\), \(r\theta\sin\theta\) and others), which are not periodic and are not used in this chapter. BARBER §8.4 (PDF pp. 132-133) gives the same solution in a table. That Michell's list is complete, that is, that every periodic biharmonic function follows from it, we quote from SADD (PDF p. 187) and do not prove here. The proof of items 1 to 3 is ours.

The lemma tells us where to look. By it, Michell's series \(\varphi = \sum_{\mathrm{n}} f_{\mathrm{n}}(r)\cos n\theta + g_{\mathrm{n}}(r)\sin n\theta\) (\(f_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(g_{\mathrm{n}}\) suitable combinations of the listed powers) solves the equation at every \(n\) separately, and the boundary conditions on the circles give for every \(n\) only a few linear equations for the constants. For a circular hole in a plate we will see that \(n = 0\) and \(n = 2\) suffice, for a beam in the shape of an arc (section 11.14) \(n = 0\) and \(n = 1\). Now let us take the simplest case, \(n = 0\).

11.12.3 The axisymmetric stress function

Let an annulus (kolobar) be loaded equally around the whole circumference. We expect stresses that do not depend on \(\theta\), so \(\varphi = \varphi(r)\). By item 1 of lemma 11.47 such functions are combinations of \(1\), \(\ln r\), \(r^2\) and \(r^2\ln r\). A constant gives no stress, since all second derivatives are zero, so three remain.

Theorem 11.48 Axisymmetric Airy function (osnosimetrična Airyjeva funkcija)

Let the annulus \(a \le r \le b\) (\(0 < a < b\)) be made of an isotropic, homogeneous, linearly elastic material with \(E > 0\) and \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\) in a state of plane stress (definition 11.32), without body force, and let \(\varphi = A\ln r + B\,r^2\ln r + C\,r^2\) with real \(A\), \(B\), \(C\). Then:

  1. the stresses that \(\varphi\) gives by lemma 11.46 are
    \[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} &= \frac{A}{r^2} + B\,(1 + 2\ln r) + 2C , \\ \sigma_{\theta\theta} &= -\frac{A}{r^2} + B\,(3 + 2\ln r) + 2C , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} &= 0 , \end{aligned} \tag{11.61}\]
    and satisfy equilibrium without body force and \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\),
  2. every displacement field on the part of the annulus with \(\theta_0 < \theta < \theta_0 + 2\pi\) whose strains are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \nu\sigma_{\theta\theta})/E\), \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = (\sigma_{\theta\theta} - \nu\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}})/E\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\) has the local components
    \[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{r}} &= \frac1E\Big[-\frac{(1+\nu)A}{r} + 2(1-\nu)B\,r\ln r \\ &\quad - (1+\nu)B\,r + 2(1-\nu)C\,r\Big] \\ &\quad + Q\cos\theta + P\sin\theta , \\ u_\theta &= \frac{4B\,r\,\theta}{E} - Q\sin\theta + P\cos\theta \\ &\quad + W\,r \end{aligned} \tag{11.62}\]
    with constants \(P\), \(Q\) and \(W\) that belong to a rigid motion (a displacement \((Q, P)\) and a rotation \(W\) about \(O\)),
  3. if \(B \ne 0\), a displacement field with the strains of item 2 does not exist on the whole annulus, because \(u_\theta\) changes by \(8\pi B\,r/E\) on going around the hole. If \(B = 0\), the stresses are Lamé's (theorem 11.27, item 1, at \(S = 0\)) with the constants \(A_{\mathrm{L}} = 2C\) and \(B_{\mathrm{L}} = -A\) of that theorem, and the displacements are those of that theorem up to a rigid motion, so they are unique.
Proof

We must show that the stresses satisfy equilibrium, that the displacements are obtained by integrating the strains, and that \(u_\theta\) is single-valued only at \(B = 0\). We start from lemma 11.46 and corollaries 11.26 and 11.21.

1. Stresses.

  1. For \(\varphi = \varphi(r)\) all derivatives with respect to \(\theta\) in (11.59) are zero, so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \varphi'/r\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \varphi''\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\). From \(\varphi' = A/r + 2B\,r\ln r + B\,r + 2C\,r\) we get \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = A/r^2 + 2B\ln r + B + 2C\), and from \(\varphi'' = -A/r^2 + 2B\ln r + 2B + B + 2C\) we get \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) of (11.61).
  2. The first equation of equilibrium in cylindrical coordinates (corollary 11.24, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\), without derivatives with respect to \(\theta\) and \(z\) and without body force) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}' + (\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \sigma_{\theta\theta})/r = 0\). By step 1, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}' = \varphi''/r - \varphi'/r^2\) and \((\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \sigma_{\theta\theta})/r = \varphi'/r^2 - \varphi''/r\), and the sum is zero. The second equation is \(0 = 0\) and the third holds because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rz}} = \sigma_{\theta \mathrm{z}} = 0\). The equation \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\) holds by item 1 of lemma 11.47.

2. Displacements.

  1. Hooke's law in local axes (corollary 11.26) at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{rz}} = \sigma_{\theta \mathrm{z}} = 0\) gives the strains of item 2 of the theorem. The relation between strains and displacements is, by corollary 11.21 with \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) and nothing depending on \(z\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial r\), \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = (u_{\mathrm{r}} + \partial u_\theta/\partial\theta)/r\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = \tfrac12\big(\tfrac1r\,\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial\theta + \partial u_\theta/\partial r - u_\theta/r\big)\).
  2. The function \(U(r) = \frac1E\big[-(1+\nu)A/r + 2(1-\nu)B\,r\ln r - (1+\nu)B\,r + 2(1-\nu)C\,r\big]\) has the derivative \(U' = (\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \nu\sigma_{\theta\theta})/E\), which we check by differentiating: the derivative of the first term is \((1+\nu)A/(E r^2)\), of the second \(2(1-\nu)B(\ln r + 1)/E\), of the third \(-(1+\nu)B/E\) and of the fourth \(2(1-\nu)C/E\), and the sum is \(\big[(1+\nu)A/r^2 + B\,(2(1-\nu)\ln r + 2(1-\nu) - (1+\nu)) + 2(1-\nu)C\big]/E\), and this is \((\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \nu\sigma_{\theta\theta})/E\) by (11.61). From \(\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial r = U'\) and corollary 1.85 on every radius we get \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = U(r) + f(\theta)\) with a function \(f\) of the angle.
  3. From the second strain, \(\partial u_\theta/\partial\theta = r\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} - u_{\mathrm{r}}\). By (11.61) \(r\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = \frac1E\big[-(1+\nu)A/r + B\,r\,(3 + 2\ln r - \nu - 2\nu\ln r) + 2(1-\nu)C\,r\big]\). The difference \(r\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} - U\) has equal terms at \(A\) and \(C\), and at \(B\) it is \(B\,r\,\big[3 + 2\ln r - \nu - 2\nu\ln r - 2(1-\nu)\ln r + (1+\nu)\big]/E = 4B\,r/E\). So \(\partial u_\theta/\partial\theta = 4B\,r/E - f(\theta)\) and \(u_\theta = 4B\,r\,\theta/E - F(\theta) + g(r)\), where \(F' = f\) and \(g\) is a function of the radius.
  4. The third strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\) gives \(\frac1r f'(\theta) + \frac{4B\theta}{E} + g'(r) - \frac1r\big(\frac{4Br\theta}{E} - F(\theta) + g(r)\big) = 0\). The terms with \(\theta\) cancel. After multiplying by \(r\) what remains is \(f'(\theta) + F(\theta) = g(r) - r\,g'(r)\). The left side is a function of \(\theta\) only and the right side of \(r\) only, so both are constant (corollary 1.85 on each side with the other variable fixed), \(= c\). From \(g - r\,g' = c\) it follows that \((g/r)' = (r g' - g)/r^2 = -c/r^2\), so \(g/r = c/r + W\) and \(g = c + W\,r\). The function \(F\) has the second derivative \(F'' = f'\) and \(F'' + F = c\), so \(G = F - c\) satisfies \(G'' + G = 0\). The functions \(W_1 = G'\cos\theta + G\sin\theta\) and \(W_2 = G\cos\theta - G'\sin\theta\) have, by theorem 8.12, the derivatives \(W_1' = (G'' + G)\cos\theta = 0\) and \(W_2' = -(G'' + G)\sin\theta = 0\), so they are constant (corollary 1.85), say \(W_1 = Q\) and \(W_2 = -P\). From \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\) we get \(G = W_1\sin\theta + W_2\cos\theta = Q\sin\theta - P\cos\theta\). Then \(f = F' = Q\cos\theta + P\sin\theta\) and \(u_\theta = 4B\,r\,\theta/E - F + g = 4B\,r\,\theta/E - Q\sin\theta + P\cos\theta - c + c + W\,r\). This is (11.62). The field \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = Q\cos\theta + P\sin\theta\), \(u_\theta = -Q\sin\theta + P\cos\theta\) is the displacement \((Q, P)\) in local components, and \(u_\theta = W\,r\) is a rotation about \(O\) by \(W\).

3. Uniqueness.

  1. The displacement of the whole annulus is a function of the point, so at the point with the same \(r\) and \(\theta\) and at \(\theta + 2\pi\) it has the same value. The local components \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(u_\theta\) then also return after going around, because \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\vek e_\theta\) are functions of the point. All terms of (11.62) except \(4B\,r\,\theta/E\) are periodic in \(\theta\) with period \(2\pi\). This one changes by \(8\pi B\,r/E\) after going around, which for \(r > 0\) differs from zero if \(B \ne 0\). So for \(B \ne 0\) there is no displacement field on the whole annulus.
  2. For \(B = 0\) the stresses are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = A/r^2 + 2C\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = -A/r^2 + 2C\), so the form \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = A_{\mathrm{L}} - B_{\mathrm{L}}/r^2\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = A_{\mathrm{L}} + B_{\mathrm{L}}/r^2\) of theorem 11.27 with \(A_{\mathrm{L}} = 2C\) and \(B_{\mathrm{L}} = -A\). At \(B = 0\) we have \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = \frac1E\big[-(1+\nu)A/r + 2(1-\nu)C\,r\big] + \dots\), which is \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = \frac{(1-\nu)A_{\mathrm{L}}}{E}\,r + \frac{(1+\nu)B_{\mathrm{L}}}{E}\,\frac1r\), the displacement of theorem 11.27 at \(S = 0\), and \(u_\theta = W r + P\cos\theta - Q\sin\theta\) is a rigid motion.

Source: SADD (8.3.7)-(8.3.9) (PDF p. 187-188, crops (8.3.7), (8.3.8), (8.3.9) read). SADD calls the constants of the function \(\varphi\) \(a_1\), \(a_2\), \(a_3\) (here \(A\), \(C\), \(B\)) and the constants of the rigid motion \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) (here \(P\), \(Q\) and \(W\)), but because the letters \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) are already taken here, we renamed them. On p. 188 SADD says that the term with \(a_3\) in \(u_\theta\) leads to multivalued displacements if a closed curve can be drawn around the origin inside the body. BARBER (PDF p. 132) says the same for the terms \(n = 0\) and \(n = 1\). The integration with the functions \(f\) and \(g\) and the solution for \(F\) are ours, and SymPy checked that \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(u_\theta\) of (11.62) satisfy all three strain equations identically.

The theorem showed three things. The three constants \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) give an axisymmetric stress field that satisfies equilibrium and the equation \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\). Displacements are obtained only by integrating the strains, because the stresses alone do not say whether the ring has a displacement field. So single-valuedness of the displacement is a separate condition, as we already saw for the ring in chapter 4 (corollary 4.113, lemma 4.120): the compatibility equations are not enough for a body with a hole. And in a whole ring this condition removes the term \(B\,r^2\ln r\), while in a ring with a cut it leaves it.

From history

Michell investigated two-dimensional problems in a paper on the direct determination of stress in an elastic solid (On the direct determination of stress in an elastic solid), published in the Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (BARBER, PDF p. 132, TIMO, PDF p. 292). BARBER attributes to him the general solution with stresses in the form of a Fourier series in \(\theta\) (definition 9.88) and calls it the Michell solution (BARBER, PDF p. 132). SADD says that Michell originally developed this solution in 1899 and that he restricts it to solutions periodic in \(\theta\), because then arbitrary boundary conditions can be treated with the Fourier method (SADD, PDF p. 187). LOVE, in the appendix on Volterra's theory of dislocations, says that Michell explicitly treated the possibility that the stress function is many-valued if the displacements are single-valued, and gives the year 1900 (LOVE, PDF p. 240). The years do not agree: 1899 (TIMO, BARBER, SADD) or 1900 (LOVE). Which year is right we cannot decide from these sources. LOVE justifies single-valued displacements like this: an actual displacement appears to be necessarily single-valued, but in a body that surrounds a hole, for example in a hollow cylinder, a many-valued displacement is also physically possible. From the cylinder we remove a thin slice between two axial planes, and the new surfaces are pressed together and joined. The body formed in this way is in an initial stress, which we obtain if the ratio of the displacement, resolved at right angles to the axial plane through the point, to the distance from the axis is many-valued with a cyclic constant, and we adjust the constant so that the corresponding points of the two axial planes coincide after the displacement (LOVE, PDF p. 240). The possibility of such an interpretation was, according to LOVE, first indicated by Weingarten in 1901, Timpe treated it in more detail for two-dimensional systems, among them the plane circular ring, and Volterra developed a more general theory in a series of notes and presented it comprehensively in 1907. Volterra calls the kind of deformations to which the theory applies "distorsioni", and Love says he ventured to call them dislocations (dislocations) (LOVE, PDF p. 240).

We asked what the term \(B\,r^2\ln r\) does in a ring. By the theorem it is absent in a whole ring, and the history tells how a many-valued displacement was given a physical meaning: a body from which a wedge is cut out and which is joined again. Let us now compute such rings, first a ring in which \(B = 0\).

Example 11.49 The tube from the Airy function (cev iz Airyjeve funkcije)

The tube of section 11.7 has inner radius \(a = 40\) mm, outer radius \(b = 60\) mm, pressure \(p = 30\) MPa in the bore, a free outer surface and free ends. This time we do not guess the displacements. We take \(\varphi = A\ln r + C\,r^2\), so \(B = 0\), because the tube surrounds a hole (theorem 11.48, item 3).

  1. On the circle \(r = a\) the outer normal of the body is \(\vek n = -\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\). The force per unit area there is \(-p\,\vek n = p\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) and must equal \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = -\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\vek e_\theta\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(a) = -p\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}(a) = 0\). At \(r = b\) we have \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) and the force is zero, so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(b) = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}(b) = 0\). The shear stress is zero everywhere by the theorem, two equations remain by the expression (11.61):
    \[\frac{A}{a^2} + 2C = -p , \qquad \frac{A}{b^2} + 2C = 0 .\]
  2. The difference of the equations is \(A\,(1/a^2 - 1/b^2) = -p\), so \(A = -p\,a^2 b^2/(b^2 - a^2) = -30 \cdot 1600 \cdot 3600/2000 = -86\,400\) MPa mm\(^2\). From the second equation \(2C = -A/b^2 = 86\,400/3600 = 24\) MPa, so \(C = 12\) MPa.
  3. The stresses are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = 24 - 86\,400/r^2\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = 24 + 86\,400/r^2\) in MPa with \(r\) in mm. At \(r = 40\), \(50\), \(60\) mm we have \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = -30\), \(-10{,}56\), \(0\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = 78\), \(58{,}56\), \(48\) MPa. These are the same results as in theorem 11.27 with \(A_{\mathrm{L}} = 24\) MPa and \(B_{\mathrm{L}} = 86\,400\) MPa mm\(^2\).
  4. Because \(B = 0\), the displacements of item 3 of theorem 11.48 are Lamé's and single-valued. Because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) at the free ends of the tube, the stresses are the same as in theorem 11.27 at \(S = 0\). There the field is shown to be an exact three-dimensional solution of the boundary problem, and by theorem 11.4 the only one up to a rigid motion.

Without the condition of single-valuedness the two boundary conditions do not determine the solution. For \(B \neq 0\) the same two conditions \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(a) = -p\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(b) = 0\) would give different \(A\) and \(C\) for every \(B\). For \(B = 10\) MPa (in the expressions we write \(\ln(r/a)\) instead of \(\ln r\), which changes only \(C\), because \(r^2\ln r = r^2\ln(r/a) + r^2\ln a\)) we get \(A = -63\,045\) MPa mm\(^2\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = 68{,}81\), \(59{,}08\), \(55{,}03\) MPa at \(r = 40\), \(50\), \(60\) mm, instead of \(78\), \(58{,}56\), \(48\) MPa. This field too is in equilibrium and satisfies the boundary conditions, but by item 3 of the theorem it has a many-valued displacement, so it is not the field of a tube loaded by pressure alone. The choice \(B = 0\) is determined by the single-valuedness of the displacement, not by a boundary condition.

The stresses of Lamé's tube do not contain \(E\) and \(\nu\). This agrees with Michell's condition from section 11.10.4: for a region with a hole the stresses are independent of the moduli if the resultant of the forces on each edge is zero. For the tube the resultant of the pressure on each of the two circles is zero by symmetry, and in that section we only stated the condition, we did not prove it.

For a loading with forces that gives an axisymmetric field, \(B = 0\) therefore always holds in a ring that surrounds a hole. But what if the ring is not loaded by forces and instead we prescribe a jump of the displacement across a cut, like the ring with shortened fibres in chapter 4?

Example 11.50 A ring with a wedge removed (obroč z izrezanim klinom)

Take the ring of chapter 4: a thin steel ring with inner radius \(a = 40\) mm, outer radius \(b = 60\) mm, thickness \(2\) mm, modulus \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\). There we shortened all the fibres around the hole by \(k = 0{,}001\) and computed that the sides of the cut move apart by \(2\pi k\,r\), that is, by \(0{,}251\) mm at \(r = 40\) mm and \(0{,}377\) mm at \(r = 60\) mm (lemma 4.120). Now we do the opposite. From a ring without stress we cut out a wedge with the angle \(\alpha = 2\pi k = 0{,}006283\) (\(0{,}36^\circ\)) with its apex at \(O\). The wedge is \(\alpha r\) wide, that is, \(0{,}251\) mm and \(0{,}377\) mm at the edges, like the gap in chapter 4. We press the sides of the cut together and weld them (figure 11.35, left). What stresses remain in a ring that no external force loads? The ring is thin and lies freely in the plane, so we take plane stress.

  1. We treat the ring with \(\varphi = A\ln(r/a) + B\,r^2\ln(r/a) + C'\,r^2\) by item 3 of lemma 11.47 (the expression \(\ln(r/a) = \ln r - \ln a\) adds only a term \(r^2\ln a\), which is part of \(C\), and changes \(A\) by a \(\ln a\) multiple of a constant). The stresses by theorem 11.48 are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = A/r^2 + B\,(1 + 2\ln(r/a)) + 2C'\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = -A/r^2 + B\,(3 + 2\ln(r/a)) + 2C'\).
  2. Before welding the ring occupies the angles \(\alpha/2 \le \theta \le 2\pi - \alpha/2\). The point \(P^+\) on the radius \(r\) at \(\theta = \alpha/2\) and the point \(P^-\) on the same radius at \(\theta = 2\pi - \alpha/2\) are apart by \(2r\sin(\alpha/2) \approx \alpha r\) in the direction \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), in which \(\vek e_\theta\) points on both sides to first order in \(\alpha\). After welding they must be at the same point, \(P^+ + \vek u^+ = P^- + \vek u^-\), so \(\vek u^- - \vek u^+ = \alpha r\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) must hold, and in local components \(u_\theta(2\pi - \alpha/2) - u_\theta(\alpha/2) = \alpha r\) (the computation is first order in \(\alpha\): we neglect the deviations of the bases \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\vek e_\theta\) between the two sides, which are of order \(\alpha = 0{,}006\), and the products of displacements with them, so the relative error is of order \(\alpha\), that is below \(1\,\%\)). By expression (11.62) the left side is \(4B\,r\,(2\pi - \alpha)/E \approx 8\pi B\,r/E\), since the rigid motion with \(P\), \(Q\) and \(W\) moves both sides equally. So \(B = E\alpha/(8\pi) = E k/4 = 49\) MPa. The jump of the displacement is thus \(2\pi k\,r\), as in chapter 4, only with the opposite sign: there the sides move apart, here we close them.
  3. The remaining constants are computed from the free surfaces, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(a) = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(b) = 0\):
    \[\frac{A}{a^2} + B + 2C' = 0 , \qquad \frac{A}{b^2} + B\,\big(1 + 2\ln\tfrac ba\big) + 2C' = 0 .\]
    The difference is \(A\,(1/a^2 - 1/b^2) = 2B\ln(b/a)\), so \(A = 2B\ln(b/a)\,a^2 b^2/(b^2 - a^2) = 114\,438\) MPa mm\(^2\), and \(2C' = -A/a^2 - B = -71{,}52 - 49 = -120{,}52\) MPa. The stresses in MPa at \(r\) in mm (figure 11.35, right):
\(r\) [mm] 40 45 50 55 60
\(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) \(0\) \(-3{,}47\) \(-3{,}88\) \(-2{,}48\) \(0\)
\(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) \(-45{,}05\) \(-18{,}49\) \(2{,}57\) \(19{,}85\) \(34{,}42\)

The hoop stress is compressive at the inner edge and tensile at the outer one, and is zero at \(r = 49{,}33\) mm. The radial stress is compressive everywhere and at most \(3{,}99\) MPa in absolute value at \(r = 48{,}3\) mm, which a ring without a hole and without a wedge would not have.

  1. The resultant of the hoop stresses on a cross section is zero. From the first equation of equilibrium in cylindrical axes, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}' + (\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \sigma_{\theta\theta})/r = 0\), we get \((r\,\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}})' = \sigma_{\theta\theta}\), so \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r = \big[r\,\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\big]_{\mathrm{a}}^b = 0\) by the free surfaces. The moment of the hoop stresses about \(O\) is not zero: \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,r\,\mathrm{d}r = 2599\) N mm per millimetre of thickness, for the thickness \(2\) mm it is \(5{,}198\) N m. Every cross section thus carries a moment without a force, compression at the inner and tension at the outer edge. We will meet the same form of \(\varphi\) in section 11.14, in a beam in the shape of an arc, where the moment is prescribed at the ends of the beam and the cut stays open.

The stresses are proportional to \(E\), because \(B = E\alpha/(8\pi)\) and \(A\) and \(C'\) are proportional to \(B\). They do not contain \(\nu\), because \(\nu\) appears neither in \(B\) nor in the equations for \(A\) and \(C'\): the datum is a jump of displacement, not a force. This is not in contradiction with Michell's independence of the moduli, which holds for a loading with forces with zero resultant on each edge. The term \(4B/E\) in \(\partial u_\theta/\partial\theta\) equals \(\alpha/(2\pi) = k\), that is, the relative shortening of the circumference by the wedge, \(\alpha r/(2\pi r)\). Because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nu(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} + \sigma_{\theta\theta})/E\) here depends on \(r\) (from \(6{,}9\cdot10^{-5}\) at \(r = 40\) mm to \(-5{,}3\cdot10^{-5}\) at \(60\) mm), the model of plane stress does not satisfy all the compatibility equations in three dimensions (theorem 11.33), so the field holds as an average over the thickness of the thin ring (theorem 11.35).

The section gave the polar form of the Airy stresses (lemma 11.46), the powers and the logarithm that solve the equation \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\) (lemma 11.47), and the axisymmetric case with the single-valuedness that removes the term \(B\,r^2\ln r\) in a whole ring (theorem 11.48). With it we computed the tube once more, this time from the stresses, and computed a ring with a wedge removed, in which the same term describes stresses without an external force. We saved the terms with \(n = 1\) and \(n = 2\) of lemma 11.47: with \(n = 2\) we will solve in section 11.13 the plane problem with a round hole, and with \(n = 0\) and \(n = 1\) in section 11.14 a beam in the shape of an arc.

11.13 A circular hole in a plate under tension

A steel plate a few millimetres thick is held at opposite edges in the jaws of a machine that pulls it with a tensile stress \(\sigma_0 = 50\) MPa. In the middle of the plate there is a circular hole of radius \(a = 10\) mm, for example for a bolt that was not inserted. Without the hole the stress would be the same everywhere, as in the tension bar of chapter 2. With the hole this is no longer so: the force that would run through the material inside the hole must run past it, and no rule so far tells where the stress is largest because of this, and by how much. There are two questions. How large is the stress at the hole? And how far from the hole does the plate still feel it?

The path is this. First we say what we assume for the plate. Then, from the Airy function of the uniform field and from the functions of lemma 11.47, we build a field with three unknown constants, which are fixed by the free hole and by the requirement that the disturbance decays with distance. We test this field on the numbers of the plate. Then, by adding two such fields, we obtain the hole in a biaxial and in a shear field, and at the end we ask what the field of the infinite plate says about a plate of finite size.

11.13.1 The plate and the hole

The plate is thin and free on both faces, loaded only in its own plane. We treat it with the model of plane stress (ravninsko napetostno stanje, definition 11.32). Its exact meaning is given by theorem 11.35: if we assume \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) throughout the plate, the thickness averages of the stresses satisfy the plane equations exactly. We understand the stresses of this section as these averages. The hole is a circle of radius \(a\) with a free edge, so there is no force per unit area on it. The material is isotropic, homogeneous and linearly elastic, and there is no body force.

The plate is much larger than the hole. For the hole \(a = 10\) mm we take a square \(200 \times 200\) mm, so the edge is \(10\) radii from the centre. Therefore we compute with a simplification: the plate is the whole plane outside the circle \(r \ge a\) (the infinite plate, neskončna plošča), and the tension acts at infinity. Let the \(x\) axis point in the direction of the pull and the origin lie at the centre of the hole. The requirement at infinity is this: as \(r \to \infty\) the stresses approach those of the plate without a hole, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_0\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\). How large an error the simplification makes for the \(200 \times 200\) mm plate we compute in the last section.

We do not prove uniqueness of the solution. Theorem 11.4 holds for bounded bodies. The infinite plate is not bounded, and a proof would need conditions at infinity, which the book does not treat. We therefore construct the field of this section and check every condition, but we do not claim that it is the only field with the given conditions.

11.13.2 The idea: a uniform field and a disturbance

We know the stresses of the plate without a hole. Their Airy function (theorem 11.36) is \(\varphi_0 = \sigma_0 y^2/2\), since \(\partial^2\varphi_0/\partial y^2 = \sigma_0 = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and the other second derivatives are zero. In polar coordinates \(y = r\sin\theta\) and by the addition theorem (corollary 8.15) \(\sin^2\theta = (1 - \cos 2\theta)/2\), so

\[\varphi_0 = \frac{\sigma_0}{2}\,r^2\sin^2\theta = \frac{\sigma_0}{4}\,r^2\,(1 - \cos 2\theta) . \tag{11.63}\]

The function contains only \(1\) and \(\cos 2\theta\) as dependence on the angle. The hole brings a disturbance, and this must decay with distance. Among the functions of lemma 11.47 with angular dependence \(1\) and \(\cos 2\theta\) the following come into question.

  • For \(n = 0\) these are \(1\), \(\ln r\), \(r^2\) and \(r^2\ln r\). The function \(1\) gives no stress, \(r^2\) is the uniform field, \(\ln r\) gives stresses that decay like \(1/r^2\). The function \(r^2\ln r\) gives stresses that grow like \(\ln r\), and by theorem 11.48 its displacement in a full ring is multivalued, so we do not take it.
  • For \(n = 2\) these are \(r^2\cos 2\theta\), \(r^4\cos 2\theta\), \(r^{-2}\cos 2\theta\) and \(\cos 2\theta\). The function \(r^2\cos 2\theta\) already appears in (11.63), \(r^4\cos 2\theta\) gives stresses that grow like \(r^2\), and what remains are \(\cos 2\theta\) with stresses that decay like \(1/r^2\) and \(r^{-2}\cos 2\theta\) with stresses that decay like \(1/r^4\).

So we try the function

\[\varphi = \frac{\sigma_0}{4}\,r^2\,(1 - \cos 2\theta) + A\ln r + \Big(\frac{C}{r^2} + D\Big)\cos 2\theta \tag{11.64}\]

with three unknown constants \(A\), \(C\), \(D\). By lemma 11.46 the stresses of such a function depend on the angle only through \(1\), \(\cos 2\theta\) and \(\sin 2\theta\), so the two conditions of the free edge of the hole will give equations for the coefficients of three functions, and three constants will suffice.

11.13.3 The Kirsch solution

Theorem 11.51 Kirsch solution for a circular hole in an infinite plate (Kirschova rešitev za krožno luknjo v neskončni plošči)

Let \(a > 0\), \(\sigma_0 > 0\), and let the plate be the region \(r \ge a\) of the plane \(x\), \(y\) with polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\) about the centre of the circle, in plane stress (definition 11.32) or plane strain (definition 11.30), of an isotropic and homogeneous material (\(E\), \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\)) and without body force. Let

\[\varphi = \frac{\sigma_0}{4}\,r^2 - \frac{a^2\sigma_0}{2}\,\ln r + \Big(-\frac{\sigma_0}{4}\,r^2 - \frac{a^4\sigma_0}{4}\,r^{-2} + \frac{a^2\sigma_0}{2}\Big)\cos 2\theta . \tag{11.65}\]

Then:

  1. The function \(\varphi\) is biharmonic on \(r > 0\), and its stresses are
    \[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} &= \frac{\sigma_0}{2}\Big(1 - \frac{a^2}{r^2}\Big) + \frac{\sigma_0}{2}\Big(1 - \frac{4a^2}{r^2} + \frac{3a^4}{r^4}\Big)\cos 2\theta , \\ \sigma_{\theta\theta} &= \frac{\sigma_0}{2}\Big(1 + \frac{a^2}{r^2}\Big) - \frac{\sigma_0}{2}\Big(1 + \frac{3a^4}{r^4}\Big)\cos 2\theta , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} &= -\frac{\sigma_0}{2}\Big(1 + \frac{2a^2}{r^2} - \frac{3a^4}{r^4}\Big)\sin 2\theta . \end{aligned} \tag{11.66}\]
    This is an equilibrium field without body force that satisfies the compatibility condition \(S_1 = 0\) (theorem 11.36, item 3).
  2. The edge of the hole is free: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(a, \theta) = \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}(a, \theta) = 0\) for every \(\theta\).
  3. The difference of each Cartesian stress component from the uniform field \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_0\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) is smaller in absolute value than \(c\,\sigma_0\,a^2/r^2\) for all \(\theta\) and \(r \ge a\), with a constant \(c\) that depends neither on \(r\) nor on \(\theta\).
  4. On the edge of the hole
    \[\sigma_{\theta\theta}(a, \theta) = \sigma_0\,(1 - 2\cos 2\theta) , \tag{11.67}\]
    the largest value is \(3\sigma_0\) at \(\theta = \pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}\), the smallest \(-\sigma_0\) at \(\theta = 0\) and \(\theta = \pi\), and zero at \(\theta = \pm\tfrac{\pi}{6}\) and \(\pm\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\).
  5. Let \(E'\), \(\nu'\) be the constants of the plane system (corollary 11.34: \(E\), \(\nu\) for plane stress, \(E^*\), \(\nu^*\) for plane strain). The displacement field
    \[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{r}} &= \frac{\sigma_0}{2E'}\Big[(1 - \nu')\,r + (1 + \nu')\frac{a^2}{r} \\ &\quad + \Big((1 + \nu')\,r + \frac{4a^2}{r} \\ &\quad - (1 + \nu')\frac{a^4}{r^3}\Big)\cos 2\theta\Big] , \\ u_\theta &= -\frac{\sigma_0}{2E'}\Big[(1 + \nu')\,r + \frac{2(1 - \nu')\,a^2}{r} \\ &\quad + (1 + \nu')\frac{a^4}{r^3}\Big]\sin 2\theta \end{aligned} \tag{11.68}\]
    has the strains that belong to the stresses (11.66), and it is single-valued: on a full turn \(\theta \to \theta + 2\pi\) it returns to the same value. The stresses (11.66) contain neither \(E\) nor \(\nu\), only the displacements depend on them.
Proof

We must show five items. The idea is this: the field (11.64) is biharmonic, its stresses follow from lemma 11.46, three conditions on the edge of the hole fix the three constants, and the displacements are obtained by integrating the strains.

  1. Item 1, biharmonicity. The functions \(r^2\), \(\ln r\), \(r^2\cos 2\theta\), \(r^{-2}\cos 2\theta\) and \(\cos 2\theta\) are biharmonic on \(r > 0\) (lemma 11.47, the cases \(n = 0\) and \(n = 2\)). The operator \(\nabla^4\) is linear (definition 11.5), so every linear combination is biharmonic, also (11.64). The function \(\varphi\) is a function of the point \((x, y)\) on \(r > 0\) with continuous derivatives of all orders, since \(r^2 = x^2 + y^2\), \(\ln r = \tfrac12\ln(x^2 + y^2)\) and \(\cos 2\theta = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta = (x^2 - y^2)/r^2\) (corollary 8.15), and all of these are smooth functions on \(r > 0\). By theorem 11.36 (item 3, \(V = 0\)) the stresses are in equilibrium and satisfy \(S_1 = 0\).

  2. Item 1, stresses. We compute the stresses of each term by lemma 11.46, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \tfrac1r\,\partial_{\mathrm{r}}\varphi + \tfrac{1}{r^2}\,\partial_\theta^2\varphi\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \partial_{\mathrm{r}}^2\varphi\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -\partial_{\mathrm{r}}\big(\tfrac1r\,\partial_\theta\varphi\big)\). The angular derivatives of \(\cos 2\theta\) are \(-2\sin 2\theta\) and \(-4\cos 2\theta\). For the term \(C\,r^{-2}\cos 2\theta\), for example, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \tfrac1r\,(-2C\,r^{-3})\cos 2\theta + \tfrac1{r^2}\,(-4C\,r^{-2})\cos 2\theta = -6C\,r^{-4}\cos 2\theta\). All terms give:

    term of \(\varphi\) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\)
    \(\tfrac{\sigma_0}{4}\,r^2\) \(\tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}\) \(\tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}\) \(0\)
    \(-\tfrac{\sigma_0}{4}\,r^2\cos 2\theta\) \(\tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}\cos 2\theta\) \(-\tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}\cos 2\theta\) \(-\tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}\sin 2\theta\)
    \(A\ln r\) \(A/r^2\) \(-A/r^2\) \(0\)
    \(C\,r^{-2}\cos 2\theta\) \(-6C\,r^{-4}\cos 2\theta\) \(6C\,r^{-4}\cos 2\theta\) \(-6C\,r^{-4}\sin 2\theta\)
    \(D\cos 2\theta\) \(-4D\,r^{-2}\cos 2\theta\) \(0\) \(-2D\,r^{-2}\sin 2\theta\)

    The first two rows are the uniform field: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \sigma_0\cos^2\theta\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_0\sin^2\theta\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -\sigma_0\sin\theta\cos\theta\) are the components of the tensor \(\sigma_0\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\otimes\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) in local axes, since \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \cos\theta\) and \(\vek e_\theta\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = -\sin\theta\).

  3. Item 2, constants. The body lies outside the circle, so the outward normal on the edge \(r = a\) is \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) and the force per unit area on the edge of the hole is \(-\ten\sigma\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) with components \(-\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) and \(-\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\). A free edge requires \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(a, \theta) = \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}(a, \theta) = 0\) for every \(\theta\). The sum of the rows of the table at \(r = a\) gives

    \[\begin{gathered} \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(a, \theta) = \Big(\frac{\sigma_0}{2} + \frac{A}{a^2}\Big) + \Big(\frac{\sigma_0}{2} - \frac{6C}{a^4} - \frac{4D}{a^2}\Big)\cos 2\theta , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}(a, \theta) = \Big(-\frac{\sigma_0}{2} - \frac{6C}{a^4} - \frac{2D}{a^2}\Big)\sin 2\theta . \end{gathered}\]

    The expression \(\alpha + \beta\cos 2\theta\) is zero for every \(\theta\) exactly when \(\alpha = \beta = 0\): at \(\theta = \pi/4\) we have \(\cos 2\theta = 0\) and get \(\alpha = 0\), at \(\theta = 0\) we get \(\alpha + \beta = 0\). The expression \(\gamma\sin 2\theta\) is zero for every \(\theta\) exactly when \(\gamma = 0\) (at \(\theta = \pi/4\)). The conditions give three equations

    \[\frac{\sigma_0}{2} + \frac{A}{a^2} = 0 , \qquad \frac{\sigma_0}{2} - \frac{6C}{a^4} - \frac{4D}{a^2} = 0 , \qquad -\frac{\sigma_0}{2} - \frac{6C}{a^4} - \frac{2D}{a^2} = 0 .\]

    The first gives \(A = -a^2\sigma_0/2\). The difference of the second and the third is \(\sigma_0 - 2D/a^2 = 0\), so \(D = a^2\sigma_0/2\), and the third gives \(-\sigma_0/2 - 6C/a^4 - \sigma_0 = 0\), so \(C = -a^4\sigma_0/4\). These are the constants in (11.65), and the edge of the hole is free.

  4. Item 1, substitution. If we insert the constants into the table and add the rows, we get (11.66). For example \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \tfrac{\sigma_0}{2} - \tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}\cos 2\theta - \tfrac{A}{r^2} + 6C\,r^{-4}\cos 2\theta = \tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}\big(1 + \tfrac{a^2}{r^2}\big) - \tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}\big(1 + \tfrac{3a^4}{r^4}\big)\cos 2\theta\).

  5. Item 3, infinity. The first two rows of the table are the uniform field. Rows 3 to 5 are smaller in absolute value than \(\big(|A| + 6|C|/a^2 + 6|D|\big)/r^2\), since \(r \ge a\) gives \(r^{-4} \le a^{-2}\,r^{-2}\) for each term, so they are smaller than \(c_1\,\sigma_0\,a^2/r^2\) with a constant \(c_1\). The Cartesian components are linear combinations of the polar ones with coefficients \(\cos^2\theta\), \(\sin^2\theta\), \(2\sin\theta\cos\theta\) and \(\pm1\) (theorem 2.42), which are at most \(1\) in absolute value. The difference from the uniform field is therefore smaller than \(c\,\sigma_0\,a^2/r^2\) with a constant \(c\).

  6. Item 4. From (11.66) at \(r = a\) we have \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}(a, \theta) = \sigma_0 - 2\sigma_0\cos 2\theta\). The function \(\cos 2\theta\) has its smallest value \(-1\) at \(\theta = \pm\pi/2\), where \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = 3\sigma_0\), its largest value \(1\) at \(\theta = 0\), \(\pi\), where \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = -\sigma_0\), and the value \(\tfrac12\) at \(2\theta = \pm\pi/3\), \(\pm 5\pi/3\), where \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = 0\).

  7. Item 5, strains. Let the constants \(E'\), \(\nu'\) be those of the plane system (11.43). For plane stress (\(E' = E\), \(\nu' = \nu\)) Hooke's law in local axes (corollary 11.26) at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) gives the same form for the local components, and for plane strain the same holds with \(E^*\), \(\nu^*\) (corollary 11.34), because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}) = \nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} + \sigma_{\theta\theta})\), since the sum of the in-plane normal stresses does not change under a rotation of the axes. So \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \nu'\sigma_{\theta\theta})/E'\), \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = (\sigma_{\theta\theta} - \nu'\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}})/E'\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = (1 + \nu')\,\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}/E'\). With the stresses (11.66) we get

    \[\begin{gathered} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = \frac{\sigma_0}{2E'}\Big[(1 - \nu') - (1 + \nu')\frac{a^2}{r^2} \\ + \Big((1 + \nu') - \frac{4a^2}{r^2} + 3(1 + \nu')\frac{a^4}{r^4}\Big)\cos 2\theta\Big] , \end{gathered}\]
    \[\begin{gathered} \varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = \frac{\sigma_0}{2E'}\Big[(1 - \nu') + (1 + \nu')\frac{a^2}{r^2} \\ - \Big((1 + \nu') - \frac{4\nu' a^2}{r^2} + 3(1 + \nu')\frac{a^4}{r^4}\Big)\cos 2\theta\Big] , \end{gathered}\]
    \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -\frac{(1 + \nu')\,\sigma_0}{2E'}\Big(1 + \frac{2a^2}{r^2} - \frac{3a^4}{r^4}\Big)\sin 2\theta .\]

  8. By corollary 11.21 \(\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial r = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}}\). The integral over \(r\) is \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) from (11.68), except that a function \(f(\theta)\) independent of \(r\) is added to it.

  9. From \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = (u_{\mathrm{r}} + \partial u_\theta/\partial\theta)/r\) we get \(\partial u_\theta/\partial\theta = r\,\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} - u_{\mathrm{r}}\). The part without \(\theta\) is therefore \(\tfrac{\sigma_0}{2E'}\big[(1 - \nu')\,r + (1 + \nu')\,a^2/r\big] - \tfrac{\sigma_0}{2E'}\big[(1 - \nu')\,r + (1 + \nu')\,a^2/r\big] = 0\). So \(u_\theta\) has no term that would grow with \(\theta\) and change the displacement after a full turn (for the ring it was given by the term \(B\,r^2\ln r\) in theorem 11.48). The part before \(\cos 2\theta\) is \(\tfrac{\sigma_0}{2E'}\big[-2(1 + \nu')\,r - 4(1 - \nu')\,a^2/r - 2(1 + \nu')\,a^4/r^3\big]\). Integration over \(\theta\), with \(\int\cos 2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \tfrac12\sin 2\theta\), gives \(u_\theta\) from (11.68), to which \(-F(\theta) + g(r)\) with \(F' = f\) is still added.

  10. The remaining relation is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = \tfrac12\big(\tfrac1r\,\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial\theta + \partial u_\theta/\partial r - u_\theta/r\big)\). Let \(P = (1 + \nu')\,r + 4a^2/r - (1 + \nu')\,a^4/r^3\) and \(Q = -(1 + \nu')\,r - 2(1 - \nu')\,a^2/r - (1 + \nu')\,a^4/r^3\), so that \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = \tfrac{\sigma_0}{2E'}\big[\dots + P\cos 2\theta\big]\) and \(u_\theta = \tfrac{\sigma_0}{2E'}\,Q\sin 2\theta + \dots\). Twice the right-hand side in the terms with \(\sin 2\theta\) is \(\tfrac{\sigma_0}{2E'}\big(-2P/r + Q' - Q/r\big)\sin 2\theta\). The terms are \(-2P/r = -2(1 + \nu') - 8a^2/r^2 + 2(1 + \nu')\,a^4/r^4\), \(Q' = -(1 + \nu') + 2(1 - \nu')\,a^2/r^2 + 3(1 + \nu')\,a^4/r^4\) and \(-Q/r = (1 + \nu') + 2(1 - \nu')\,a^2/r^2 + (1 + \nu')\,a^4/r^4\). The sum is \((1 + \nu')\big(-2 - 4a^2/r^2 + 6a^4/r^4\big)\) and half of the expression \(\tfrac{\sigma_0}{2E'}(\dots)\sin 2\theta\) is indeed \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\) from step 7. The remaining terms give \(r\,g' - g = -(F'' + F)\). The left side depends only on \(r\), the right only on \(\theta\), so both equal a constant \(\kappa\). Then \(g = c_3\,r - \kappa\) and \(F = -\kappa + c_1\cos\theta + c_2\sin\theta\), which is a rigid displacement (translation \(f = F'\) and small rotation \(c_3\,r\)) that we leave out.

  11. The functions \(\cos 2\theta\) and \(\sin 2\theta\) have period \(\pi\), so the field (11.68) returns to the same value after a turn \(\theta \to \theta + 2\pi\). The components \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(u_\theta\) are components of the field \(\vek u = u_{\mathrm{r}}\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} + u_\theta\vek e_\theta\), in which \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\vek e_\theta\) are functions of the point, so \(\vek u\) is single-valued too. The constants \(A\), \(C\), \(D\) from step 3 are fixed by the force conditions, so the stresses contain neither \(E\) nor \(\nu\).

Source: SADD, example 8.7, (8.4.11) to (8.4.17), PDF pp. 192 to 194, CM, example 7.5.7, PDF pp. 335 to 337, BARBER §8.4.1, (8.60), PDF p. 133. Displacements: the integration procedure from BARBER §9.2, PDF pp. 141 to 143, where the same computation is done for a hole in a shear field. The formulas (11.68) were computed and checked with SymPy (rbe, part I). Uniqueness of the solution of the infinite plate is not proved.

The proof showed that the three conditions of the free edge determine the three constants exactly, and gave a field that we can check on numbers. Equilibrium and compatibility are consequences of biharmonicity, the free edge of the hole is the first two conditions of step 3, and the uniform field at infinity is the first two rows of the table.

11.13.4 The stress at the hole

For the plate from the beginning \(a = 10\) mm and \(\sigma_0 = 50\) MPa. By (11.67) the hoop stress on the edge of the hole is \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}(a, \theta) = 50\,(1 - 2\cos 2\theta)\) MPa. At \(\theta = 90^\circ\), at the ends of the diameter perpendicular to the pull, it is \(150\) MPa. At \(\theta = 0\), at the ends of the diameter in the direction of the pull, it is \(-50\) MPa. This is compression, although nowhere do we press the plate. It is zero at \(\theta = 30^\circ\), which SADD also writes (PDF p. 194). Figure 11.36 shows the hoop stress around the hole.

The ratio of the largest stress to the stress in the plate without a hole is called the stress concentration factor (faktor koncentracije napetosti), \(K_{\mathrm{t}} = \sigma_{\max}/\sigma_0\), where \(\sigma_{\max}\) is the largest principal stress in the plate. On the edge of the hole \(K_{\mathrm{t}} = 3\). That there is no larger principal stress anywhere in the plate we did not prove. We checked it on a grid of about \(1{,}4\) million points over \(1 \le r/a \le 40\) and \(0 \le \theta \le 2\pi\): the largest principal stress is \(3\sigma_0\) on the edge of the hole, the smallest \(-\sigma_0\) where \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = -\sigma_0\). On the edge of the hole \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\), so the state there is uniaxial and the von Mises stress (definition 2.76) is \(|\sigma_{\theta\theta}| = 150\) MPa. Take a yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa. The von Mises stress is largest on the edge of the hole on the same grid, so the steel starts to yield at the hole when \(3\sigma_0 = 220\) MPa, that is at \(\sigma_0 = 73{,}33\) MPa, a third of the yield stress of the plate without a hole.

We get the Cartesian components on both axes from (11.66). On the \(y\) axis (\(\theta = \pi/2\)) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\theta\theta}\), so

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(0, y) = \sigma_0\Big(1 + \frac{a^2}{2y^2} + \frac{3a^4}{2y^4}\Big) , \tag{11.69}\]

and on the \(x\) axis (\(\theta = 0\)) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\theta\theta}\),

\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(x, 0) &= \sigma_0\Big(1 - \frac{5a^2}{2x^2} + \frac{3a^4}{2x^4}\Big) , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}(x, 0) &= \frac{\sigma_0}{2}\,\frac{a^2}{x^2}\Big(1 - \frac{3a^2}{x^2}\Big) . \end{aligned} \tag{11.70}\]
\(r/a\) \(1\) \(1{,}5\) \(2\) \(3\) \(5\) \(10\)
\(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\sigma_0\) on the \(y\) axis \(3{,}0000\) \(1{,}5185\) \(1{,}2188\) \(1{,}0741\) \(1{,}0224\) \(1{,}0051\)
\(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\sigma_0\) on the \(x\) axis \(0\) \(0{,}1852\) \(0{,}4688\) \(0{,}7407\) \(0{,}9024\) \(0{,}9752\)
\(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}/\sigma_0\) on the \(x\) axis \(-1{,}0000\) \(-0{,}0741\) \(0{,}0313\) \(0{,}0370\) \(0{,}0176\) \(0{,}0049\)

Figure 11.37 shows the same values as curves. On the \(x\) axis \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is slightly negative just next to the hole, since by (11.70) it equals \(\sigma_0\,(1 - a^2/x^2)\,(1 - 3a^2/(2x^2))\), so it is zero at \(x = a\) and at \(x = \sqrt{3/2}\,a\) and has its minimum \(-\sigma_0/24 \approx -0{,}042\,\sigma_0\) at \(x = \sqrt{6/5}\,a \approx 1{,}095\,a\).

How far, then, does the hole disturb the plate? The disturbance is positive on the \(y\) axis and smaller, negative on the \(x\) axis and larger. Why? From (11.69) the leading term on the \(y\) axis is \(+\tfrac12(a/r)^2\). It comes only from the term \(A\ln r\) in (11.64), since the term \(D\cos 2\theta\) gives \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = 0\) (the table of step 2). On the \(x\) axis by (11.70) the leading term is \(-\tfrac52(a/r)^2\), composed of the term \(A\ln r\) with \(-\tfrac12\) and the term \(D\cos 2\theta\) with \(-2\), which have the same sign there. The deviation from \(\sigma_0\) is at most \(5\) % at \(r \ge 3{,}53\,a\) on the \(y\) axis and \(r \ge 7{,}03\,a\) on the \(x\) axis, and at most \(1\) % at \(7{,}27\,a\) and \(15{,}79\,a\) (solutions of (11.69) and (11.70)). For the hoop stress on the \(y\) axis SADD writes that the disturbance essentially disappears at \(r > 5a\) (PDF p. 194), which corresponds to \(2{,}2\) % at \(r = 5a\).

Where does the force go that the hole cannot carry? Through the section \(x = 0\), in the plate without a hole, a force \(2a\,\sigma_0\) per unit thickness passes over the width \(2a\). The excess of stress at the hole is by (11.69)

\[2\int_{\mathrm{a}}^\infty \big(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(0, y) - \sigma_0\big)\,\mathrm{d}y = 2\sigma_0\int_{\mathrm{a}}^\infty\Big(\frac{a^2}{2y^2} + \frac{3a^4}{2y^4}\Big)\mathrm{d}y = 2\sigma_0\Big(\frac a2 + \frac a2\Big) = 2a\,\sigma_0 ,\]

exactly what the cut-out part would carry. Here \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^\infty y^{-2}\,\mathrm{d}y = 1/a\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^\infty y^{-4}\,\mathrm{d}y = 1/(3a^3)\). The force that would pass through the hole therefore flows past it along the narrow ligaments next to the hole, and the ligaments carry more than they would without the hole.

Why does the disturbance decay like \((a/r)^2\) and not exponentially, as in the strip in section 11.11? The field (11.66) is the sum of the uniform field and a disturbance. The uniform field on the edge of the hole (outward normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\)) has the force per unit area \(-\ten\sigma^{(0)}\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\), and the sum must be zero, so the load of the disturbance on the edge of the hole is \(+\ten\sigma^{(0)}\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\). This load is self-equilibrated (definition 11.44). Its resultant over the circle is \(a\,\ten\sigma^{(0)}\int_0^{2\pi}\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \vek 0\), since the components \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) cancel over the full circle. The moment about the centre has only the component \(a^2\int_0^{2\pi}\sigma^{(0)}_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\,\mathrm{d}\theta = -\tfrac{a^2\sigma_0}{2}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin 2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = 0\). The disturbance is therefore the response to a self-equilibrated load on a part of the edge of size \(2a\), as in section 11.11, and we computed that the stress decays. It decays algebraically because among the functions of lemma 11.47 with angular dependence \(1\) and \(\cos 2\theta\) the slowest decaying is \(\ln r\), with stresses that decay like \(r^{-2}\). SADD gives the same rate \(O(1/r^2)\) for a hole under pressure (PDF p. 191). In the strip the decaying solutions with a complex exponent \(\lambda\) remain (lemma 11.45), because the conditions of the free edges of the strip give an equation for \(\lambda\) with such solutions.

From history

The stresses around a circular hole in a plate that is pulled uniformly in one direction were analysed by G. Kirsch in 1898 (TIMO, PDF p. 346, footnote). He showed that the largest stress is on the edge of the hole, at the ends of the diameter perpendicular to the direction of the pull, and that it is three times larger than the applied stress (TIMO, PDF p. 346). According to the text of TIMO it was thereby probably shown for the first time how essential it is to study the local irregularities in the stress distribution produced by holes, and since then engineers have studied stress concentrations intensively, theoretically and experimentally (TIMO, PDF p. 346). With our numbers this means that the stress far from the hole is \(50\) MPa and right next to the hole \(150\) MPa, and a computation with the average over the cross section does not detect this. The plate of finite width with a hole on the axis of symmetry was considered by R. C. J. Howland (TIMO, PDF p. 346), and we replaced it by an infinite plate.

We looked at a plate with a hole under a pull of \(50\) MPa and asked for the stress at the hole and the reach of the disturbance. The Kirsch field gave \(3\sigma_0 = 150\) MPa on the edge of the hole and a disturbance that decays like \((a/r)^2\), and the history showed why this computation was important. We now use the same field for two other loads.

11.13.5 Biaxial tension and pure shear

A plate in a structure is often pulled in two directions or loaded in shear. Linearity of the equations lets us obtain these two fields from the Kirsch field without a new computation. The equations and the boundary condition of the free edge in polar coordinates do not contain the angle \(\theta\) explicitly (lemma 11.46), so besides \(\varphi(r, \theta)\) also \(\varphi(r, \theta - \pi/2)\) is a solution, namely for the pull \(\tau\) in the direction of the \(y\) axis. Since \(\cos 2(\theta - \tfrac{\pi}{2}) = -\cos 2\theta\) and \(\sin 2(\theta - \tfrac{\pi}{2}) = -\sin 2\theta\), the components of the rotated field are

\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} &= \frac{\tau}{2}\Big(1 - \frac{a^2}{r^2}\Big) - \frac{\tau}{2}\Big(1 - \frac{4a^2}{r^2} + \frac{3a^4}{r^4}\Big)\cos 2\theta , \\ \sigma_{\theta\theta} &= \frac{\tau}{2}\Big(1 + \frac{a^2}{r^2}\Big) + \frac{\tau}{2}\Big(1 + \frac{3a^4}{r^4}\Big)\cos 2\theta , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} &= \frac{\tau}{2}\Big(1 + \frac{2a^2}{r^2} - \frac{3a^4}{r^4}\Big)\sin 2\theta . \end{aligned} \tag{11.71}\]
Corollary 11.52 A hole in a biaxial and a shear field (luknja v dvoosnem in strižnem polju)

Let the plate be as in theorem 11.51. Then:

  1. The field (11.66), added to the field (11.71) for \(\tau = \sigma_0\), has a free edge of the hole and at infinity the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} \to \sigma_0\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} \to \sigma_0\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} \to 0\) (biaxial tension). Its stresses are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \sigma_0\,(1 - a^2/r^2)\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_0\,(1 + a^2/r^2)\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\). On the edge of the hole \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}(a, \theta) = 2\sigma_0\) for every \(\theta\), so \(K_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\).
  2. The field (11.66), added to the field (11.71) for \(\tau = -\sigma_0\), has a free edge of the hole and at infinity the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} \to \sigma_0\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} \to -\sigma_0\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} \to 0\) (pure shear \(\sigma_0\) on planes rotated by \(45^\circ\)). Its stresses are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \sigma_0\,(1 - 4a^2/r^2 + 3a^4/r^4)\cos 2\theta\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = -\sigma_0\,(1 + 3a^4/r^4)\cos 2\theta\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -\sigma_0\,(1 + 2a^2/r^2 - 3a^4/r^4)\sin 2\theta\). On the edge of the hole \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}(a, \theta) = -4\sigma_0\cos 2\theta\), the largest value is \(4\sigma_0\) at \(\theta = \pm\pi/2\), so \(K_{\mathrm{t}} = 4\).
Proof

We must show that the sum satisfies the conditions of theorem 11.51 with the second condition at infinity. The idea is linearity.

  1. The field (11.71) is a solution: under the replacement \(\theta \to \theta - \pi/2\) the polar equations from lemma 11.46 and the condition \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(a, \cdot) = \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}(a, \cdot) = 0\) are preserved, because \(\theta\) does not appear in them explicitly. The displacements rotate in the same way, so they stay single-valued. At infinity the uniform field \(\sigma_0\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\otimes\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) is rotated into \(\tau\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\otimes\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) (theorem 2.42).
  2. The equations of equilibrium, Hooke's law and compatibility are linear and the edge of the hole is free for both fields, so the sum of the solutions is a solution of this problem with the sum of the data at infinity (the idea of corollary 11.3, without uniqueness, because the plate is infinite). For \(\tau = \sigma_0\) the terms with \(\cos 2\theta\) and \(\sin 2\theta\) cancel and the terms without the angle add: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = 2\cdot\tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}(1 - a^2/r^2)\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = 2\cdot\tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}(1 + a^2/r^2)\). For \(\tau = -\sigma_0\) the terms without the angle cancel and the terms with \(\cos 2\theta\) and \(\sin 2\theta\) add.
  3. At \(r = a\) by (11.67) and (11.71) \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_0\,(1 - 2\cos 2\theta) + \tau\,(1 + 2\cos 2\theta)\). For \(\tau = \sigma_0\) this is \(2\sigma_0\), for \(\tau = -\sigma_0\) it is \(-4\sigma_0\cos 2\theta\).
  4. The tensor \(\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_0, -\sigma_0)\) in axes rotated by \(45^\circ\) has by theorem 2.42 normal components \(0\) and a shear component of absolute value \(\sigma_0\). This is pure shear.

Source: SADD, §8.4.2 and §8.4.3, (8.4.9), (8.4.10), (8.4.18), PDF pp. 191 to 192 and 195 to 196.

Why is biaxial tension more favourable than uniaxial, and shear less favourable? Look at the end of the vertical diameter, \(\theta = 90^\circ\). The pull in the direction \(x\) gives \(3\sigma_0\) there, and the pull \(\tau\) in the direction \(y\) gives \(\tau\,(1 + 2\cos 180^\circ) = -\tau\). For \(\tau = \sigma_0\) the sum is \(2\sigma_0\): the pull in the direction \(y\) lowers the stress there, because at the end of the horizontal diameter it has its concentration, and at the end of the vertical diameter compression. For \(\tau = -\sigma_0\) the sum is \(3\sigma_0 + \sigma_0 = 4\sigma_0\), because the compression in the direction \(y\) raises the stress there. SADD remarks that an additional pull in the other direction lowers the concentration (PDF p. 194). Figure 11.38 shows the hoop stress for all three fields.

The field (11.71) at \(\tau = \sigma_0\) is in the sum of item 1 the field of the Lamé tube from theorem 11.27 at \(p_{\mathrm{a}} = 0\) and \(p_{\mathrm{b}} = -\sigma_0\) (tensile pressure), when the outer radius \(b \to \infty\): the constants (11.34) are then \(A \to \sigma_0\) and \(B \to \sigma_0\,a^2\) and the stresses (11.36) are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \sigma_0\,(1 - a^2/r^2)\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_0\,(1 + a^2/r^2)\). This agrees with item 1 and is the path by which SADD derives this field (PDF p. 191).

11.13.6 The finite plate

The Kirsch field is a solution for the infinite plate. The plate from the introduction is \(200 \times 200\) mm with a hole of radius \(a = 10\) mm, so the middle of the edge is \(10\) radii from the centre. What error do we make if we take the plate to be infinite?

The real plate has on the edge \(x = \pm 100\) mm a force per unit area \(\sigma_0\) in the direction \(x\) and \(0\) in the direction \(y\), and on the edge \(y = \pm 100\) mm it has \(0\). We compute the Kirsch field at the points of the edge by (11.66) and rotate it into Cartesian components (theorem 2.42). On the edge \(x = 100\) mm \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) lies between \(48{,}758\) and \(50{,}248\) MPa, and the shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is up to \(0{,}574\) MPa in absolute value, instead of \(50\) and \(0\). On the edge \(y = 100\) mm \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}| \le 0{,}743\) MPa and \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}| \le 0{,}291\) MPa, instead of \(0\) (rbe, part I). The largest deviation is therefore \(1{,}242\) MPa, which is \(2{,}5\) % of the stress \(\sigma_0\). Why exactly this much? The middle of the edge \(x = 100\) mm is on the \(x\) axis at \(r = 10a\) and (11.70) gives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_0\,\big(1 - \tfrac52\cdot 10^{-2} + \tfrac32\cdot 10^{-4}\big) = 0{,}97515\,\sigma_0 = 48{,}758\) MPa. The largest deviation is therefore the leading term of the disturbance \(-\tfrac52(a/r)^2\) at \(r = 10a\). Figure 11.39 shows the forces on the edge that the Kirsch field requires, with the deviation enlarged \(20\) times.

What does this say about the real plate? The Kirsch field solves the problem of the \(200 \times 200\) mm plate with an edge load that differs from the real one by \(\Delta\bar{\vek t}\), and this is at most \(2{,}5\) % of \(\sigma_0\) in absolute value. If the problem of the plate with the edge load \(-\Delta\bar{\vek t}\) and a free hole has a solution (existence is not proved in the book, section 11.1), the real solution is the sum of the Kirsch field and this solution by corollary 11.3, and by theorem 11.4 it is the only one (the finite plate is a bounded body). The load \(\Delta\bar{\vek t}\) is self-equilibrated: the Kirsch field is in equilibrium in a plate with a free hole, so the forces on the outer edge have resultant and moment zero, and the same holds for two opposite uniform pulls. By the principle of Saint-Venant (section 11.11) we expect the correction at the hole, which is \(10\) radii away from the edge, to be small. We do not compute the correction in the interior. We computed only the error of the load on the edge, at most \(2{,}5\) % of \(\sigma_0\). The plate of finite width with a hole was considered by Howland (TIMO, PDF p. 346).

SADD writes that the solution of the infinite plate is a good approximation for finite plates with edges that are more than about five radii from the centre of the hole (PDF p. 196). Our numbers complement this rule: at \(5a\) the deviation is still \(9{,}8\) % on the \(x\) axis and \(2{,}2\) % on the \(y\) axis, and at \(10a\) it is \(2{,}5\) % on the \(x\) axis. The rule of five radii therefore holds for the order of magnitude of the error and not for accuracy below a few per cent.

11.13.7 What we have shown

The question was how large the stress at the hole is and how far the hole disturbs the plate. With the Airy function in polar coordinates we built a field that has a free hole and a uniform pull at infinity: the function of the uniform field, three biharmonic functions that decay, and three equations from the free edge. The field is constructed and checked, but not proved to be the only one. The hoop stress on the edge of the hole is \(\sigma_0\,(1 - 2\cos 2\theta)\) with the largest value \(3\sigma_0 = 150\) MPa and the smallest \(-50\) MPa, and the disturbance decays like \((a/r)^2\), on the \(y\) axis to \(2{,}2\) % at \(5a\) and on the \(x\) axis to \(9{,}8\) % at \(5a\). The stresses do not depend on \(E\) and \(\nu\). A hole in a biaxial field gives \(2\sigma_0\), in a shear field \(4\sigma_0\). The \(200 \times 200\) mm plate deviates from the infinite one by at most \(2{,}5\) % of the stress \(\sigma_0\) on the edge, and the first yield is at \(\sigma_0 = 73{,}33\) MPa.

11.14 The curved beam

The ring of chapter 4 is a steel ring with inner radius \(a = 40\) mm, outer radius \(b = 60\) mm and thickness \(t = 2\) mm. There we cut it with a plane through the axis and showed that the cut ring is simply connected (lemma 4.109). Now we leave the cut open and attach one couple to each of the two faces of the cut, so that the couples open or close the ring. This gives a curved beam (ukrivljeni nosilec): a body whose axis is a circular arc. The axis runs midway between the inner and the outer edge, that is along the radius \(c = (a + b)/2 = 50\) mm, and the height of the section is \(h = b - a = 20\) mm.
