Chapter 5 treated straight beams and named, as a limit of its theory, the exact plane solutions of elasticity that this chapter provides. For a circular edge the polar form of the Airy function from section 11.12 is suitable.

Does the formula \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = N/A - M\,y/I\) of theorem 5.35 hold for this beam? Let us see what the formula assumes. In a straight beam all fibres between two sections have the same length. When the two sections turn against each other, each fibre is lengthened or shortened by a displacement proportional to its distance from the axis, and so the strain is proportional to the distance from the axis. In our piece the inner fibre (\(r = 40\) mm) between two sections that enclose an angle \(\Delta\theta\) (in radians, definition 8.7) is \(40\,\Delta\theta\) mm long and the outer one (\(r = 60\) mm) is \(60\,\Delta\theta\) mm long, that is half as long again. So we expect the formula to be wrong for this beam, and the question is by how much. The answer comes from the exact solution of the plane problem, not from a model of the section. We compute it with the Airy function in polar coordinates and compare it with the formula.

11.14.1 Internal forces of a curved beam

First we agree on what the force and the moment on a section of a curved beam are, so that the comparison with chapter 5 has the same sign. A curved beam is a piece of an annulus \(a \le r \le b\), \(\theta_1 \le \theta \le \theta_2\) with \(\theta_2 - \theta_1 < 2\pi\) (figure 11.40), in plane stress (definition 11.32). The section at angle \(\theta\) is the radial segment \(\theta = \text{const}\), \(a \le r \le b\). Chapter 5 defined the internal forces of a straight beam as the resultant and the moment of the stress vector on the face with outward normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), that is as what the part at larger \(x\) exerts on the part at smaller \(x\) (lemma 5.9). We take the same rule here, only the direction of the axis of the beam is \(\vek e_\theta\) instead of \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The stress vector on the face with normal \(+\vek e_\theta\) is \(\ten\sigma\,\vek e_\theta = \sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\vek e_\theta + \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\), because the first index gives the normal of the face (definition 11.19). The centroid of the section is at the point \(r = c\) (definition 5.21). The point of the section with radius \(r\) has the position vector \((r - c)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) relative to the centroid, and since \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\times\vek e_\theta = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) in the right-handed system \((r, \theta, z)\), the \(z\) component of the moment of the stress vector of this point is \((r - c)\,\sigma_{\theta\theta}\). The shear force \(V\) is the component of the resultant in the direction of the axis \(y\) of chapter 5. Since this axis points here towards the centre \(O\) (\(\vek e_\theta\times(-\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}) = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), as \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) for a straight beam), it is the component in the direction \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\). We compute the plane problem per unit thickness, so the integrals run over \(r\) only. Plane stress is a model of a thin plate: the stresses of this section are stresses of the model, and by theorem 11.35 they are averages over the thickness of the exact three-dimensional solution when \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\).

Definition 11.53 Internal forces of a curved beam (notranje količine ukrivljenega nosilca)

Let a curved beam be a piece of an annulus \(a \le r \le b\), \(\theta_1 \le \theta \le \theta_2\) with \(\theta_2 - \theta_1 < 2\pi\), of an isotropic, homogeneous, linearly elastic material in plane stress, and let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\) be continuous functions on it. Let \(c = (a + b)/2\) be the radius of the centroids of the sections and \(t\) the thickness of the beam. The internal forces of the section at \(\theta\) are the axial force, the shear force and the bending moment per unit thickness,

\[\begin{aligned} N(\theta) &= \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r , \\ V(\theta) &= -\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r , \\ M(\theta) &= \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b (r - c)\,\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r . \end{aligned} \tag{11.72}\]

These are the component \(\vek e_\theta\) and the component \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) (the direction of the axis \(y\)) of the resultant and the component \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) of the moment about the centroid of the stress vector \(\ten\sigma\,\vek e_\theta\) on the section, per unit thickness. At thickness \(t\) the force and the moment of the beam are \(t\,N\), \(t\,V\) and \(t\,M\).

Source: The definition is ours, by the same rule as lemma 5.9. SADD (8.4.58) (PDF p. 211, crop read) writes \(\int\sigma_\theta\,r\,\mathrm{d}r = -M\), so with the opposite sign to this definition, by which \(\int\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,r\,\mathrm{d}r = M\) at zero axial force. BARBER (10.9) (PDF p. 150, crop read) has \(\int\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,r\,\mathrm{d}r = M_0\), like us.

What does the sign mean? At \(M > 0\) we have \(\int (r - c)\,\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r > 0\), so the hoop stress is larger at larger \(r\): the outer fibres are more in tension, the inner ones more in compression, and the couples close the piece of the annulus, that is they increase its curvature. For the straight beam of chapter 5 it is the same: at \(M > 0\) we have \(v'' > 0\), the beam bends towards the positive direction of the axis \(y\) and the fibres on that side are compressed (figure 5.36). In the curved beam the axis \(y\), which forms a right-handed system with the axis of the beam \(\vek e_\theta\) (\(\vek e_\theta\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\)), points towards the centre \(O\), so \(y = c - r\), and \(M = -\int y\,\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r\) is the same expression as in lemma 5.9. The elementary formula (5.25) at \(A = h\) and \(I = h^3/12\) gives for a beam that would be straight

\[\sigma_{\theta\theta} \approx \frac{N}{h} + \frac{12\,M}{h^3}\,(r - c) , \tag{11.73}\]

and this is the object of comparison in this section. For the beam made of the ring with \(h = 20\) mm the largest hoop stress at \(N = 0\) is \(6\,|M|/h^2\) at both edges.

11.14.2 Pure bending

First take a beam loaded at its ends by couples only, without force. The part of the beam between the end \(\theta_1\) and the section at \(\theta_0\) is in equilibrium: the field on it is the solution of the boundary value problem for this part with the data that it itself gives. On it are the load of the end \(\theta_1\), the free arcs \(r = a\) and \(r = b\) and the stress vector \(\ten\sigma\,\vek e_\theta\) on the section at \(\theta_0\). By lemma 11.2 the sum of the forces is zero. The load of the end has no force resultant, so \(N(\theta_0) = V(\theta_0) = 0\) on every section. With zero resultant the moment does not depend on the point about which we measure it (lemma 2.34). The end \(\theta_1\) has the outward normal \(-\vek e_\theta\), its stress vector is therefore \(-\ten\sigma\,\vek e_\theta\) and its moment is \(-M(\theta_1)\). The sum of the moments is zero, so \(M(\theta_0) - M(\theta_1) = 0\): the moment is the same on every section, \(M(\theta_0) = M\). Since all sections are loaded in the same way, we look for stresses that do not depend on the angle \(\theta\), that is for an Airy function \(\varphi(r)\). By lemma 11.47 such functions are combinations of the functions \(\ln r\), \(r^2\ln r\) and \(r^2\), that is the function of theorem 11.48. There the term \(B\,r^2\ln r\) is forbidden in a whole ring, because its displacement \(u_\theta = 4B\,r\,\theta/E\) is not equal to the initial one after a circuit around the hole. Our beam is a piece of an annulus with \(\theta_2 - \theta_1 < 2\pi\), where the points at \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) are different, so there is no jump here and the term is allowed.

Theorem 11.54 Pure bending of a curved beam (čisti upogib ukrivljenega nosilca)

Let the curved beam be as in definition 11.53, of an isotropic, homogeneous, linearly elastic material with \(E > 0\) and \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\) in plane stress, without body force. Let \(M\) be a real number, \(L = \ln(b/a)\) and

\[\Delta = (b^2 - a^2)^2 - 4\,a^2 b^2 L^2 .\]

Then:

  1. \(\Delta > 0\) and the function \(\varphi = A\ln(r/a) + B\,r^2\ln(r/a) + C\,r^2\) with
    \[\begin{aligned} A &= \frac{4M\,a^2 b^2 L}{\Delta} , \\ B &= \frac{2M\,(b^2 - a^2)}{\Delta} , \\ C &= \frac{M\,(a^2 - b^2 - 2b^2 L)}{\Delta} \end{aligned} \tag{11.74}\]
    is the only function of this form for which the faces \(r = a\) and \(r = b\) are free and \(M(\theta) = M\),
  2. the stresses given by \(\varphi\) are
    \[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} &= \frac{4M}{\Delta}\Big[\frac{a^2 b^2}{r^2}\,L + b^2\ln\frac rb \\ &\quad + a^2\ln\frac ar\Big] , \\ \sigma_{\theta\theta} &= \frac{4M}{\Delta}\Big[-\frac{a^2 b^2}{r^2}\,L + b^2\ln\frac rb \\ &\quad + a^2\ln\frac ar + b^2 - a^2\Big] , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} &= 0 , \end{aligned} \tag{11.75}\]
    do not depend on \(\theta\) and satisfy equilibrium,
  3. on every section \(N(\theta) = 0\), \(V(\theta) = 0\) and \(M(\theta) = M\), the faces \(r = a\) and \(r = b\) are free,
  4. the stress field (11.75) is the only stress field of the beam whose arcs are free and whose ends carry the stress vector \(\mp\sigma_{\theta\theta}(r)\,\vek e_\theta\) from item 2, and the displacement is unique up to a rigid motion,
  5. the sections \(\theta = \text{const}\) stay plane to first order: the displacement \(u_\theta\) is a linear function of \(r\) on every section, the section at \(\theta\) turns by \(4B\,\theta/E + W\) with some rigid rotation \(W\), so the sections at \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) turn against each other by \(4B\,(\theta_2 - \theta_1)/E\).
Proof

We have to show that the constants (11.74) solve the three conditions, that the stresses satisfy equilibrium and that the displacement field exists. For the displacements we use theorem 11.48. Since \(r^2\ln r = r^2\ln(r/a) + r^2\ln a\) and \(\ln r = \ln(r/a) + \ln a\), the function of theorem 11.48 with its own constants \(A\), \(B\), \(C_0\) equals the function \(\varphi\) of this theorem with \(C = C_0 + B\ln a\) up to a constant that gives no stresses. The stresses are therefore by that theorem \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = A/r^2 + B\,(1 + 2\ln(r/a)) + 2C\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = -A/r^2 + B\,(3 + 2\ln(r/a)) + 2C\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\).

  1. By lemma 11.46, for \(\varphi(r)\) the stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \varphi'/r\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \varphi''\). The arcs \(r = a\) and \(r = b\) have the outward normal \(\mp\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) and the stress vector \(\mp(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\,\vek e_\theta)\), so they are free exactly when \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(a) = \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(b) = 0\) (the shear stress is zero everywhere). This is \(\varphi'(a) = \varphi'(b) = 0\).
  2. By the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.40) \(N = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b\varphi''\,\mathrm{d}r = \varphi'(b) - \varphi'(a) = 0\). For the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b r\,\varphi''\,\mathrm{d}r\) we have \((r\varphi')' = \varphi' + r\varphi''\), so \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b r\varphi''\,\mathrm{d}r = \big[r\varphi'\big]_{\mathrm{a}}^b - \big[\varphi\big]_{\mathrm{a}}^b = \varphi(a) - \varphi(b)\). At \(N = 0\) we get \(M(\theta) = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b (r - c)\,\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b r\,\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r - c\,N = \varphi(a) - \varphi(b)\). Free arcs and zero axial force therefore follow from the form of the function, and the condition \(\varphi(a) - \varphi(b) = M\) remains.
  3. The conditions are three linear equations for \(A\), \(B\), \(C\). From \(\varphi' = A/r + 2B\,r\ln(r/a) + B\,r + 2C\,r\) the condition \(\varphi'(a) = 0\) is \(A/a^2 + B + 2C = 0\) and \(\varphi'(b) = 0\) is \(A/b^2 + B\,(1 + 2L) + 2C = 0\). The difference of the two is \(A\,(1/b^2 - 1/a^2) + 2BL = 0\), so \(A = 2BL\,a^2 b^2/(b^2 - a^2)\). The first equation gives \(C = -\tfrac12\,(A/a^2 + B)\).
  4. The function has \(\varphi(a) = C\,a^2\) and \(\varphi(b) = A L + B\,b^2 L + C\,b^2\), so \(\varphi(a) - \varphi(b) = -AL - B\,b^2 L - C\,(b^2 - a^2)\). We insert \(C\) from step 3: \(M = A\big[\frac{b^2 - a^2}{2a^2} - L\big] + B\big[\frac{b^2 - a^2}{2} - b^2 L\big]\). With \(A\) from step 3 the first term is \(B L b^2 - 2BL^2 a^2 b^2/(b^2 - a^2)\), and the sum of both terms is \(M = B\big[\frac{b^2 - a^2}{2} - \frac{2a^2 b^2 L^2}{b^2 - a^2}\big] = \frac{B\,\Delta}{2\,(b^2 - a^2)}\).
  5. \(\Delta > 0\): we factor \(\Delta = (b^2 - a^2 - 2abL)(b^2 - a^2 + 2abL)\). The second factor is positive, because \(b > a\) and \(L > 0\). At \(s = b/a > 1\) the first factor is \(a^2 s\,k(s)\) with \(k(s) = s - 1/s - 2\ln s\), \(k(1) = 0\) and \(k'(s) = 1 + 1/s^2 - 2/s = (1 - 1/s)^2 > 0\) for \(s > 1\). By the mean value theorem (theorem 1.84) \(k(s) - k(1) = k'(\xi)\,(s - 1) > 0\), so \(k(s) > 0\) and \(\Delta > 0\). Therefore step 4 gives \(B = 2M\,(b^2 - a^2)/\Delta\), step 3 gives \(A = 4M\,a^2 b^2 L/\Delta\) and \(C = M\,(a^2 - b^2 - 2b^2 L)/\Delta\), and all steps were equivalent transformations. This is item 1.
  6. We insert into the stresses. For \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) the sum is
    \[\begin{gathered} \frac{M}{\Delta}\big[\frac{4a^2 b^2 L}{r^2} + 2(b^2 - a^2)\,(1 + 2\ln\frac ra) + 2(a^2 - b^2 - 2b^2 L)\big] \\ = \frac{4M}{\Delta}\big[\frac{a^2 b^2 L}{r^2} + (b^2 - a^2)\ln\frac ra - b^2 L\big] \end{gathered}\]
    and the last two terms are \(b^2\ln\frac rb + a^2\ln\frac ar\), because \(\ln\frac ra - L = \ln\frac rb\). For \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) the sum is \(3B + 2C = \frac{M}{\Delta}\,(4(b^2 - a^2) - 4b^2 L)\) and the same writing of the terms with logarithms. This is (11.75). Equilibrium and \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\) hold by item 1 of theorem 11.48, and the stresses do not depend on \(\theta\).
  7. Item 3: \(N = 0\) and \(M(\theta) = M\) by step 2, \(V = 0\) because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\). The arcs are free by step 1.
  8. Item 4. The stresses are continuous, they satisfy equilibrium without body force (step 6), the arcs are free and the ends carry the prescribed stress vector, so the field is a solution of the traction problem (definition 11.1 with empty \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\)). If any solution has the same data, it has by theorem 11.4 the same stresses, and the displacement differs by a small rigid motion. That the displacement exists is shown by theorem 11.48, item 2: the field (11.62) satisfies all three strain equations identically (checked with SymPy) and on a piece with \(\theta_2 - \theta_1 < 2\pi\) it is a function of the point.
  9. Item 5. From (11.62) the displacement on the section \(\theta = \theta_0\) is \(u_\theta = (4B\,\theta_0/E + W)\,r - Q\sin\theta_0 + P\cos\theta_0\), a linear function of \(r\) (the terms with \(Q\) and \(P\) are constant at given \(\theta_0\)). The point with radius \(r\) therefore moves by \(u_{\mathrm{r}}(r)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} + u_\theta(r)\,\vek e_\theta\). The radial part moves it only along the section, and the tangential part \(u_\theta\) is a linear function of the original \(r\). Expressed with the new radius \(r + u_{\mathrm{r}}\) it differs from a linear function by a product of two small quantities (the rotation and \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\)), which we neglect to first order, so the section stays plane and turns by \(\partial u_\theta/\partial r = 4B\,\theta_0/E + W\). The difference of the rotations at \(\theta_2\) and \(\theta_1\) is \(4B\,(\theta_2 - \theta_1)/E\).

Source: SADD example 8.9, (8.4.58)-(8.4.61) (PDF pp. 211 to 212, crops (8.4.58) and (8.4.64) read, the form of the solution in SADD has constants \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) and \(N\) from (8.4.60), \(N_{\text{SADD}}\) is our \(\Delta\) up to the order of the terms). BARBER §10.1.1, (10.1)-(10.16) (PDF pp. 149 to 151). The form (11.75) with logarithms was checked with SymPy (the difference of the two forms is zero) and with the form from TIMO in rbe.py part J. The sign of \(M\) is ours (definition 11.53), SADD has \(\int\sigma_\theta\,r\,\mathrm{d}r = -M\), BARBER (10.9) has \(\int\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,r\,\mathrm{d}r = M_0\) as we do. Steps 2 (with \(\int r\varphi''\,\mathrm{d}r\)) and 5 (\(\Delta > 0\)) are ours, SADD and BARBER solve the linear system in words only.

The proof showed three things. The conditions of free arcs and zero force are already satisfied by the form of the function \(\varphi(r)\), since \(\varphi'(a) = \varphi'(b) = 0\) is enough for \(N = 0\). The moment gives only the difference \(\varphi(a) - \varphi(b)\). And the exact solution has sections that stay plane, like the elementary theory, but a different distribution of stress. Let us take the ring of chapter 4.

Example 11.55 The cut ring under couples (obroč z rezom pod dvojicama)

Take the ring with \(a = 40\) mm, \(b = 60\) mm, \(t = 2\) mm of steel with \(E = 196\) GPa and, at the ends of the cut, couples that open the ring, with total moment \(t\,M = -5\) N m. The sign is negative, because by definition 11.53 the couples open the piece, the outer fibres are in compression and the inner ones in tension. Per unit thickness \(M = -5000\ \text{N mm}/2\ \text{mm} = -2500\) N.

  1. At \(L = \ln 1{,}5 = 0{,}405465\) we have \(\Delta = 2000^2 - 4\cdot 1600\cdot 3600\cdot L^2 = 212\,179\ \text{mm}^4\) (SymPy), positive, as it must be. The constants (11.74) are \(A = -110\,071\ \text{N}\), \(B = -47{,}13\ \text{N/mm}^2\) and \(C = 57{,}96\ \text{N/mm}^2\) (units N and mm, stresses in MPa).
  2. The stresses (11.75) at five radii (in MPa) and the elementary formula (11.73), which at \(N = 0\) equals \(12\,M\,(r - c)/h^3 = -3{,}75\,(r - 50)\) MPa at \(r\) in mm:
\(r\) [mm] 40 45 50 55 60
\(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) (exact) \(43{,}33\) \(17{,}79\) \(-2{,}47\) \(-19{,}10\) \(-33{,}11\)
\(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) (elementary) \(37{,}50\) \(18{,}75\) \(0\) \(-18{,}75\) \(-37{,}50\)
\(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) (exact) \(0\) \(3{,}34\) \(3{,}73\) \(2{,}39\) \(0\)
  1. At the inner edge the exact stress is \(15{,}5\,\%\) larger than the elementary one (\(43{,}33/37{,}50 = 1{,}155\)), at the outer edge \(11{,}7\,\%\) smaller in absolute value (\(33{,}11/37{,}50 = 0{,}883\)). The elementary formula underestimates the inner edge and overestimates the outer one. The stress is zero at \(r = 49{,}33\) mm (SymPy), \(0{,}67\) mm towards the centre from the centroid at \(50\) mm. The conditions of the theorem are confirmed by SymPy: \(\int_{40}^{60}\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r = 0\) and \(\int_{40}^{60}\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,r\,\mathrm{d}r = -2500\) N, which is \(M\) at \(N = 0\).

Figure 11.41 shows this example. The hoop stress is not a linear function of \(r\) but curves around the zero, and next to it is the radial stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\), which the elementary formula does not know.

Why is the inner fibre loaded more? Take two sections that enclose an angle \(\Delta\theta\). Since they stay plane, the displacement of the points of the section along the axis varies linearly with the radius, so the fibre at radius \(r\) is lengthened by \(\Delta\omega\,(r - r_0)\), where \(\Delta\omega\) is the relative rotation of the sections and \(r_0\) the radius of the fibre without elongation. The length of the fibre before loading is \(r\,\Delta\theta\), so the strain is

\[\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} \approx \frac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta\theta}\,\frac{r - r_0}{r} .\]

In a straight beam the denominator would be constant, here it is \(r\), so the same elongation at the inner fibre (\(r = 40\)) is spread over a shorter length than at the outer one (\(r = 60\)). In the exact solution \(r\,\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = r\,(\sigma_{\theta\theta} - \nu\,\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}})/E\) is a linear function of \(r\) to within \(1{,}5\,\%\) of its range (SymPy), so the idea holds. At \(r_0 = 49{,}33\) mm the ratio \((r - r_0)/r\) between the inner and the outer edge is in absolute value \((9{,}33/40)/(10{,}67/60) = 0{,}2333/0{,}1778 = 1{,}31\). At both edges \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = 0\), so the ratio of the strains of the inner and the outer fibre equals the ratio of the stresses, \(43{,}33/33{,}11 = 1{,}31\), while the elementary formula gives \(1\). The elementary theory gets the rotation of the sections right: by item 5 of the theorem the relative rotation of the sections per radian of the angle between them is \(4|B|/E = 9{,}618\cdot 10^{-4}\), and the elementary formula (\(12\,|M|\,c/(E h^3)\), because the distance between the sections on the axis is \(c\,\Delta\theta\) and the rotation per unit length is \(12\,|M|/(E h^3)\)) gives \(9{,}566\cdot 10^{-4}\), the difference is \(0{,}54\,\%\). The rotation of the sections is therefore almost exact in the elementary theory, but the stress at the edge is not.

The radial stresses, which the elementary formula does not contain, have their cause in equilibrium. The first equilibrium equation in cylindrical coordinates (corollary 11.24) at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\) and independence of \(\theta\) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}' + (\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \sigma_{\theta\theta})/r = 0\), which is \((r\,\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}})' = \sigma_{\theta\theta}\). At the inner edge \(r\,\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = 0\). As long as \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} > 0\) (inner fibres, tension), \(r\,\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) grows, that is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) is tensile. A fibre in hoop tension is curved and pulls towards the centre of curvature \(O\), so it separates from the layer outside it, which is radial tension. At \(r_0 = 49{,}33\) mm, where the hoop stress changes sign, \(r\,\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \int_{40}^{r_0}\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r = 187{,}45\) N per mm of thickness. This is the largest value, and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) is largest a little earlier because of the division by \(r\), \(3{,}84\) MPa at \(r = 48{,}3\) mm (SymPy), which is \(8{,}9\,\%\) of the largest hoop stress. For a couple of opposite sign \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) is compressive everywhere. In the elementary theory the fibres are in uniaxial stress (assumption 6 of chapter 5), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = 0\).

From history

Navier and Bresse calculated displacements and stresses of curved bars by formulas derived for straight prismatic bars. TIMO says that this way is adequate when the dimensions of the cross section are small in comparison with the radius of curvature of the axis, and that in hooks, rings, chains and links this condition is not fulfilled, so the formulas for straight bars are not reliable enough (TIMO, PDF p. 161). Winkler published his paper on curved bars soon after finishing his studies, in the year 1858 according to a footnote in TIMO (TIMO, PDF p. 160), and his main contribution to strength of materials is the theory of bending of curved bars (TIMO, PDF p. 161). Winkler kept the assumption that cross sections stay plane in bending, but took into account that, because of the initial curvature, the longitudinal fibres between two sections have different lengths, so the stresses are no longer proportional to the distance from the neutral axis and this axis does not pass through the centroid of the section (TIMO, PDF p. 161). He applied his theory to stresses in hooks, rings of various sections and chain links and showed that the elementary bending formula for straight beams loses its value when the dimensions of the section are not small in comparison with the radius \(r\), and that the new theory is then needed (TIMO, PDF p. 162). Winkler therefore kept plane sections and assumed that the longitudinal fibres do not press upon each other (TIMO, PDF p. 161), so in his theory there are no radial stresses. Golovin, however, was interested in the deformations and stresses of circular arches of constant thickness, treated the problem as a two-dimensional problem of the theory of elasticity and solved it for pure bending and for bending by a force at the end (TIMO, PDF p. 290, figure 209). In pure bending he found that the cross sections stay plane, as the elementary theory assumes, but that his stress distribution differs from the elementary one, because the elementary theory assumes that the longitudinal fibres are in simple tension or compression only, while Golovin shows that there are also radial stresses (TIMO, PDF p. 290). The work appeared in 1880 and 1881 (TIMO, PDF p. 290, footnote). For a force at the end there are, besides normal stresses, also shear stresses on every section and their distribution is not parabolic, as the elementary theory assumes (TIMO, PDF p. 290). Golovin also computed the deflection of arches and with it solved a statically indeterminate arch with built-in ends, and for usual proportions of arches the elementary theory is accurate enough for practice (TIMO, PDF p. 290), which we will see in this section in numbers for the ratio \(b/a\). TIMO calls Golovin's work the first attempt to use the theory of elasticity in the stress analysis of arches (TIMO, PDF p. 290).

We asked whether the formula \(\sigma = -My/I\) holds for the curved beam made of the ring with \(a = 40\) mm and \(b = 60\) mm. In pure bending it does not hold exactly: at the same moment the stress at the inner edge is \(15{,}5\,\%\) larger, at the outer one \(11{,}7\,\%\) smaller, the neutral fibre moves by \(0{,}67\) mm towards the centre and a radial stress of up to \(3{,}84\) MPa appears. The sections, however, stay plane and the rotation is almost the one that the formula gives. We now test the same on a beam loaded by a force.

11.14.3 A cantilever with a force at its end

Pure bending has the same moment on every section and no force. A curved beam with a force at its end has on the section also an axial and a shear force, and the moment is proportional to the distance from the force. Take a quarter of the annulus \(a \le r \le b\), \(0 \le \theta \le \pi/2\). At the end \(\theta = 0\) acts a force in the direction of the radius that passes through the centre \(O\), at the other end the beam is clamped (figure 11.42). Let the force per unit thickness be \(P\) and let it point in the direction \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) (\(P > 0\) pulls the end away from \(O\)). The force \(P\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}(0) = P\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) at the end must be balanced on every section. The part of the beam between the end and the section at \(\theta\) is in equilibrium, so the resultant of the stress vector on the section is \(-P\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). In the basis \((\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}, \vek e_\theta)\) this vector has the components \(-P\cos\theta\) and \(P\sin\theta\), because \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} = \cos\theta\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\vek e_\theta = -\sin\theta\). We therefore expect stresses that depend on the angle as \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\). By lemma 11.47, item 2, such terms are the functions \(r^3\sin\theta\), \(r^{-1}\sin\theta\), \(r\sin\theta\) and \(r\ln r\,\sin\theta\).

Theorem 11.56 Curved cantilever with an end force (ukrivljena konzola s silo na koncu)

Let the curved beam be as in definition 11.53 with \(\theta_1 = 0\) and \(\theta_2 = \pi/2\), in plane stress, without body force. Let \(P\) be a real number, \(L = \ln(b/a)\) and \(K = (b^2 - a^2) - (a^2 + b^2)\,L\). Then:

  1. \(K < 0\) and the function \(\varphi = (A\,r^3 + B/r + D\,r\ln r)\sin\theta\) with
    \[A = \frac{P}{2K} , \qquad B = -\frac{P\,a^2 b^2}{2K} , \qquad D = -\frac{P\,(a^2 + b^2)}{K} \tag{11.76}\]
    is biharmonic and is the only function of this form for which the arcs \(r = a\) and \(r = b\) are free and the resultant of the stress vector on the end \(\theta = 0\) is \(P\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\),
  2. the stresses are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = g(r)\sin\theta\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = h(r)\sin\theta\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -g(r)\cos\theta\) with \(g(r) = 2A\,r - 2B/r^3 + D/r\) and \(h(r) = 6A\,r + 2B/r^3 + D/r\),
  3. the end \(\theta = 0\) carries only the radial stress vector \(g(r)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\), and the internal forces of the section at every \(\theta\) are (definition 11.53)
    \[N(\theta) = P\,\sin\theta , \qquad V(\theta) = P\,\cos\theta , \qquad M(\theta) = -c\,P\,\sin\theta , \tag{11.77}\]
  4. the field is the only stress field of the beam with free arcs that has on the end \(\theta = 0\) the stress vector \(g(r)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) and on the end \(\theta = \pi/2\) the stress vector \(\ten\sigma\,\vek e_\theta\) from item 2, and the displacement is unique up to a rigid motion.
Proof

We have to show that the constants (11.76) solve the three conditions and that we get exactly these stresses and section quantities.

  1. Each of the functions \(r^3\sin\theta\), \(r^{-1}\sin\theta\) and \(r\ln r\,\sin\theta\) is biharmonic (lemma 11.47, item 2). The function \(r\sin\theta = y\) has all second derivatives zero and gives no stresses, so it is omitted.
  2. Let \(f(r) = A\,r^3 + B/r + D\,r\ln r\) and \(\varphi = f(r)\sin\theta\). By lemma 11.46 \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = (f'/r - f/r^2)\sin\theta\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = f''\sin\theta\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -(f/r)'\cos\theta\). From \(f' = 3Ar^2 - B/r^2 + D\ln r + D\) we get
    \[\begin{gathered} f'/r - f/r^2 = (3Ar - B/r^3 + D\ln r/r + D/r) - (Ar + B/r^3 + D\ln r/r) \\ = 2Ar - 2B/r^3 + D/r = g \end{gathered}\]
    . From \(f'' = 6Ar + 2B/r^3 + D/r\) we get \(h\) and from \(f/r = Ar^2 + B/r^2 + D\ln r\) we get \((f/r)' = 2Ar - 2B/r^3 + D/r = g\). This is item 2.
  3. The arcs \(r = a\) and \(r = b\) are free exactly when the stress vector \(\mp(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\,\vek e_\theta) = \mp g\,(\sin\theta\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} - \cos\theta\,\vek e_\theta)\) is zero there, that is \(g(a) = g(b) = 0\) (both components are proportional to \(g\)). The end \(\theta = 0\) has the outward normal \(-\vek e_\theta\) and the stress vector \(-\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\vek e_\theta - \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} = g(r)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\), because \(\sin 0 = 0\) and \(\cos 0 = 1\). The resultant \(P\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) means \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b g\,\mathrm{d}r = P\).
  4. The conditions \(g(a) = 0\), \(g(b) = 0\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b g\,\mathrm{d}r = P\) are, after multiplying the first two by \(a\) and \(b\), the equations \(2Aa^2 - 2B/a^2 + D = 0\), \(2Ab^2 - 2B/b^2 + D = 0\) and \(A\,(b^2 - a^2) + B\,(1/b^2 - 1/a^2) + DL = P\). The difference of the first two is \(2A\,(a^2 - b^2) = 2B\,(1/a^2 - 1/b^2)\), so \(B = -A\,a^2 b^2\), and from the first \(D = -2Aa^2 + 2B/a^2 = -2A\,(a^2 + b^2)\). The third gives \(B\,(1/b^2 - 1/a^2) = A\,(b^2 - a^2)\) and \(P = 2A\,(b^2 - a^2) - 2A\,(a^2 + b^2)\,L = 2A\,K\).
  5. \(K < 0\): at \(s = b/a > 1\) the inequality \(K < 0\) is \(\ln s > (s^2 - 1)/(s^2 + 1)\). The function \(m(s) = \ln s - (s^2 - 1)/(s^2 + 1)\) has \(m(1) = 0\) and \(m'(s) = 1/s - 4s/(s^2 + 1)^2 = (s^2 - 1)^2/(s\,(s^2 + 1)^2) > 0\) for \(s > 1\), so by the mean value theorem (theorem 1.84) \(m(s) > 0\). Since \(K \ne 0\), the system of step 4 has exactly one solution, which is (11.76), and all steps were equivalent transformations. This proves item 1.
  6. Item 3. The field satisfies equilibrium without body force (theorem 11.36), so the piece of the beam from the end \(\theta = 0\) to the section at \(\theta_0\) is in equilibrium and by lemma 11.2 the stress vector on its surface has resultant zero and moment about \(O\) zero. The arcs are free, the end \(\theta = 0\) has the stress vector \(g\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) with resultant \(P\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and moment about \(O\) zero, because the position vector of the point is parallel to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\). The section at \(\theta_0\) therefore has resultant \(-P\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and moment about \(O\) zero. The components of the resultant are \(N = -P\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\vek e_\theta = P\sin\theta_0\) and \(V = -P\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot(-\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}) = P\cos\theta_0\). The moment about \(O\) is the \(z\) component of \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b r\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\times(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\vek e_\theta + \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}})\,\mathrm{d}r = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b r\,\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r\), so \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b r\,\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r = 0\). By definition 11.53 \(M = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b (r - c)\,\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r = 0 - c\,N = -cP\sin\theta_0\).
  7. Item 4 like item 4 of theorem 11.54: the field is a solution of the traction problem that corresponds to the equilibrium of the whole body (step 6), and by theorem 11.4 it is the only one up to a rigid motion.

Source: SADD §8.4.12, (8.4.62)-(8.4.64) (PDF pp. 212 to 215, crops (8.4.62) and (8.4.64) read). SADD writes the conditions at the ends with the forces \(P\) at \(\theta = 0\) and \(-P\) at \(\theta = \pi/2\) and \(\int\tau_{\mathrm{r}\theta}(r, 0)\,\mathrm{d}r = P\), and we reversed the sign of \(P\) so that \(P\) points in the direction \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) (our convention, all stress fields agree up to the sign of \(P\), checked in rbe.py part J2). BARBER §10.1.2 (PDF pp. 152 to 153). Step 6 (section quantities from the equilibrium of the whole piece) and step 5 (\(K < 0\)) are ours.

Here too the conditions \(g(a) = g(b) = 0\) mean two conditions for three constants and the force gives the third, and the moment of the section is not a condition but a consequence of equilibrium. Let us test it on the ring.

Example 11.57 A quarter of the ring with an end force (četrtina obroča s silo na koncu)

A quarter of the ring with \(a = 40\) mm, \(b = 60\) mm, \(t = 2\) mm, steel, at the end \(\theta = 0\) a force \(100\) N in the direction \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\), so \(P = 100\ \text{N}/2\ \text{mm} = 50\) N/mm, and the clamp at \(\theta = \pi/2\) (figure 11.42).

  1. At \(L = 0{,}405465\) we have \(K = 2000 - 5200\,L = -108{,}42\ \text{mm}^2\) and the constants (11.76) are \(A = -0{,}2306\ \text{N/mm}^3\), \(B = 1{,}3282\cdot 10^6\ \text{N mm}\) and \(D = 2398{,}1\ \text{N/mm}\) (SymPy). Check: \(g(40) = g(60) = 0\) and \(\int_{40}^{60} g\,\mathrm{d}r = 50\) N/mm.
  2. The internal forces on the clamped section by equation (11.77) at \(\theta = \pi/2\): \(N = 50\) N/mm, \(V = 0\), \(M = -50\ \text{mm}\cdot 50\ \text{N/mm} = -2500\) N, so at thickness \(2\) mm the force \(100\) N and the moment \(-5\) N m. SymPy, integrating \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}(r, \pi/2)\), confirms \(N = 100{,}000\) N and \(M = -5{,}0000\) N m. The moment equals the moment of the force \(100\) N about the centroid of the section, since the line of action of the force is at the distance \(c = 50\) mm from the centroid of the section.
  3. The hoop stress on the clamped section is \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}(r, \pi/2) = h(r)\): \(46{,}12\) MPa at \(r = 40\) mm, \(0{,}04\) MPa at \(50\) mm and \(-30{,}75\) MPa at \(60\) mm. The elementary formula (11.73) with \(N/h = 2{,}5\) MPa and \(12\,M\,(r - c)/h^3 = -3{,}75\,(r - 50)\) MPa gives \(40{,}0\) MPa at the inner edge and \(-35{,}0\) MPa at the outer one. The exact value is \(15{,}3\,\%\) larger at the inner edge and \(12{,}2\,\%\) smaller in absolute value at the outer one.
  4. The shear stress at the end \(\theta = 0\) is \(-g(r)\). At the middle (\(r = 50\) mm) it is \(-3{,}65\) MPa, at both edges zero. The elementary parabola (\(3F/(2A)\) for a straight beam, theorem 5.39) gives \(1{,}5\cdot 100\ \text{N}/(2\cdot 20\ \text{mm}^2) = 3{,}75\) MPa, the difference is \(2{,}6\,\%\). The shear stress therefore almost agrees with the elementary one at this load, the hoop stress does not.
  5. The radial stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = g\,\sin\theta\) is largest at the clamp, there \(3{,}80\) MPa (SymPy, maximum over \(r\)), and falls towards zero at the force.

Figure 11.42 shows the beam and the comparison of the hoop stress at the clamp with the elementary formula.

11.14.4 How far the elementary formula holds

So when may we use the formula of the straight beam? The answer depends on the ratio \(b/a\) or, equivalently, on the ratio of the radius of the axis to the height, \(c/h\). For pure bending at every \(b/a\) we compute the stress at the inner and the outer edge from theorem 11.54 and divide it by the elementary value \(6\,|M|/h^2\). The quotients \(f_{\mathrm{a}} = \sigma_{\theta\theta}(a)/(6|M|/h^2)\) and \(f_{\mathrm{b}} = \sigma_{\theta\theta}(b)/(6|M|/h^2)\) (in absolute value, the inner one in tension and the outer one in compression at \(M < 0\)) are equal to \(1\) in the elementary formula. For the ring of the example (\(b/a = 1{,}5\)) they are \(1{,}155\) and \(0{,}883\). Figure 11.43 shows \(f_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(f_{\mathrm{b}}\) for \(b/a\) from \(1{,}1\) to \(4\).

\(b/a\) 1,1 1,2 1,5 2 3 4
\(f_{\mathrm{a}}\) (inner edge) 1,033 1,065 1,155 1,293 1,528 1,727
\(f_{\mathrm{b}}\) (outer edge) 0,969 0,943 0,883 0,820 0,753 0,719

The elementary formula at the inner edge falls below \(5\,\%\) deviation if \(b/a \le 1{,}153\), that is \(c/h \ge 7{,}0\), below \(10\,\%\) at \(b/a \le 1{,}31\) (SymPy, bisection). At the outer edge the limits are \(1{,}17\) and \(1{,}40\). BARBER says that the elementary theory deviates significantly from the exact solution when \(a/b < 0{,}5\), that is \(b/a > 2\), and that the theory of curved beams, which keeps plane sections but takes into account the different lengths of the fibres, is much better (BARBER, PDF p. 151). At \(b/a = 2\) the elementary formula at the inner edge is, by our table, \(29\,\%\) too small. At \(b/a = 4\) SADD compares the exact solution with the theory of curved beams from strength of materials in its appendix D.4, which keeps plane sections and has a nonlinear distribution of stress, and says that the differences are very small (SADD, PDF pp. 212 and 581 to 583). This theory is not the formula of the straight beam with which we compare: the exact solution gives at \(b/a = 4\) the quotients \(1{,}727\) and \(0{,}719\) relative to the formula of the straight beam.

Hooks and chain links have a large ratio \(b/a\): a hook with inner radius equal to the height of the section (\(a = h\), \(b/a = 2\)) has at the inner edge a stress \(29\,\%\) larger than the elementary one, a chain link with \(a = h/2\) (\(b/a = 3\)) \(53\,\%\) larger. This is why TIMO names precisely hooks, rings, chains and links as examples where the formulas of the straight beam do not suffice (TIMO, PDF p. 161). For the cantilever of example 11.57 the deviation of the hoop stress at the clamp (by \(15{,}3\,\%\) and \(12{,}2\,\%\)) is similar to pure bending, and the shear stress agrees with the elementary one to within \(2{,}6\,\%\).

This section solved the curved beam with the Airy function in polar coordinates. Pure bending gives with \(\varphi(r)\) stresses independent of the angle, determined by the free arcs and the moment, and the term \(B\,r^2\ln r\), which uniqueness of the displacement forbids in a whole ring, is allowed in a piece of an annulus (theorem 11.54). The cantilever with an end force gives stresses that vary as \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) (theorem 11.56). For the ring with \(a = 40\) mm and \(b = 60\) mm the elementary formula underestimates the stress at the inner edge by \(15{,}5\,\%\) in bending and by \(15{,}3\,\%\) under the force and overestimates the outer edge by \(11{,}7\,\%\) and \(12{,}2\,\%\), a radial stress of up to \(3{,}84\) MPa appears, and the formula gets the rotation of the sections right to within \(0{,}54\,\%\). The formula holds to within \(5\,\%\) at \(b/a \le 1{,}15\). The answer to the question from the beginning is therefore: not exactly, but plane sections are a good model of the deformation, and at small radii of curvature we must compute the stress from the exact solution or from the theory of curved beams.

11.15 A body on several separate supports

In chapter 4 we found that the equation of virtual forces, if it holds for every statically admissible virtual stress field, gives a displacement field with the given strains (theorem 4.124). We also proved that this field agrees with the prescribed displacement on the support when the support is one single piece (theorem 4.130) and when the body is a bar welded at both ends (corollary 4.131). We did not treat a body on several separate supports, for example a straight strip glued to the ground at three places. We wrote that we need statically admissible fields that carry a force and a moment from one support to another, and that in general we get them only by solving boundary value problems. So we moved this question to this section. Does the equation of virtual forces ensure the support condition here too?

The answer has two parts, which we separate from the start. For the plane case, where we write the fields with an Airy function, we prove the answer for the rectangular strip, and for another plane region given a function that still has to be found. For a body in space we prove a theorem that holds if such fields exist, but we do not prove that they exist. At the end we say which is which.

The route is this. First we say what can happen with several pieces of support, and from that we write down what field of stress we need, namely one that carries a force and a moment from one support to another. Then we prove the theorem that concludes the support condition from the existence of such fields. Then we look at the plane case, where the mismatch of the supports is a plane rigid displacement and where we write such fields with one function, and then the strip on three supports with numbers. At the end we say what remains for a body in space.

11.15.1 What can go wrong

Take a steel strip, 300 mm long, 20 mm high and 10 mm thick. On its bottom face it is glued to the ground at three places, under the left end, under the middle and under the right end, each time over a length of 20 mm (figure 11.44). Let the origin \(O\) be at the centre of the left end of the strip, the \(x\) axis along the strip, the \(y\) axis upwards and the \(z\) axis towards the viewer. The supports are three pieces (kosi) \(S_1\), \(S_2\), \(S_3\) of the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) where the displacement is prescribed. Let the prescribed displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) be the same on all three pieces: the ground settles as a whole by 0,1 mm. Let the strains of the strip be zero, so the displacement field of the strip is a small rigid displacement \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) (theorem 1.134). Is this possible? Yes: the strip settles as a whole, by 0,1 mm at each support. But if only the middle support settles, by 0,1 mm, while the end supports stay, this is not possible. A rigid displacement that is zero at two points is a rotation about the line through them (subsection 4.7.11), and this rotation moves every point off the line. A rigid displacement that is zero on both end supports is therefore zero everywhere, while at the middle support it would have to be 0,1 mm downwards. The equation of virtual forces must detect such a difference.

How does this relate to theorem 4.130? There we proved for every rectangle of the support that the mismatch is a rigid displacement (lemma 4.129), and for neighbouring rectangles that it is the same, because otherwise it would differ by a rotation about the common side, which the field from a bump around this side detects. The pieces \(S_1\), \(S_2\) and \(S_3\) have no common side, so this field does not help. The mismatch has its own rigid displacement \(\vek R_{\mathrm{m}} = \vek a_{\mathrm{m}} + \mat W_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek r\) on each piece, and the difference of two pieces is a rigid displacement. Which virtual fields detect it? The work of a statically admissible field on a rigid displacement that is the same on all pieces is zero: the surface integral \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek R\,\mathrm{d}A\) is zero for a rigid displacement \(\vek R\) (lemma 4.81, as in step 8 of the proof of theorem 4.130), and on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) we have \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\). The work is therefore nonzero only for a field whose forces on the pieces of the support are not in equilibrium each on its own. Such fields carry a force and a moment through the body from one piece to another, like the six fields of the bar between two walls (figure 4.107). EP (p. 198) derives the support condition from the statement that the virtual stresses in the body and on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) are independently arbitrary. For statically admissible fields this is not true, because equilibrium ties the forces on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) together. So we must either assume or prove the existence of fields that carry force.

11.15.2 Transmitting fields and the theorem

Let us write what it means to "carry a force". Let \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) be the union of the pieces \(S_1, \dots, S_{\mathrm{k}}\), where every piece is a union of rectangles of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and the pieces have no common rectangles. For a statically admissible virtual stress field \(\delta\ten\sigma\) (definition 4.96) the force and the moment of the virtual support forces on the piece \(S_{\mathrm{j}}\) about the origin \(O\) are

\[\vek F_{\mathrm{j}} = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{j}} \delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A , \qquad \vek M_{\mathrm{j}} = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{j}} \vek r\times(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{11.78}\]

where \(\vek r\) is the position vector from \(O\) to the point of the face. The integrals are sums of surface integrals over the rectangles of the piece.

Definition 11.58 Transmitting field (prenosno polje)

Let the body \(V\) with the parts \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) be as in theorem 4.130, and let \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) be the union of the pieces \(S_1, \dots, S_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(k \ge 2\), as above. Let \(2 \le m \le k\) and let \(\vek F\) and \(\vek M\) be vectors with three components each. A statically admissible virtual stress field \(\delta\ten\sigma\) is a transmitting field from the piece \(S_{\mathrm{m}}\) to the piece \(S_1\) with force \(\vek F\) and moment \(\vek M\) if \(\vek F_{\mathrm{m}} = \vek F\), \(\vek M_{\mathrm{m}} = \vek M\), \(\vek F_1 = -\vek F\), \(\vek M_1 = -\vek M\), and \(\vek F_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek 0\) and \(\vek M_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek 0\) for every other piece \(S_{\mathrm{j}}\), where \(\vek F_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\vek M_{\mathrm{j}}\) are as in (11.78).

Source: The definition is not from the sources.

A transmitting field is thus a matrix of functions that is in equilibrium in the body, free on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), and whose forces on the support are "force \(\vek F\) and moment \(\vek M\) on the piece \(S_{\mathrm{m}}\), the opposite force and moment on the piece \(S_1\), zero elsewhere". With the pieces \(S_1\), \(S_2\), \(S_3\) and \(m = 2\) the field has an upward resultant on the middle support, an equally large downward one on the left, and zero on the right. We state the theorem. For \(k = 1\) there is nothing to carry, and the theorem is theorem 4.130.

Theorem 11.59 Converse of the principle of virtual forces at supports in several pieces (obrat načela virtualnih sil na podporah v več kosih)

Let the body \(V\), the parts of the surface \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) and the functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) be as in theorem 4.124, and let the equation of virtual forces

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\bar{\vek u}\,\mathrm{d}A \tag{11.79}\]

hold for every statically admissible virtual stress field. Assume further:

  1. the set of interior points of the body is connected and simply connected,
  2. the prescribed displacement on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) equals a field \(\bar{\vek u}\) whose components have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on an open set containing the body,
  3. \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is the union of the pieces \(S_1, \dots, S_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(k \ge 2\), without common rectangles, and every piece on its own satisfies condition 3 of theorem 4.130: any two of its rectangles are joined by a chain of its rectangles in which neighbouring rectangles have a common side and the cells of the body containing this side are not exactly two cells without a common face,
  4. for every \(m = 2, \dots, k\) and every pair of vectors \(\vek F\), \(\vek M\) there is a transmitting field from the piece \(S_{\mathrm{m}}\) to the piece \(S_1\) with force \(\vek F\) and moment \(\vek M\) (definition 11.58).

Then there is a displacement field \(\tilde{\vek u}\), defined at the interior points of the body, with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order, whose small strain tensor components equal \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at every interior point and whose extension to the cell of every rectangle of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) (lemma 4.127) equals \(\bar{\vek u}\) on this rectangle.

Proof

We have to show that the mismatch is the same rigid displacement on all pieces. On each piece there is one rigid displacement by theorem 4.130, and the transmitting fields detect the differences between the pieces.

1. The field and the mismatch on a piece.

  1. By theorem 4.124, point 2, which we may apply because of assumption 1, there is a displacement field \(\vek u\) at the interior points of the body with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order and strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By lemma 4.127 it has an extension \(\vek U_{\mathrm{C}}\) to every cell \(C\) of the body. For a rectangle \(F\) of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) with cell \(C\), the mismatch \(\vek w_{\mathrm{F}} = \vek U_{\mathrm{C}} - \bar{\vek u}\) is, by lemma 4.129, which we may apply because of assumption 2, a rigid displacement \(\vek R_{\mathrm{F}} = \vek a_{\mathrm{F}} + \mat W_{\mathrm{F}}\,\vek r\).
  2. Let \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) be neighbouring rectangles of the chain of assumption 3 for the piece \(S_{\mathrm{m}}\), with common side \(E\). Steps 3 to 11 of the proof of theorem 4.130 use only the rectangles \(F_1\) and \(F_2\), the cells of the mesh at the side \(E\), for which the condition of assumption 3 holds, the equality (4.80) and the field from bumps around \(E\), which by step 7 of that proof is zero on the whole surface except on \(F_1\) and \(F_2\). This field is therefore statically admissible regardless of the other pieces, and the steps need nothing about the other rectangles of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). Steps 3 to 11 therefore hold here too and give \(\vek R_{\mathrm{F}_1} = \vek R_{\mathrm{F}_2}\).
  3. Any two rectangles of the piece \(S_{\mathrm{m}}\) are joined by the chain of assumption 3, in which neighbours have the same rigid displacement by step 2. As in step 12 of the proof of theorem 4.130, all rectangles of the piece \(S_{\mathrm{m}}\) therefore have the same rigid displacement \(\vek R_{\mathrm{m}} = \vek a_{\mathrm{m}} + \mat W_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek r\).

2. The work on the mismatch.

  1. By lemma 4.128, which we may apply because of equation (11.79), we have \(\sum_{\mathrm{F}} \int_{\mathrm{F}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek w_{\mathrm{F}}\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\) for every statically admissible virtual stress field. By step 3, \(\vek w_{\mathrm{F}} = \vek R_{\mathrm{m}}\) on every rectangle of the piece \(S_{\mathrm{m}}\), so
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{m}=1}^{k} \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{m}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek R_{\mathrm{m}}\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 . \tag{11.80}\]
  2. Let \(\boldsymbol\omega_{\mathrm{m}} = (W_{\mathrm{zy}}, W_{\mathrm{xz}}, W_{\mathrm{yx}})\) be the triple of entries of the matrix \(\mat W_{\mathrm{m}}\). Since \(\mat W_{\mathrm{m}}\) is antisymmetric, \((\mat W_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek r)\cdot\vek t = \boldsymbol\omega_{\mathrm{m}}\cdot(\vek r\times\vek t)\) for every vector \(\vek t\), as we saw for the bar between two walls (equation (4.81)): we multiply the components \((\mat W\,\vek r)_{\mathrm{x}} = -W_{\mathrm{yx}}\,y + W_{\mathrm{xz}}\,z\), \((\mat W\,\vek r)_{\mathrm{y}} = W_{\mathrm{yx}}\,x - W_{\mathrm{zy}}\,z\) and \((\mat W\,\vek r)_{\mathrm{z}} = -W_{\mathrm{xz}}\,x + W_{\mathrm{zy}}\,y\) by the components of the vector \(\vek t\) and compare with the components of the vector product \(\vek r\times\vek t\) (definition 2.30). Therefore, by (11.78),
    \[\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{m}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek R_{\mathrm{m}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \vek a_{\mathrm{m}}\cdot\vek F_{\mathrm{m}} + \boldsymbol\omega_{\mathrm{m}}\cdot\vek M_{\mathrm{m}} . \tag{11.81}\]
  3. Let \(2 \le m \le k\), let \(\vek F\) and \(\vek M\) be arbitrary vectors and \(\delta\ten\sigma\) a transmitting field from \(S_{\mathrm{m}}\) to \(S_1\) with force \(\vek F\) and moment \(\vek M\), which exists by assumption 4. The sum (11.80) has, by (11.81), only the terms of the pieces \(S_{\mathrm{m}}\) and \(S_1\), the others are zero, so
    \[\vek F\cdot(\vek a_{\mathrm{m}} - \vek a_1) + \vek M\cdot(\boldsymbol\omega_{\mathrm{m}} - \boldsymbol\omega_1) = 0 . \tag{11.82}\]

3. One rigid displacement.

  1. Equation (11.82) holds for every pair \(\vek F\), \(\vek M\). With \(\vek F = \vek a_{\mathrm{m}} - \vek a_1\) and \(\vek M = \vek 0\) we get \(|\vek a_{\mathrm{m}} - \vek a_1|^2 = 0\), and with \(\vek F = \vek 0\) and \(\vek M = \boldsymbol\omega_{\mathrm{m}} - \boldsymbol\omega_1\) we get \(|\boldsymbol\omega_{\mathrm{m}} - \boldsymbol\omega_1|^2 = 0\). Therefore \(\vek a_{\mathrm{m}} = \vek a_1\) and \(\boldsymbol\omega_{\mathrm{m}} = \boldsymbol\omega_1\). The entries \(W_{\mathrm{zy}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{yx}}\) determine an antisymmetric matrix, so \(\mat W_{\mathrm{m}} = \mat W_1\) and \(\vek R_{\mathrm{m}} = \vek R_1 =: \vek R\) for every \(m\).
  2. Let \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u - \vek R\) at the interior points of the body. The field \(\vek R\) has constant first partial derivatives and a zero small strain tensor (theorem 1.134, point 2), so \(\tilde{\vek u}\) has continuous partial derivatives of first and second order and strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). For a cell \(C\), \(\vek U_{\mathrm{C}} - \vek R\) is continuous on \(C\) and equals \(\tilde{\vek u}\) at the interior points, so it is the extension of the field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) to \(C\).
  3. On a rectangle \(F\) of the piece \(S_{\mathrm{m}}\) with cell \(C\), by steps 3 and 7, \(\vek U_{\mathrm{C}} - \vek R = \bar{\vek u} + \vek w_{\mathrm{F}} - \vek R_{\mathrm{m}} = \bar{\vek u}\).

Source: Lemma 4.129, theorem 4.130 and lemma 4.128 of chapter 4. EP (4.4.10) (p. 198) writes the support condition without an analysis of the supports. The theorem and the proof are not from the sources.

The proof reduced the mismatch on each piece to one rigid displacement with the fields around common sides, as for one piece, and the differences between pieces to six numbers, which the transmitting fields detect: three components of the displacement and three of the rotation. The opposite direction is the principle of virtual forces: if there is a displacement field with the given strains that is continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body with its surface and equals \(\bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), the equation holds for every statically admissible field (theorem 4.97). When transmitting fields exist, the equation of virtual forces thus ensures a field that agrees with the supports, and conversely such a field, if it is continuously differentiable up to the surface, ensures the equation.

For the bar between two walls we wrote the transmitting fields with formulas (figure 4.107). For a body of arbitrary shape their existence is not self-evident. Where can we write them?

11.15.3 The plane case

Take a prism \(V = A \times [-c, c]\), where \(A\) is a region in the \(xy\) plane made of finitely many cells \(R_{\mathrm{i}}\) of the mesh of some rectangle, and let the body have the cells \(R_{\mathrm{i}} \times [-c, c]\). We put the pieces of the support on the lateral boundary, from face to face over the whole height: a rectangle of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is \(e \times [-c, c]\) for a side \(e\) of some rectangle \(R_{\mathrm{i}}\) on the boundary of the region \(A\). The strains are plane if \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) are functions of \(x\) and \(y\) only. The prescribed displacement is plane if \(\bar{\vek u} = (\bar u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y), \bar u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y), 0)\). The strip of the introduction is such a case with \(A = [0, 300] \times [-10, 10]\) mm and \(c = 5\) mm, with the mesh that cuts it at \(x = 20\), \(140\), \(160\) and \(280\) mm into five cells, and with the pieces \(S_1\), \(S_2\), \(S_3\) on the bottom face.

In the plane case the mismatch is simpler than the general lemma gives: a plane rigid displacement has only three numbers, \(a_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{y}}\) and one rotation about the \(z\) axis. So we need only three fields instead of six. We prove this before we write the fields.

Lemma 11.60 The mismatch for plane data is a plane rigid displacement (neujemanje pri ravninskih podatkih je ravninski togi premik)

Let \(V = A \times [-c, c]\), \(c > 0\), be a prism over a region \(A\) of the \(xy\) plane made of finitely many cells \(R_{\mathrm{i}}\) of the mesh of some rectangle, with the cells \(R_{\mathrm{i}} \times [-c, c]\), let the interior of the region \(A\) be connected and simply connected, and let \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) be a union of rectangles of the form \(e \times [-c, c]\), where \(e\) is a side of a rectangle \(R_{\mathrm{i}}\) on the boundary of the region \(A\). Let the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) be as in theorem 4.124 and plane, the prescribed displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) plane with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on an open set containing the body, and let equation (11.79) hold for every statically admissible virtual stress field. Then:

  1. there is a displacement field \(\vek u\) at the interior points of the body with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order and strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) which is plane: \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) independent of \(z\),
  2. for such a field \(\vek u\) the mismatch \(\vek w_{\mathrm{F}}\) on every rectangle \(F\) of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is a plane rigid displacement, \(\vek w_{\mathrm{F}} = (a_{\mathrm{x}} - \omega\,y,\ a_{\mathrm{y}} + \omega\,x,\ 0)\) with constant \(a_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\omega\).
Proof

We have to show two things. The field from theorem 4.124 differs from a plane field by a rigid displacement, which we subtract, and the plane mismatch follows from the fact that a plane function does not change over the height.

1. A plane field.

  1. The interior of the body is connected and simply connected because the interior of the region \(A\) is (as in step 1 of the proof of lemma 11.37 for a prism over a simply connected region). By theorem 4.124, point 2, there is a displacement field \(\vek u\) with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order and strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  2. The field \(\vek v = \partial\vek u/\partial z\) is continuously differentiable. By corollary 1.126 on the independence of the order of differentiation, \(\tfrac12\,(\partial v_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \partial v_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}) = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial z\), and this derivative is zero because the components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are either zero or independent of \(z\). By theorem 1.134 therefore \(\vek v = \vek b + \mat\Omega\,\vek r\) with a constant \(\vek b\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat\Omega\).
  3. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = v_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), we have \(b_{\mathrm{z}} + \Omega_{\mathrm{zx}}\,x + \Omega_{\mathrm{zy}}\,y = 0\) at every interior point. The interior contains three points with different pairs \((x, y)\) that do not lie on one line, so \(b_{\mathrm{z}} = \Omega_{\mathrm{zx}} = \Omega_{\mathrm{zy}} = 0\), and by antisymmetry also \(\Omega_{\mathrm{xz}} = \Omega_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\). What remains is \(v_{\mathrm{x}} = b_{\mathrm{x}} + \Omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\,y\) and \(v_{\mathrm{y}} = b_{\mathrm{y}} - \Omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\,x\).
  4. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12\,(v_{\mathrm{x}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x) = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = \tfrac12\,(v_{\mathrm{y}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial y) = 0\), we have \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x = -b_{\mathrm{x}} - \Omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\,y\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial y = -b_{\mathrm{y}} + \Omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\,x\). By theorem 1.125 the second mixed derivative of the function \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) does not depend on the order: \(-\Omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = \Omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\), so \(\Omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) and \(\vek v = (b_{\mathrm{x}}, b_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\).
  5. Let \(\vek r_0 = (b_{\mathrm{x}}\,z,\ b_{\mathrm{y}}\,z,\ -b_{\mathrm{x}}\,x - b_{\mathrm{y}}\,y)\). This is a field of the form \(\mat W\,\vek r\) with an antisymmetric matrix (\(W_{\mathrm{xz}} = b_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{zx}} = -b_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{yz}} = b_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{zy}} = -b_{\mathrm{y}}\), the others zero), so it has zero strains (theorem 1.134, point 2). The field \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u - \vek r_0\) therefore has continuous derivatives up to second order and strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Its derivatives \(\partial\tilde u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z = v_{\mathrm{x}} - b_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\partial\tilde u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial z = v_{\mathrm{y}} - b_{\mathrm{y}}\) are zero by step 4. The component \(\tilde u_{\mathrm{z}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} + b_{\mathrm{x}}\,x + b_{\mathrm{y}}\,y\) has zero derivatives in \(x\) and \(y\) by step 4, and its derivative in \(z\) is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\).
  6. The field \((0, 0, \tilde u_{\mathrm{z}})\) has a zero gradient by step 5, so zero strains. By theorem 1.134, point 1, it is \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\), and by point 2 its gradient is \(\mat W\), so \(\mat W = \mat 0\) and the field is constant, \((0, 0, \zeta_0)\). The field \(\vek u - \vek r_0 - (0, 0, \zeta_0)\) therefore has a zero third component. Its \(x\) and \(y\) components have zero derivative in \(z\) by step 5, so by corollary 1.85 they do not change along any vertical segment in the body and are functions of \(x\) and \(y\) only. The field has strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and continuous derivatives up to second order (the fields \((0, 0, \zeta_0)\) and \(\vek r_0\) have zero strains), so it is the plane field we look for.

2. The mismatch is plane.

  1. Let \(\vek u\) be the plane field of point 1, \(C\) the cell of the rectangle \(F\) and \(M\) the centre of the cell. The points \(P = (x_0, y_0, z)\) and \(P' = (x_0, y_0, z')\) of the cell have the sequences of interior points \(P + \tfrac1n\,\overrightarrow{PM}\) and \(P' + \tfrac1n\,\overrightarrow{P'M}\) with the same \(x\) and \(y\) coordinates. On both sequences the field \(\vek u\) is the same in \(x\) and \(y\) and has a zero third component. The extension \(\vek U_{\mathrm{C}}\) (lemma 4.127) is continuous on \(C\) and equals \(\vek u\) at the interior points, so by lemma 1.68 \(\vek U_{\mathrm{C}}(P) = \vek U_{\mathrm{C}}(P')\) and \(U_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). The field \(\bar{\vek u}\) is plane too, so the mismatch \(\vek w_{\mathrm{F}}\) on \(F\) is plane: \(w_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) independent of \(z\).
  2. By lemma 4.129, \(\vek w_{\mathrm{F}} = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) on \(F\), which we take in the plane \(x = c_0\), \(F = \{c_0\} \times [y_1, y_2] \times [-c, c]\) with \(y_1 < y_2\). The \(x\) component, \(a_{\mathrm{x}} + W_{\mathrm{xy}}\,y + W_{\mathrm{xz}}\,z\), does not depend on \(z\) at two points with the same \(y\) and different \(z\), so \(W_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0\). In the same way \(W_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\) from the \(y\) component, \(a_{\mathrm{y}} + W_{\mathrm{yx}}\,c_0 + W_{\mathrm{yz}}\,z\). The \(z\) component, \(a_{\mathrm{z}} + W_{\mathrm{zx}}\,c_0 + W_{\mathrm{zy}}\,y\), is zero at \(y_1\) and \(y_2\), so \(W_{\mathrm{zy}} = 0\), by antisymmetry also \(W_{\mathrm{zx}} = -W_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0\), and therefore \(a_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). With \(\omega = W_{\mathrm{yx}} = -W_{\mathrm{xy}}\) what remains is \(\vek w_{\mathrm{F}} = (a_{\mathrm{x}} - \omega\,y,\ a_{\mathrm{y}} + \omega\,x,\ 0)\). For a rectangle in the plane \(y = d_0\) the computation is the same with the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) exchanged.

Source: The lemma and the proof are not from the sources.

The proof showed that for plane data it suffices to look for plane mismatches: three numbers per piece. Detecting the difference of the pieces \(S_{\mathrm{m}}\) and \(S_1\) therefore means detecting the difference of \((a_{\mathrm{x}}, a_{\mathrm{y}}, \omega)\), which needs only transmitting fields with the components \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{z}}\). We now build such fields from one function.

The field (4.77) of chapter 4, which is independent of \(z\), is statically admissible if it gives zero force on the free faces: on a free face we need \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\). For an Airy function the forces on the boundary are differences of first derivatives (lemma 11.38). The free arcs of the boundary therefore only require that the two derivatives of the function have a constant value along the arc. The plane forces and the moment of a piece are differences of values between the neighbouring arcs. Let us write this precisely.

Lemma 11.61 Transmitting fields from an Airy function (prenosna polja iz Airyjeve funkcije)

Let \(V = A \times [-c, c]\) be as in lemma 11.60, and let the boundary of the region \(A\) be a closed curve of segments without self-contact, which, walked in the positive direction (region \(A\) on the left), we divide into the arcs \(S_1, A_1, S_2, A_2, \dots, S_{\mathrm{k}}, A_{\mathrm{k}}\) in this order, each of positive length and each made of sides of the cells \(R_{\mathrm{i}}\). Let the pieces of the support be \(S_{\mathrm{j}} \times [-c, c]\) and let the part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) of the surface consist of the faces \(A_{\mathrm{j}} \times [-c, c]\) and the faces \(z = \pm c\). Let \(\varphi(x, y)\) be a function with continuous partial derivatives of first, second and third order in the plane whose two first derivatives are constant on every arc \(A_{\mathrm{j}}\), \(\partial\varphi/\partial x = \beta_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\partial\varphi/\partial y = \gamma_{\mathrm{j}}\), and let \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\) be the value of the function \(\varphi - \beta_{\mathrm{j}}\,x - \gamma_{\mathrm{j}}\,y\) at the starting point of the arc \(A_{\mathrm{j}}\). Write \((\alpha_0, \beta_0, \gamma_0) = (\alpha_{\mathrm{k}}, \beta_{\mathrm{k}}, \gamma_{\mathrm{k}})\). Then:

  1. the field (4.77) with the function \(\varphi\) is a statically admissible virtual stress field,
  2. for \(j = 1, \dots, k\) the forces and moments (11.78) of the pieces of the support are
    \[\begin{aligned} \vek F_{\mathrm{j}} &= 2c\,\big(\gamma_{\mathrm{j}} - \gamma_{\mathrm{j}-1},\ -(\beta_{\mathrm{j}} - \beta_{\mathrm{j}-1}) \\ &\quad ,\ 0\big) , \\ \vek M_{\mathrm{j}} &= 2c\,\big(0,\ 0,\ \alpha_{\mathrm{j}} - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}-1}\big) , \end{aligned} \tag{11.83}\]
  3. if \((\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}, \beta_{\mathrm{j}}, \gamma_{\mathrm{j}}) = (0, 0, 0)\) for \(j < m\) and \((\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}, \beta_{\mathrm{j}}, \gamma_{\mathrm{j}}) = (\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) for \(j \ge m\), where \(2 \le m \le k\), the field is a transmitting field from the piece \(S_{\mathrm{m}}\) to the piece \(S_1\) with force \(2c\,(\gamma, -\beta, 0)\) and moment \(2c\,(0, 0, \alpha)\). For arbitrary \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{z}}\) we may choose \(\alpha = M_{\mathrm{z}}/(2c)\), \(\beta = -F_{\mathrm{y}}/(2c)\), \(\gamma = F_{\mathrm{x}}/(2c)\).
Proof

We have to show that the field is in equilibrium and free on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), and that the lemma on the boundary forces gives the differences. The boundary is made of segments, so we apply lemma 11.38 to each segment separately and add the differences.

  1. We take the function \(\varphi\) as a function of three variables that does not depend on \(z\). Its partial derivatives up to third order are derivatives in \(x\) and \(y\) or zero, and they are continuous in space, because the projections of two points onto the \(xy\) plane are at most as far apart as the points. By lemma 4.121, point 1, the field (4.77) is therefore symmetric, continuously differentiable in the whole space and in equilibrium without body force. The field does not depend on \(z\), and the components \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) are zero.
  2. On the faces \(z = \pm c\) we have \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \pm(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}, \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}) = \vek 0\). On the face \(A_{\mathrm{j}} \times [-c, c]\) the normal is \(\vek n = (y', -x', 0)\) for an arc \((x(s), y(s))\) with the body on the left, and by lemma 11.38, point 1, applied to each segment of the arc, \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) is the derivative along the segment of the vector \((\partial\varphi/\partial y, -\partial\varphi/\partial x)\), which is constant on \(A_{\mathrm{j}}\), \((\gamma_{\mathrm{j}}, -\beta_{\mathrm{j}})\). Therefore \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\) on the whole surface \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) and the field is statically admissible (definition 4.96). This is point 1.
  3. On every segment of the arc \(A_{\mathrm{j}}\) the function \(\varphi - \beta_{\mathrm{j}}\,x - \gamma_{\mathrm{j}}\,y\) has, by the chain rule, the derivative along the segment \(\varphi_{\mathrm{x}} x' + \varphi_{\mathrm{y}} y' - \beta_{\mathrm{j}} x' - \gamma_{\mathrm{j}} y' = 0\), where \(\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{y}}\) are the first derivatives, so it is constant on the segment (corollary 1.85), as in step 5 of the proof of lemma 11.38. The function is continuous, so it is constant on the whole arc, and \(\varphi = \alpha_{\mathrm{j}} + \beta_{\mathrm{j}}\,x + \gamma_{\mathrm{j}}\,y\) on \(A_{\mathrm{j}}\). Let \(S_{\mathrm{j}}\) run from the point \(P_{\mathrm{j}}\), which is the end of the arc \(A_{\mathrm{j}-1}\), to the point \(Q_{\mathrm{j}}\), which is the start of the arc \(A_{\mathrm{j}}\). The points lie on the closed arcs \(A_{\mathrm{j}-1}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{j}}\), and the derivatives of the function \(\varphi\) are continuous, so the values of \(\varphi\), \(\partial\varphi/\partial x\) and \(\partial\varphi/\partial y\) at \(P_{\mathrm{j}}\) are the values of the linear function \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}-1} + \beta_{\mathrm{j}-1}\,x + \gamma_{\mathrm{j}-1}\,y\) and its derivatives, and at \(Q_{\mathrm{j}}\) the values of the linear function \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}} + \beta_{\mathrm{j}}\,x + \gamma_{\mathrm{j}}\,y\).
  4. By lemma 11.38, point 2, the force per unit height on \(S_{\mathrm{j}}\) is, on each segment, the difference of the values of the vector \((\partial\varphi/\partial y, -\partial\varphi/\partial x)\) between the ends, and the sum over the segments gives the difference between \(Q_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(P_{\mathrm{j}}\), because the intermediate values are continuous: \((\gamma_{\mathrm{j}} - \gamma_{\mathrm{j}-1},\ -(\beta_{\mathrm{j}} - \beta_{\mathrm{j}-1}))\). The same holds for the moment, \(\varphi - x\,\partial\varphi/\partial x - y\,\partial\varphi/\partial y\), which for a linear function \(\alpha + \beta x + \gamma y\) equals \(\alpha\). The moment about \(O\) around the \(z\) axis per unit height is therefore \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}} - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}-1}\).
  5. The virtual force \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) does not depend on \(z\) and has no \(z\) component. The integral over the height \(-c \le z \le c\) gives a factor \(2c\). The moment components \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = -\int z\,t_{\mathrm{y}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) and \(M_{\mathrm{y}} = \int z\,t_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) are zero because the integral of an odd function of \(z\) over a symmetric interval is zero. This is point 2.
  6. With the choice of point 3, \(\vek F_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\vek M_{\mathrm{j}}\) by (11.83) for \(j = m\) equal \(2c\,(\gamma, -\beta, 0)\) and \(2c\,(0, 0, \alpha)\), because \((\alpha_{\mathrm{m}}, \beta_{\mathrm{m}}, \gamma_{\mathrm{m}}) - (\alpha_{\mathrm{m}-1}, \beta_{\mathrm{m}-1}, \gamma_{\mathrm{m}-1}) = (\alpha, \beta, \gamma) - (0, 0, 0)\). For \(j = 1\) we have \((\alpha_1, \beta_1, \gamma_1) - (\alpha_{\mathrm{k}}, \beta_{\mathrm{k}}, \gamma_{\mathrm{k}}) = -(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\). For \(1 < j < m\) and for \(j > m\) the difference is zero. This is point 3.

Source: The lemma and the proof are not from the sources. SADD §7.5 (PDF p. 159) only mentions that the traction condition can be written with first-order derivatives of the stress function, without derivation. Lemma 11.38 is ours.

The lemma turned transmitting fields into the search for a function \(\varphi\) with given constant derivatives on the free arcs. The function need not satisfy the equation \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\), because the virtual field has only to be in equilibrium, not also compatible. Do such functions exist? For a general region we need a function that is smooth, zero on one part of the boundary and equal to a linear function on another. Such a function would come from a construction of analysis called mollification (zglajevanje), which the book does not have, so we do not use it. For the strip we write the function directly from the steps of chapter 4.

For \(\alpha < \beta\) let \(q_{\alpha\beta}(t) = (t - \alpha)^4\,(\beta - t)^4\) on the interval \([\alpha, \beta]\) and zero elsewhere (lemma 4.122), and

\[s_{\alpha\beta}(t) = \frac{\int_\alpha^t q_{\alpha\beta}(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau}{\int_\alpha^\beta q_{\alpha\beta}(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau} \ \ (\alpha \le t \le \beta) , \qquad s_{\alpha\beta} = 0 \ \text{for}\ t < \alpha , \qquad s_{\alpha\beta} = 1 \ \text{for}\ t > \beta .\]

The function \(s_{\alpha\beta}\) is a "smooth step" from zero to one. Since \(q_{\alpha\beta}\) is zero outside the interval \([\alpha, \beta]\), we have \(s_{\alpha\beta}(t) = \int_\alpha^t q_{\alpha\beta}(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau \big/ \int_\alpha^\beta q_{\alpha\beta}(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau\) for every \(t\), and by the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.40, point 2, its first derivative is \(q_{\alpha\beta}/\int q_{\alpha\beta}\), which by lemma 4.122, point 1, has continuous derivatives up to third order, equal to zero at \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Therefore \(s_{\alpha\beta}\) has continuous derivatives up to fourth order on the whole line, and these derivatives are zero at \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) and outside the interval.

Corollary 11.62 Converse at supports in several pieces for a plane body (obrat na podporah v več kosih za ravninsko telo)

Let \(V = A \times [-c, c]\), the parts \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), the pieces \(S_1, \dots, S_{\mathrm{k}}\) with \(k \ge 2\) and the arcs \(A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{k}}\) be as in lemma 11.61, the functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and the field \(\bar{\vek u}\) plane as in lemma 11.60, let equation (11.79) hold for every statically admissible virtual stress field and let every piece \(S_{\mathrm{m}}\) satisfy condition 3 of theorem 11.59. Let there be, for every \(m = 2, \dots, k\) and every linear function \(L(x, y) = \alpha + \beta x + \gamma y\), a function \(\varphi\) as in lemma 11.61 which on the arcs \(A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{m}-1}\) has the value \(0\) and derivatives \(0\), and on the arcs \(A_{\mathrm{m}}, \dots, A_{\mathrm{k}}\) the value \(L\) and derivatives \(\partial L/\partial x\), \(\partial L/\partial y\). Then the conclusion of theorem 11.59 holds.

The assumption on the function \(\varphi\) and condition 3 hold for the rectangular strip \(A = [0, X] \times [-b, b]\) with the pieces \(S_{\mathrm{j}}\) on the bottom face \(y = -b\) over the intervals \([x_{\mathrm{j}}^-, x_{\mathrm{j}}^+]\), where \(0 \le x_1^- < x_1^+ < x_2^- < \dots < x_{\mathrm{k}}^+ \le X\), and with the mesh that cuts the strip at all \(x_{\mathrm{j}}^\pm\) between \(0\) and \(X\). For the strip the conclusion therefore holds without the assumption on the function \(\varphi\).

Proof

We have to show that the theorem need not be used in full. We need only steps 1 to 3 of its proof and transmitting fields for three of the six numbers, so we repeat the proof with the fields of lemma 11.61. For the strip we show that the function of the assumption exists.

1. The converse from plane transmitting fields.

  1. By lemma 11.60 there is a plane field \(\vek u\) with strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) whose mismatch on every rectangle is a plane rigid displacement. Steps 1 to 3 of the proof of theorem 11.59 (the same rigid displacement on all rectangles of one piece) hold for this field in place of the field of step 1, because they use only that the field has strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and they give on the piece \(S_{\mathrm{m}}\) a plane rigid displacement \(\vek R_{\mathrm{m}} = (a_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{x}} - \omega_{\mathrm{m}}\,y,\ a_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{y}} + \omega_{\mathrm{m}}\,x,\ 0)\), in the notation of the theorem \(\vek a_{\mathrm{m}} = (a_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{x}}, a_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{y}}, 0)\) and \(\boldsymbol\omega_{\mathrm{m}} = (0, 0, \omega_{\mathrm{m}})\).
  2. Steps 4 to 6 of the proof of theorem 11.59 (equations (11.80), (11.81) and (11.82)) hold for every transmitting field, whatever its origin. For a transmitting field of lemma 11.61 we have \(F_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) and \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = M_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\), so equation (11.82) becomes
    \[F_{\mathrm{x}}\,(a_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{x}} - a_{1,\mathrm{x}}) + F_{\mathrm{y}}\,(a_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{y}} - a_{1,\mathrm{y}}) + M_{\mathrm{z}}\,(\omega_{\mathrm{m}} - \omega_1) = 0 .\]
  3. For \(m \ge 2\) take the functions \(\varphi\) of the assumption with \(L = 1\), \(L = x\) and \(L = y\), that is with \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma) = (1, 0, 0)\), \((0, 1, 0)\) and \((0, 0, 1)\). By point 3 of lemma 11.61 these are transmitting fields from \(S_{\mathrm{m}}\) to \(S_1\) with \((F_{\mathrm{x}}, F_{\mathrm{y}}, M_{\mathrm{z}}) = (0, 0, 2c)\), \((0, -2c, 0)\) and \((2c, 0, 0)\). The equation of step 2 gives in turn \(\omega_{\mathrm{m}} = \omega_1\), \(a_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{y}} = a_{1,\mathrm{y}}\) and \(a_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{x}} = a_{1,\mathrm{x}}\).
  4. Therefore all \(\vek R_{\mathrm{m}}\) are equal, \(\vek R_{\mathrm{m}} = \vek R_1 = \vek R\), and \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u - \vek R\) is the field we look for, as in steps 8 and 9 of the proof of theorem 11.59.

2. The function for the strip.

  1. Let \(g(x)\) and \(k(y)\) be the functions \(g = s_{\mathrm{x}_1^- \mathrm{x}_1^+} - s_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{m}^- \mathrm{x}_\mathrm{m}^+}\) and \(k = 1 - s_{-\mathrm{b}\,\mathrm{b}}\). The function \(g\) is zero for \(x \le x_1^-\) and for \(x \ge x_{\mathrm{m}}^+\), one on the interval \([x_1^+, x_{\mathrm{m}}^-]\), and the function \(k\) is one at \(y = -b\) and zero at \(y = b\). Both have continuous derivatives up to fourth order, which are zero at the points where they change (at \(x_1^\pm\), \(x_{\mathrm{m}}^\pm\), \(\pm b\)) and zero at the points outside the interval of change.
  2. Let \(\varphi = L\,(1 - g(x)\,k(y))\). The functions \(g(x)\), \(k(y)\) and \(L\) have continuous derivatives up to fourth order, so by the product rule so does \(\varphi\), like the product of bumps in point 2 of lemma 4.122, in particular up to third order.
